stem_md: In a group of mathematicians, every mathematician has some friends (the relation of friend is reciprocal). Prove that there exists a mathematician, such that the average of the number of friends of all his friends is no less than the average of the number of friends of all these mathematicians.
solution_md:
Denote all mathematicians by a graph  $G$  with vertices  $v_1,v_2,\ldots ,v_n$ . We can assume that  $deg(v_i)\geq 1$  for each  $i,1\leq i\leq n$ , because if the proposition is true for this case, then it is true for the general case which there is at least one  $i,1\leq i\leq n$  such that  $deg(v_i)\geq 1$ . $($ It is because if we add new points to a graph  $Q$  which each of  $Q$ 's vertices degree is  $\geq 1$ (without adding new edges), then the average of the number of friends of all mathematicians will be decrease, and for each vertice  $v_i$  of  $Q$ , the average of the number of friends of all  $v_i$ 's friends won't be change $)$ .
Now suppose the contrary. Let  $k_i$  is the total number of friends of  $v_i$ . Then  $k_i=deg(v_i)$ . Let  $a_i$  is the total number of friends of friends of  $v_i$ .(This means if  $w_1,w_2,\ldots ,w_{k_i}$  are all friends of  $v_i$ , then  $a_i=\sum_{j=1}^{k_i}deg(w_j)$ ). Call a subgraph  $x$  of  $G$   $good$  if and only if  $x$  has  $3$  vertices  $v_i,v_j,v_k$  in total and  $deg(v_i)=deg(v_j)=1$  and  $deg(v_k)=2$  on  $x$ . Let  $Y$  is the total number of good subgraphs of  $G$ . Then  $Y=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{deg(v_i)\choose 2}$ . Let  $t$  is the total number of friends of all mathematicians. Then  $t=\sum_{i=1}^{n}deg(v_i)$ . Since  $\frac{a_i}{k_i}<\frac{t}{n}$  for each  $i,1\leq i\leq n$ ;  $A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{a_i}<\frac{t}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{k_i}=\frac{t^2}{n}$ . Select a  $v_i$ ,  $1\leq i\leq n$ . Let  $g_i$  is the number of good subgraphs of  $G$  which  $v_i$  is a point of each of them and $deg(v_i)=1$  on each of them. Then  $v_i$  counts exactly  $deg(v_i)+g_i$  times in  $A$  ( $deg(v_i)$  times while counting the friends of friends of  $v_i$ , and  $g_i$  times while counting the friends of friends of  $v_j$ 's, such that  $j\neq i$ , $1\leq j\leq n$ ). Then  $A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{a_i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}deg(v_i)+g_i$ . Since we count each good subgraph  of  $G$  exactly  $2$  times in  $\sum_{i=1}^{n}{g_i}$ ;  $\sum_{i=1}^{n}{g_i}=2Y=2\sum_{i=1}^{n}{deg(v_i)\choose 2}$  is true. Thus  $A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{a_i}=(\sum_{i=1}^{n}deg(v_i))+2\sum_{i=1}^{n}{deg(v_i)\choose 2}=$   $(\sum_{i=1}^{n}deg(v_i))+2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{deg(v_i)(deg(v_i)-1)}{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{(deg(v_i))^2}$ . Thus $A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{(deg(v_i))^2}<\frac{t^2}{n}={(\sum_{i=1}^{n}deg(v_i))^2}\frac{1}{n}$   $(*)$ . But since  $deg(v_i)\geq 1$  for  $1\leq i\leq n$ , by Root Mean Square-Arithmetic Mean Inequality,  $\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(deg(v_i))^2}{n}}\geq \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}deg(v_i)}{n}$  so  $\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{(deg(v_i))^2}}{n}\geq \frac{(\sum_{i=1}^{n}deg(v_i))^2}{n^2}$  is true which contradicts with  $(*)$ .

Let  $M_1,M_2,...M_n$  be those mathematicians, and  $M_i$  has  $k_i$  friends. Denote  $S_{i}$  be the average of the number of friends of all  $M_i$  friends.
We are going to prove  $ \frac{\sum_{j = 1}^{n}S_{j}}{n}$  is not less than the average of the number of friends of all these mathematicians.
Actually  $\sum_{j = 1}^{n}S_{j}$  is equal to  $\sum_{M_i,M_j are friends}{} \frac{k_i}{k_j}$ . By AM-GM,  $ \frac{k_i}{k_j} + \frac{k_j}{k_i} \ge2 $ Therefore  $\sum_{M_i,M_j are friends}{} \frac{k_i}{k_j} \ge \sum_{M_i,M_j are friends}{} 1 = \sum_{j= 1}^{n}k_{j}$ As a result,  $ \frac{\sum_{j = 1}^{n}S_{j}}{n} \ge \frac{\sum_{j= 1}^{n}k_{j}}{n}$ . This means exists a  $j$  such that  $S_{j} \ge \frac{\sum_{j= 1}^{n}k_{j}}{n}$ , the average of  the number of friends of all these mathematicians. The proof is complete.

I cannot resist using the symbol that Donald Knuth made so popular. Given a boolean predicate  $\mathcal{P}$ , denote  $[[\mathcal{P}]] =1$  if  $\mathcal{P}$  is true, while  $[[\mathcal{P}]]=0$  if  $\mathcal{P}$  is false. Now, interpret the problem in graph theoretical terminology, where we have a graph  $G$  whose vertices are the mathematicians, and the edges the friendship relations. Let  $|V(G)| = n$ , and denote  $N(v) = \{w \in V(G) \mid vw \in E(G)\}$ .

Then  $ \sum_{i=1}^n \dfrac {1} {\deg v_i} \sum_{j = 1}^n \deg v_{j} [[v_iv_j \in E(G)]] =$   $ \sum_{i=1}^n  \sum_{j= 1}^n  \dfrac {\deg v_{j}} {\deg v_i} [[v_iv_j \in E(G)]] = $   $\sum_{1\leq i\leq j \leq n} \left ( \dfrac {\deg v_{j}} {\deg v_i} +\dfrac {\deg v_{i}} {\deg v_j} \right ) [[v_iv_j \in E(G)]] \geq $   $ 2\sum_{1\leq i\leq j \leq n} [[v_iv_j \in E(G)]] = $   $ 2|E(G)| = $   $ \sum_{k=1}^n \deg v_k$ . 
This means there exists an index  $i$  such that  $d(N(v_i)) = \dfrac {1} {\deg v_i} \sum_{j = 1}^n \deg v_{j} [[v_iv_j \in E(G)]] \geq  \dfrac {1} {n} \sum_{k=1}^n \deg v_k = d(G)$ .

Suppose we have a connected graph  $G$  of order  $n$ . Let's assume the negation of the problem statement, which says that for every vertex  $v_i\in G$ ,  the average degree of its neighbors is less than the average degree of all vertices in  $G$ . Let  $N(v_i)$  denote the set of neighbors of  $v_i$ . Then for every  $v_i\in G$ , we have   $$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{deg(v_i)}\sum_{x\in N(v_i)}deg(x) < \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v_j\in G}deg(v_j) $$     $$ \displaystyle\sum_{x\in N(v_i)}deg(x) < \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}deg(v_i)\sum_{v_j\in G}deg(v_j)  $$   

If we sum over all  $v_i$ , we get:   $$ \displaystyle\sum_{v_i\in G}\sum_{x\in N(v_i)}deg(x) < \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v_i\in G}deg(v_i)\sum_{v_j\in G}deg(v_j) = \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}{\left(\sum_{v_i\in G}deg(v_i)\right)}^2 $$   

Notice that in the sum on the left-most side, for any particular vertex  $x \in G$ , the term  $deg(x)$  will show up  $deg(x)$  times. Hence, we obtain:   $$ \displaystyle\sum_{v_i\in G}deg(v_i)^2 < \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}{\left(\sum_{v_i\in G}deg(v_i)\right)}^2 $$    $$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v_i\in G}deg(v_i)^2 < \displaystyle{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{v_i\in G}deg(v_i)\right)}^2 $$   
The function  $f(x)=x^2$  is convex, so according to Jensen's Inequality, this gives a contradiction, as required.

stem_md: Six cities  $A, B, C, D, E$ , and  $F$  are located on the vertices of a regular hexagon in that order.  $G$  is the center of the hexagon. The sides of the hexagon are the roads connecting these cities. Further more, there are roads connecting cities  $B, C, E, F$  and  $G$ , respectively. Because of raining, one or more roads maybe destroyed. The probability of the road keeping undestroyed between two consecutive cities is  $p$ . Determine the probability of the road between cities  $A$  and  $D$  is undestroyed.
solution_md:
graph theory! awesome!

let your graph be called  $W$  then we are interested in  $\kappa (x,y,W)=$  the number of x-y paths in W

then what you are looking for is exactly  $P(1\le \kappa (A,D,W))=(1-p^2)P(1 \le \kappa(B,D,W_1))$  where  $W_1 $  is W with the point A and its edges taken out $=(1-p^2)(1-p) \left[P(1\le \kappa( C,D, W_2))+P(1 \le \kappa(G,D,W_2))\right]$  where  $W_2$  is  $W_1$  with the point B and its edges taken out $=(1-p^2)(1-p) \left[ (1-p)+p(1-p)P(1\le \kappa(G,D,W_3) +(1-p)^2 +(1-(1-p)^2)P(1\le \kappa(G,D,W_3))\right]$  
where  $W_3$  is  $W_2$  with the point C and its edges removed $=(1-p^2)(1-p) \left[ (2-p)(1-p)+p(3-2p)P(1\le \kappa(G,D,W_3) \right]$  $= (1-p^2)(1-p) \left[ (2-p)(1-p)+p(3-2p)(1-p)P(1\le \kappa(G,E,W_4) \right]$  where  $W_4$  is now the triangle  $GEF$  $=(1-p^2)(1-p)^2 \left[ (2-p) + p(3-2p) \left( (1-p)+ p(1-p)^2 \right) \right]$  $= (1-p^2)(1-p)^2(-2p^5+7p^4-6p^3-2p^2+2p+2)$  which seems pretty unfactorable

stem_md: We call a set  $S$  on the real line  $R$  "superinvariant", if for any stretching  $A$  of the set  $S$  by the transformation taking  $x$  to  $A(x) = x_0 + a(x - x_0)$ , where  $a > 0$ , there exists a transformation  $B, B(x) = x + b$ , such that the images of  $S$  under  $A$  and  $B$  agree; i.e., for any  $x \in S$ , there is  $y \in S$  such that  $A(x) = B(y)$ , and for any  $t \in S$ , there is a  $u  \in S$  such that  $B(t) = A(u).$  Determine all superinvariant sets.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Remarks</summary>$(1)$  I use the convention where if  $f$  is a function with domain  $D$ , and  $S\subset D$ , then  $f(S)$  denotes the set of all images of elements of  $S$ .  $(2)$  It might be useful to notice that if  $S$  is superinvariant, then so is its complement (with respect to the reals). $(3)$   $A(x)$  and  $B(x)$  are bijections and have inverses.  $(4)$  I use the variable  $c$  instead of  $x_0$ .</details>

This is only a partial solution; can anybody try completing it?

Let  $S$  be a superinvariant set. 
Let  $p(a,b,c)$  be the proposition that  $A(S)=B(S)$ , where  $A(x) = c + a(x-c)$  and  $B(x) = x+b$ .

Problem statement: for every pair  $(a,c)$ , where  $a>0$ , there exists some true  $p(a,b,c)$ .
Trivial case: if  $a=1$ , then choose  $b=0$ , and we have  $p(a,b,c)$ . So assume  $a\neq 1$ .

Implications of  $p(a,b,c)$ : If  $x \in S$ , then so is  $f(x) = B^{-1}A(x)$ , and so is every <details><summary>integer power </summary>By integer power, here I mean  $f$  composed with itself any number of times, or  $f^{-1}$  composed with itself any number of times.</details> of  $f(x)$ . Evaluating  $f(x)$  gives   $$ f(x) = \gamma + a(x-\gamma) \text{ where } \gamma = c + \frac{b}{a-1} \text{ noting } a\neq 1 $$   I write it in this form to make it clear that this is a dilation with center  $\gamma$  and scale factor  $a$ . Hence, we have the following condition on the set  $S$  for all valid  $p(a,b,c)$ :  $x\in S \iff [\gamma + a(x-\gamma)] \in S$ . Perhaps one interesting point is that  $\gamma$  must be an accumulation point of  $S$ . 

Although  $\gamma$  depends on  $(a,b,c)$  we can make it equal to come constant  $\Gamma$  by always choosing  $b = (\Gamma -c)(a-1).$  Let us do just that. Now let us draw the implications of  $p(a, (\Gamma-c)(a-1), c)$  over all  $(a,c)$ , where  $a>0$  and  $a\neq 1$ . It would put the following restrictions on  $S$ : For all  $a$ ,  $x\in S \iff [\Gamma + a(x-\Gamma)] \in S$ .

This leads to a number of possible sets  $S$ , based on answers to the following questions:  $(1)$  Does  $S$  contain an element less than  $\Gamma$ ? Then  $S$  must contain all reals less than  $\Gamma$ .  $(2)$  Does  $S$  contain an element more than  $\Gamma$ ? Then  $S$  must contain all reals more than  $\Gamma$ .  $(3)$  Does  $S$  contain  $\Gamma$ ? Then  $S$  must contain  $\Gamma$  (obviously). Accordingly, there are  $8$  possible sets  $S$  that can result: $S = \o$  $S = \{\Gamma\}$  $S = (-\infty, \Gamma) $  $S = (-\infty, \Gamma]$  $S = (\Gamma, \infty)$  $S = [\Gamma, \infty)$  $S = (-\infty, \Gamma) \cup (\Gamma, \infty)$  $S = (-\infty, \infty) $ Any set of this form, for any  $\Gamma$ , is superinvariant. 

If, on the other hand, the value of  $\gamma$  is not constant over all  $(a,b,c)$ , I'm stuck. Though I suspect that it would give  $S=(-\infty, \infty)$

stem_md: 1990 mathematicians attend a meeting, every mathematician has at least 1327 friends (the relation of friend is reciprocal). Prove that there exist four mathematicians among them such that any two of them are friends.
solution_md:
Analogously: If each of  $1990$  vertices of a graph has degree at least  $1327,$  there exists within the graph a complete subgraph on four vertices  $K_4$ .

Now, if each vertex has degree at least  $1327$ , then the graph has at least  $1327 \cdot 995 = 1320365$  edges. However, Turan's theorem on  $n = 1990, r= 3$  gives an upper bound of  $\left\lfloor\frac{1}{3}(1327^2)\right\rfloor = 1320033$  edges for the graph to be  $K_4-$ free. Since  $1320365 > 1320033, K_4$  exists within the graph, and the proof is complete.

More generally: Replace  $1990$  and  $1327$  with  $n$  and  $\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{3}\right\rfloor + 1$  and the result will still hold.  $(n \ge 4)$

stem_md: Could the three-dimensional space be expressed as the union of disjoint circumferences?
solution_md:
Seems like a silly question, unless I misunderstand...

I assume "circumference" means "boundary of circle." We first partition  $\mathbb{R} ^3$  into a "stack" of planes. Then we partition each plane into concentric circles. 

<details><summary>Slightly more formal solution</summary>Denote  $C(r,t)$  to be the set of points  $\{(x,y,z) | \sqrt{x^2+y^2} = r \text{ and } z=t\}$ . In other words,  $C(r,t)$  is the circle with radius  $r$  that is centered about  $(0,0,t)$  and that is parallel to the  $xy$ -plane.

It is clear that sets of this form partition the three dimensional space. To ensure this, we need only show that every point in  $\mathbb{R} ^3$  belongs to exactly one of the sets  $C(r,t)$ . But this is obvious: any point  $(x,y,z)$  belongs to  $C(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}, z)$ , and only to this set.</details>

EDIT: I think I misunderstood. I would imagine the intention of the question is that circumferences of radius 0 are not allowed, in which case it is not as simple as I say above.

stem_md: Point  $O$  is interior to triangle  $ABC$ . Through  $O$ , draw three lines  $DE \parallel BC, FG \parallel CA$ , and  $HI \parallel AB$ , where  $D, G$  are on  $AB$ ,  $I, F$  are on  $BC$  and  $E, H$  are on  $CA$ . Denote by  $S_1$  the area of hexagon  $DGHEFI$ , and  $S_2$  the area of triangle  $ABC$ . Prove that  $S_1 \geq \frac 23 S_2.$
solution_md:
Claim:  $AGOH$ ,  $CEOF$ , and  $BIOD$  are all parallelograms. This follows from parallel lines.

Now, partition triangle  $ABC$  into the following triangles, and denote their areas as follows:   $$ [AGH] = [OHG] = x $$     $$ [BID] = [ODI] = y $$     $$ [CEF] = [OFE] = z $$     $$ [OIF] = a $$     $$ [HOE] = b $$     $$ [GDO] = c $$   where  $[X]$  denotes the area of polygon  $X$ .

Plugging into the problem statement gives  $a+b+c \geq x + y +z$ , so this is all we must prove.

Claim:  $a+b \geq 2z$  <details><summary>Proof</summary>Due to parallel lines,  $OIF$  is similar to  $HOE$ , so we have:  $$ \frac{OI^2}{OH^2}\ = \frac{[OIF]}{[HOE]} = \frac{a}{b} $$  Meanwhile,  $OIC$  and  $OHC$  have the same altitude from  $C$ , so we have:  $$ \frac{OI}{OH}\ = \frac{[OIC]}{[OHC]} = \frac{[OIF] + [OFC]}{[OHE] + [OEC]}
= \frac{[OIF] + \frac{1}{2}[CEOF]}{[OHE] + \frac{1}{2}[CEOF]} = \frac{[OIF] + [OFE]}{[OHE] + [OFE]} = \frac{a+z}{b+z} $$  Combining the two pieces of information gives   $$ \frac{a}{b} = \frac{(a+z)^2}{(b+z)^2} $$  Simplifying gives  $$ ab=z^2 $$  Finally, applying AM-GM Inequality gives the required result:  $$ a+b\geq 2z $$</details>

Similarly, we have  $b+c \geq 2x$  and  $c+a \geq 2y$ . The sum of the three inequalities gives the desired result.

stem_md:
Find the real number  $t$ , such that the following system of equations has a unique real solution  $(x, y, z, v)$ :

\[ \left\{\begin{array}{cc}x+y+z+v=0 (xy + yz +zv)+t(xz+xv+yv)=0\end{array}\right. \]
solution_md:
Find the real number $t$ , such that the following system of equations has a unique real solution $(x, y, z, v)$ : \[ \left\{\begin{array}{cc}x+y+z+v=0 (xy + yz +zv)+t(xz+xv+yv)=0\end{array}\right. \]
Setting $v=-x-y-z$ and plugging in second equation, we get $z^2+z(x+ty)+t(x^2+2xy+y^2)-xy=0$ We want that the quadratic has roots, and so its discriminant need to be $\ge 0$ and so : $x^2(1-4t)+2xy(2-3t)+t^2y^2-4ty^2\ge 0$ If $t<\frac 14$ , this inequality has infinitely many solutions $(x,y)$ and so we have infinitely many $(x,y,z,v)$ If $t=\frac 14$ , this becomes $(8x-3y)y\ge 0$ which has also infinitely many solutions $(x,y)$ and so infinitely many $(x,y,z,v)$ So we need $t>\frac 14$ , and so the discriminant of the quadratic in $x$ must be $\ge 0$ : $4y^2(2-3t)^2-4y^2(1-4t)(t^2-4t)\ge 0$ $16y^2(t+1)(t^2-3t+1)\ge 0$ If $(t+1)(t^2-3t+1)\ge 0$ , we have then infinitely many values for $y$ , and so for $x,y,z,v$ So we need $t>\frac 14$ and $(t+1)(t^2-3t+1)< 0$ and indeed this would imply $y=0$ , then $x=0$ , then $z=0$ and then $v=0$ Hence the answer : $\boxed{t\in(\frac{3-\sqrt 5}2,\frac{3+\sqrt 5}2)}$

stem_md: Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers  $n$  such that the number  $\frac{1^2+2^2+\cdots+n^2}{n}$  is a perfect square. Obviously,  $1$  is the least integer having this property. Find the next two least integers having this property.
solution_md:
Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that the number $\frac{1^2+2^2+\cdots+n^2}{n}$ is a perfect square. Obviously, $1$ is the least integer having this property. Find the next two least integers having this property.
The equation is $(n+1)(2n+1)=6p^2$ $\iff$ $(4n+3)^2-48p^2=1$ The Pell equation $x^2-48y^2$ has infinitely many solutions built from $(7,1)$ thru the transformation $(x,y)\to(7x+48y,x+7y)$ In order to have $x\equiv 3\pmod 4$ , we need to take only one solution upon two and so $(x,y)\to(97x+672y,14x+97y)$ So, the solutions of $(4n+3)^2-48p^2=1$ are obtained from $(1,1)$ thru the transformation $(n,p)\to(97n+168p+72,56n+97p+42)$ So we have infinitely many solutions and the three first are $\boxed{(1,1),(337,195),(65521,37829)}$

stem_md:
Function  $f(n), n \in \mathbb N$ , is defined as follows:
Let  $\frac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1000)!} = \frac{A(n)}{B(n)}$  , where  $A(n), B(n)$  are coprime positive integers; if  $B(n) = 1$ , then  $f(n) = 1$ ; if  $B(n) \neq 1$ , then  $f(n)$  is the largest prime factor of  $B(n)$ . Prove that the values of  $f(n)$  are finite, and find the maximum value of  $f(n).$
solution_md:
When  $n=999$ , denominator of  $ \frac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1000)!}$  is divisible by  $1999$ , a prime, where numerator of it cannot. Therefore  $B(999)=1999$ .
We are going to prove that  $B(n)$  must be less than  $2000$ For all prime  $p$  and  $n\ge 1000$ , we consider this  $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^i}\rfloor -\lfloor \frac{n}{p^i}\rfloor -\lfloor \frac{n+1000}{p^i}\rfloor$ . If  $p=B(n)$ , the sumation is less than zero. That means exist a  $i$  such that  $\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^i}\rfloor -\lfloor \frac{n}{p^i}\rfloor -\lfloor \frac{n+1000}{p^i}\rfloor<0$ We will use a fact that  $\lfloor a+b \rfloor \ge \lfloor a \rfloor +\lfloor b \rfloor $ . $\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^i}\rfloor -\lfloor \frac{n}{p^i}\rfloor \ge \lfloor \frac{n}{p^i}\rfloor $  And  $\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^i}\rfloor -\lfloor \frac{n+1000}{p^i}\rfloor \ge \lfloor \frac{n-1000}{p^i}\rfloor $ . This means  $ \lfloor \frac{n}{p^i}\rfloor < \lfloor \frac{n+1000}{p^i}\rfloor$  And   $ \lfloor \frac{n-1000}{p^i}\rfloor < \lfloor \frac{n}{p^i}\rfloor$ . This is equivalent to a multiple of  $p^{i}$  is lying between  $n-1000$  and  $n$  and another multiple of  $p^{i}$  is lying between  $n$  and  $n+1000$ . As a result  $p^{i}<2000$ . Therefore the maximum of  $B(n)=1999$  and its value are finite since  $B(n)\ge 1$ .

stem_md: Let  $S = \{1, 2, \ldots, 1990\}$ . A  $31$ -element subset of  $S$  is called "good" if the sum of its elements is divisible by  $5$ . Find the number of good subsets of  $S.$
solution_md:
Just to make the claim for symmetry a bit more substantiated: 

Instead of thinking of the set  $S=\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, \dots 1989, 1990\}$ , think of the multiset  $S_m = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 1, 2, \dots 4, 0\}$ , where each element is a residue class, and each residue class appears equally as often, thanks to the fact that  $1990$  is divisible by  $5$ . 

Let us just consider  $3$ -element subsets of  $S_m$ , for simplicity (rather than  $31$ -element subsets). How many ways are there to pick a certain  $3$ -element subset from  $S_m$ ? You can verify that it only depends on the relative multiplicities of each element in the subset. For example,  $\{0,0,0\}$  can be chosen in just as many ways as can  $\{1,1,1\}$ , and  $\{0,3,3\}$  can be chosen in just as many ways as can  $\{0,0,1\}$ .

Now we create a  $5$ -way bijection, so to speak, where we group together the following  $3$ -element subsets, for any (not necessarily distinct)  $a,b,c$ : $\{a,b,c\} \text{   } \{a+1,b+1,c+1\} \text{   } \{a+2,b+2,c+2\}\text{   } \{a+3,b+3,c+3\} \text{   }\{a+4,b+4,c+4\} $ These  $5$  subsets sum to the five distinct residues  $0, 1, 2, 3,$  and  $4$  (and this is due to the fact that  $3$ , just like  $31$ , is relatively prime to  $5$ ). Moreover, each of the subsets contains elements with the same multiplicities, and therefore can be chosen in the same number of ways from  $S_m$ . 

It follows that the number ways of choosing a  $3$ -element subset of  $S_m$ , whose elements sum to  $0$ , is exactly  $1/5$  of the total number of ways of choosing a  $3$ -element subset from  $S_m$ . Therefore, the number of  $3$ -element subsets of  $S$ , whose elements sum to  $0$ , is exactly  $1/5$  of the total number of  $3$ -element subsets of  $S$ . All the above reasoning works if you substitute  $31$  for  $3$ .

stem_md:
Prove that if  $|x| < 1$ , then
\[ \frac{x}{(1-x)^2}+\frac{x^2}{(1+x^2)^2} + \frac{x^3}{(1-x^3)^2}+\cdots=\frac{x}{1-x}+\frac{2x^2}{1+x^2}+\frac{3x^3}{1-x^3}+\cdots\]
solution_md:
We have  $ \frac{1}{1-x^n} =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} x^{kn} $  and  $ \frac{1}{1+x^k} =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (-1)^k x^{kn} $  which, upon differentiation and simplification, gives us \[ \frac{x^n}{(1-x^n)^2} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} kx^{kn},  \frac{x^n}{(1+x^n)^2} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (-1)^{k+1} kx^{kn} \]

Thus, \[ \frac{x}{(1-x)^2} = x+2x^2 + 3x^3 + 4x^4 + \cdots \]

\[ \frac{x^2}{(1+x^2)^2} = x^2 -2x^4 + 3x^6 - \cdots \]

\[ \frac{x^3}{(1-x^3)^2} = x^3+ 2x^6 + 3x^9 + \cdots \]

.. etc. 

Summing the first terms of the sums, then the second, third, etc gives

\[ \frac{x}{(1-x)^{2}}+\frac{x^{2}}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}+\frac{x^{3}}{(1-x^{3})^{2}}+\cdots \]

\[ = \left(x + x^2+x^3+ \cdots \right) + 2\left( x^2 - x^4 + x^4 - \cdots \right) + 3\left( x^3 + x^6 + x^9 + \cdots \right) + \cdots  \]

which are each geometric series which sum to the required terms.

stem_md: Let  $n$  be an arbitrary positive integer. Calculate  $S_n = \sum_{r=0}^n 2^{r-2n} \binom{2n-r}{n}.$
solution_md:
We have: $ S_n = \sum_{r=0}^{n}2^{r-2n}\binom{2n-r}{n} = \sum_{r=0}^{n}2^{r-2n}\binom{2n-r}{n-r} = $  $ = \sum_{s=0}^{n} 2^{-s-n}\binom{n+s}{s} $ .


Let denote  $ a_n = \sum_{s=0}^{n} 2^{-s}\binom{n+s}{s}$  . We get: $ a_n = 1+ \sum_{s=1}^n \binom{n-1+s}{s} 2^{-s} + \sum_{s=1}^n \binom{n+s-1}{s-1} 2^{-s} = $  $= a_{n-1} + \binom{2n-1}{n}2^{-n} + \frac{1}{2} a_n - \binom{2n}{n}2^{-(n+1)} \, \Rightarrow$  $a_n = 2 a_{n-1}$ .

From  $a_0=1 \, \Rightarrow \, a_n = 2^n$ .

Obviously  $S_n = 2^{-n} a_n = 1$ .

See also: http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?f=38&t=52544

stem_md: Prove that for any positive integer  $n$ , the number of odd integers among the binomial coefficients  $\binom nh \ ( 0 \leq h \leq n)$  is a power of 2.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>This is kind of hard to explain without diagrams, so I'll use a black dot for odd numbers and a white dot for an even number. We then proceed by induction.

The base case is the first two rows. All three of these dots are black dots, so each row has a power of two number of dots. The inductive step is to prove that given that each of the first  $2^n$  rows have a power of two number of black dots, the rows  $2^n+1$  to  $2^{n+1}$  also have a power of two number of black dots.

Because the  $2^n$  row is all black dots, each of the  $2^n-1$  dots beneath these black dots must be white. This is because the binomial coefficients are the terms of Pascal's Triangle and the sum of any two odd numbers is even. Each of the  $2^n-2$  terms beneath these are also white, since even+even=odd. This logic continues until there's a lone white dot on the  $2^{n+1}-1$  row. 

Now let us examine the remaining dots on the  $2^n+1$  row; these are the two edge dots, which must be black (they are 1). Since I don't have a diagram, I will call the pyramid starting at the left point which I just mentioned the start of Triangle A. (Triangle A starts on row  $2^n+1$  and ends on  $2^{n+1}$ .) By symmetry, the triangle on the right side is equivalent to Triangle A, so we'll call this Triangle A'. 

Note that up to the  $2^{n+1}-1$ th row, both sides of Triangle A are lined with white dots (the left side is filled with 0's). Thus, each row thereafter must have the same parity as the corresponding row in Triangle B. Thus, the first  $2^n-1$  rows of Triangle A match those of Triangle B. Because the  $2^n$ th row of Triangle A is the sum of the previous row's terms, the  $2^n$ th row of Triangle A also matches that of Triangle B. Thus, Triangle A == Triangle A' == Triangle B. Thus, the mth row of Triangle B has the same number of black dots as the mth row of each of Triangle A's and Triangle A''s. 

Thus, the  $2^n+m$  row of the Pascal's triangle has twice the number of dots as the mth row. By the inductive hypothesis, the mth row has a power of two number of black dots, and hence the  $2^n+m$ th row must also have a power of two number of black dots. Therefore, the number of odd integers among the binomial coefficients  $\binom nh$  is a power of 2.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/International Contests/IMO Longlists/1990 IMO Longlists/367438.json

We can generalize the problem.
If  $ab,ac,bc$  is not a square ,  $ \sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt{c} $  is irrational.

Assume  $ \sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt{c} $  is rational, then  $[ \sqrt a+\sqrt b+\sqrt{c} ]^{2} $  is also rational. 
That means  $ \sqrt {ab}+\sqrt {bc}+\sqrt{ca} $  is rational. Moreover  $[ \sqrt {ab}+\sqrt {bc}+\sqrt{ca} ]^{2}$  is rational too.
This means that  $ c.\sqrt {ab} +a.\sqrt {bc} + b. \sqrt{ac} $  is rational.
Also  $ c.\sqrt {ab} +a.\sqrt {bc} + b. \sqrt{ac} - a.\sqrt {ab}-a.\sqrt {bc}-a.\sqrt{ca} $  is rational.
In other words,  $ (c-a).\sqrt {ab}+ (b-a). \sqrt{ac}$  is rational.
This is equipvalent to  $a^{2}.bc$  is a square, which contradicts to  $ bc $  is not a square.
Suppose it is rational. Then it is sum of algebraic integers, hence rational integer. However, this contradicts  $$ 47 < \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{1990} < 48. $$

I think we can use the following lemma:**Lemma** If  $a,b,c$  and  $\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}+\sqrt{c}$  are rational, then  $\sqrt{a},\sqrt{b},\sqrt{c}$  are also rational.
*Proof*  Let  $x=\sqrt{a}+\sqrt{b}+\sqrt{c}$ . Square both sides of  $x-\sqrt{a}=\sqrt{b}+\sqrt{c}$  to get   $x^2+a-2x\sqrt{a}=b+c+2\sqrt{bc}$ . Square both sides of  $x^2+a-2x\sqrt{a}-b-c=2\sqrt{bc}$  and after that only  $\sqrt{a}$  will remain in the equation, from which it is clear that  $\sqrt{a}$  is rational.

Now assume that  $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{1990}$  is rational. Then  $\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3},\sqrt{1990}$  are all rational, which is not true. Therefore, the given sum must be irrational.

stem_md:
During the class interval,  $n$  children sit in a circle and play the game described below. The teacher goes around the children clockwisely and hands out candies to them according to the following regulations: Select a child, give him a candy; and give the child next to the first child a candy too; then skip over one child and give next child a candy; then skip over two children; give the next child a candy; then skip over three children; give the next child a candy;...

Find the value of  $n$  for which the teacher can ensure that every child get at least one candy eventually (maybe after many circles).
solution_md:
LOL this appeared as an AIME-style problem (with slight modifications) in one of my classes

For all nonnegative integer  $q$  and integer  $r$  such that  $1 \le r \le n$ , suppose the  $qn + r$ th child means the  $r$ th child. The teacher gives candy to the  $0$ th child, then to the  $1$ st child, then the  $1 + 2$ nd child, then the  $1 + 2 + 3$ rd child, and so on, giving candy to the  $1 + 2 + \cdots + k = \frac{k(k+1)}{2}$ th child on his  $(k+1)$ th candy. The teacher gives candies to all children if and only if for all positive integers  $m$ , there exists nonnegative integer  $k$  such that  $\frac{k(k+1)}{2} \equiv m \pmod n.$  This is equivalent to  $k(k+1) \equiv 2m \pmod {2n}.$ We claim that, if the teacher has enough candy, he gives all students a candy if and only if  $n$  is of the form  $2^s$  with  $s$  a nonnegative integer.

First, let's prove that, if  $n = 2^s$  with  $s$  a nonnegative integer, and the teacher has enough candy, every child will get a candy. That is, for all positive integers  $m$ , there exists nonnegative integer  $k$  such that  $k(k+1) \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{s+1}}$ . We do this by induction on  $s$ .

The base case is where  $s = 0$ . We wish to prove there exists  $k$  with  $k(k+1) \equiv 2m \pmod 2$  for all positive integers  $m$ . This is equivalent to  $k(k+1) \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ . Choosing  $k=0$  makes the equivalence true because  $0 \cdot 1 = 0 \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ .

For the induction case, let's assume  $a^2 + a \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+1}}$ . Our goal is to prove that there exists  $k$  such that  $k^2 + k \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+2}}$ . We must have either  $a^2 + a \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+2}}$  or  $a^2 + a \equiv 2m + 2^{t+1} \pmod {2^{t+2}}$ . We go into cases for this.

In the case with  $a^2 + a \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+2}}$ , we choose  $k=a$  and we're done.

Otherwise we assume  $a^2 + a \equiv 2m + 2^{t+1} \pmod {2^{t+2}}$ . Let's choose  $k = a + 2^{t+1}$ . We wish to prove  $$ (a + 2^{t+1})^2 + a + 2^{t+1} \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+2}} $$  This expands to  $$ a^2 + 2^{t+2} + 2^{2t+2} + a + 2^{t+1} \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+2}} $$  By our assumption for this case, our goal is equivalent to  $$ 2^{t+2} + 2^{2t+2} + (2m + 2^{t+1}) + 2^{t+1} \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+2}} $$  This is equivalent to  $$ 2^{t+2} + 2^{2t+2} + 2m + 2^{t+2} \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+2}} $$  After we eliminate the terms divisible by  $2^{t+2}$ , we are left with  $2m \equiv 2m \pmod {2^{t+2}}$  as our goal, which is true. This completes the induction. We have proven one direction of the "if and only if" claim.

Now, we must prove that, if  $n$  is not of the form  $2^s$  with  $s$  a nonnegative integer, it is not true that for all positive integers  $m$ , there exists  $k$  such that  $k^2 + k \equiv 2m \pmod {2n}$ . We prove this by contradiction. In this case, there must be an odd prime that divides  $n$ . Suppose the prime factorization of  $n$  is  $n = 2^{e_0}p_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\ldots p_h^{e_h}$ , with all the  $p_i$  distinct odd primes. Here,  $e_0$  is not necessarily positive, but all of the other  $e_i$  are.

By Chinese Remainder Theorem, there is a unique solution $\pmod {2n}$  to the system  $$ x \equiv a_0 \pmod {2^{e_0+1}} $$    $$ x \equiv a_1 \pmod {p_1^{e_1}} $$    $$ x \equiv a_2 \pmod {p_2^{e_2}} $$    $$ \ldots $$    $$ x \equiv a_h \pmod {p_h^{e_h}} $$  In particular, if  $a_0$  is even, then  $2m \pmod {2n}$  is the solution to this system for some positive integer  $m$ . This also means that there must exist  $k$  such that  $k(k+1)$  is a solution to this system. Let's focus on the congruence  $$ x \equiv a_1 \pmod {p_1^{e_1}} $$  Now,  $a_1$  can be any integer, and as long as  $a_0$  is even, we can have  $2m$  be a solution to the system. Thus, for all integer  $a_1$ , there exists  $m$  such that  $2m \equiv a_1 \pmod {p_1^{e_1}}$ . We also assume that, for all  $m$ , there exists  $k$  such that  $k(k+1) \equiv 2m \pmod{2n}$ . This implies that for all integer  $a_1$ , there exists  $k$  with  $$ k(k+1) \equiv a_1 \pmod {p_1^{e_1}}. $$  This implies that, for all  $p_1^{e_1}$  residues mod  $p_1^{e_1}$ , there exists  $k$  such that  $k(k+1)$  achieves the residue. Notice that  $$ (k + p_1^{e_1})(k + p_1^{e_1} + 1) \equiv k(k+1) \equiv a_1 \pmod {p_1^{e_1}}, $$  which implies that, as  $k$  increases, the residues of  $k(k+1) \pmod {p_1^{e_1}}$  repeat with period  $p_1^{e_1}$ . This implies that all possible residues mod  $p_1^{e_1}$  are achieved by  $k(k+1)$  with  $1 \le k \le p_1^{e_1}$  in some order. In particular, all of these residues must be distinct.

Now, with  $k=1$ , we get  $1(1+1) \equiv 2 \pmod {p_1^{e_1}}$ . However, with  $k = p_1^{e_1} - 2$ , we get  $(p_1^{e_1} - 2)(p_1^{e_1} - 1) \equiv (-2)(-1) \equiv 2 \pmod {p_1^{e_1}}$ . Not all of the residues of  $k(k+1)$  mod  $p_1^{e_1}$  for  $1 \le k \le p_1^{e_1}$  are distinct, but we previously showed that they are. We have arrived at a contradiction, completing the proof.

\[\begin{cases}x^3+y^3 &=1x^5+y^5 &=1\end{cases}\]
solution_md:
Find the real solution(s) for the system of equations \[\{\begin{array}{cc}x^3+y^3=1x^5+y^5=1\end{array}\]
$(x,y)=(0,1)$ and $(x,y)=(1,0)$ are trivial roots. We'll look now for solutions such that $x,y\notin\{0,1\}$ $x,y$ cant be both negative, so WLOG say $x>0$ . $(x,y)$ solution $\implies$ $(\frac 1x,-\frac yx)$ solution. So WLOG say $1>x>0$ System implies $(1-x^3)^5=(1-x^5)^3$ . But $1>x>0$ $\implies$ $x^51-x^5>1-x^3>0$ $\implies$ $(1-x^5)^3>(1-x^3)^3>(1-x^3)^5$ and so no solution Hence the only two solutions : $\boxed{(x,y)\in\{(0,1),(1,0)\}}$

stem_md:
Let  $M = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$  and  $\phi : M \to M$  be a bijection.

(i) Prove that there exist bijections  $\phi_1, \phi_2 : M \to M$  such that  $\phi_1 \cdot \phi_2 = \phi , \phi_1^2 =\phi_2^2=E$ , where  $E$  is the identity mapping.

(ii) Prove that the conclusion in (i) is also true if  $M$  is the set of all positive integers.
solution_md:
I assume the dots in the problem are the composition function, not the multiplication function.

We know that the inverse  $\phi^{-1}(x)$  is well defined.  Let some number in the interval be  $a_0$ .  Then define  $a_1, a_2, \ldots$  as  $\phi(a_0)=a_1, \phi(a_1)=a_2, \ldots$  and define  $a_{-1}, a_{-2}, \ldots$  as  $a_{-1}=\phi^{-1}(a_0), a_{-2}=\phi^{-1}(a_{-1}), \ldots$ .  Thus  $\phi(a_{k})=a_{k+1}$ .  If this becomes a cycle, so be it.  If there are numbers left over, then define new sequences  $\ldots b_{-2}, b_{-1}, b_0, b_1, b_2\ldots$ ,  $\ldots c_{-2}, c_{-1}, c_0, c_1, c_2\ldots$  and so on.  Note that these sequences are disjoint.

Define  $\phi_1(a_n)=a_{1-n}$  and  $\phi_2(a_n)=a_{-n}$ , and analogously with the other sequences.  We see that  $\phi_1(\phi_1(a_n))=\phi_1(a_{1-n})=a_n$  and  $\phi_2(\phi_2(a_n))=\phi_2(a_{-n})=a_n$ .  Also we can see that  $\phi_1(\phi_2(a_n))=\phi_1(a_{-n})=a_{n+1}=\phi(a_n)$  for all numbers in the set, even if it's infinite.

The only potential problem is if the  $a$ 's become cyclic, then multiple values for the function may be assigned.  We can check that if  $a_k=a_{n+k}$  for some  $k$ , then for all  $m$ ,  $a_m=a_{n+m}$ .  We then know that  $\phi_1(a_m)=a_{1-m}=a_{n+(1-m-n)}=a_{1-m-n}=\phi_1(a_{m+n})$ and $\phi_2(a_m)=a_{-m}=a_{n+(-m-n)}=a_{-m-n}=\phi_2(a_{m+n})$ .  Thus there is no worry about multiple assignments of the two functions.

stem_md: The sequence  $\{u_n\}$  is defined by  $u_1 = 1, u_2 = 1, u_n = u_{n-1} + 2u_{n-2} for n \geq 3$ . Prove that for any positive integers  $n, p \  (p > 1), u_{n+p} = u_{n+1}u_{p} + 2u_nu_{p-1}$ . Also find the greatest common divisor of  $u_n$  and  $u_{n+3}.$
solution_md:
$u_n=\frac{1}{3}(2^n-(-1)^n)$ , which can be proved by induction, and which was found using the characteristic polynomial  $x^2-x-2=0$  which gives  $(x-2)(x+1)=0$ . The first statement is just tedious algebraic manipulation of the formula for  $u_n$ .

For the second, $gcd(\frac{1}{3}(2^{n+3}-(-1)^{n+3}),\frac{1}{3}(2^{n}-(-1)^{n}))=\frac{1}{3}gcd(8\cdot 2^n + (-1)^n, 2^n- (-1)^n)=\frac{1}{3}gcd(8\cdot 2^n + (-1)^n, 8\cdot 2^n- 8(-1)^n)|\frac{1}{3}gcd(9(-1)^n, 8\cdot 2^n- 8(-1)^n)|\frac{1}{3} \cdot 9=3$ So therefore, the  $gcd$  is  $1$  or  $3$ . Looking at the sequence mod  $3$ , we get for  $n=1,2,3,...$  the sequence  $1,1,0,2,2,0,1,1,0,2,2,0,...$  where the pattern is easy to prove by induction, and thus gives the  $gcd$  being  $1$  when  $n$  is not a multiple of  $3$ , and  $3$  if  $n$  is a multiple of  $3$ .

Cheers,

Rofler

stem_md:
Given eight real numbers  $a_1 \leq a_2 \leq  \cdots \leq a_7 \leq a_8$ . Let  $x = \frac{ a_1 + a_2 +  \cdots + a_7 + a_8}{8}$ ,  $y = \frac{ a_1^2 + a_2^2 +  \cdots + a_7^2 + a_8^2}{8}$ . Prove that 
\[2 \sqrt{y-x^2} \leq a_8  - a_1 \leq 4 \sqrt{y-x^2}.\]
solution_md:
Given eight real numbers $a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots \leq a_7 \leq a_8$ . Let $x = \frac{ a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_7 + a_8}{8}$ , $y = \frac{ a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \cdots + a_7^2 + a_8^2}{8}$ . Prove that \[2 \sqrt{y-x^2} \leq a_8 - a_1 \leq 4 \sqrt{y-x^2}.\]
RHS let $z = \frac{{a_2 + \cdots + a_7 }}{6}$ , then $a_1 \le z \le a_8 $ , and $4\sqrt {y - x^2 } = 4\sqrt {\frac{{8\left( {a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \cdots + a_7^2 + a_8^2 } \right) - \left( {a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_7 + a_8 } \right)^2 }}{{64}}} $ $ \ge 4\sqrt {\frac{{8\left( {a_1^2 + 6z^2 + a_8^2 } \right) - \left( {a_1 + 6z + a_8 } \right)^2 }}{{64}}} $ $ = \sqrt {\frac{{3\left( {a_1 - 2z + a_8 } \right)^2 + 4\left( {a_1 - a_8 } \right)^2 }}{4}} $ $ \ge a_8 - a_1 .$ generalization see also: http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?f=52&t=366469 LHS $\left( {a_i - a_1 } \right)\left( {a_i - a_8 } \right) \le 0 \Leftrightarrow a_i^2 \le \left( {a_1 + a_8 } \right)a_i - a_1 a_8 \;(i = 1,2,...,8)$ , so $2\sqrt {y - x^2 } = 2\sqrt {\frac{{8\left( {a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \cdots + a_7^2 + a_8^2 } \right) - \left( {a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_7 + a_8 } \right)^2 }}{{64}}} $ $ \le 2\sqrt {\frac{{8\left( {a_1 + a_8 } \right)\left( {a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_7 + a_8 } \right) - 64a_1 a_8 - \left( {a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_7 + a_8 } \right)^2 }}{{64}}} $ $ = \frac{{\sqrt {\left( {7a_8 - 6z - a_1 } \right)\left( {a_8 + 6z - 7a_1 } \right)} }}{4}$ $ \le \frac{{\left( {7a_8 - 6z - a_1 } \right) + \left( {a_8 + 6z - 7a_1 } \right)}}{8}$ $=a_8-a_1.$ [mod edit - merge posts]

Find all the continuous bounded functions  $f: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$  such that 
\[(f(x))^2 -(f(y))^2  = f(x + y)f(x - y) \text{  for all } x, y \in \mathbb R.\]
solution_md:

Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(x)^2-f(y)^2=f(x+y)f(x-y)$ $f(x)=0$ $\forall x$ is a solution. So let us from now look for non all-zero functions. So let $u$ such that $f(u)\ne 0$ 1) $f(x)$ is an odd function and $f(0)=0$ ============================= $P(\frac{u+x}2,\frac{u-x}2)$ $\implies$ $f(\frac{u+x}2)^2-f(\frac{u-x}2)^2=f(u)f(x)$ $P(\frac{u-x}2,\frac{u+x}2)$ $\implies$ $f(\frac{u-x}2)^2-f(\frac{u+x}2)^2=f(u)f(-x)$ Adding these two lines, we get $f(-x)=-f(x)$ Q.E.D. 2) $\exists v>0$ such that $f(v)=0$ ======================== If $f(x)$ is injective, it is monotonous (since continuous) and, since monotonous and bounded, limits at $\pm\infty$ exist : Let then $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L$ and $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=l$ $P(x+u,x)$ $\implies$ $f(x+u)^2-f(x)^2=f(2x+u)f(u)$ Setting $x\to+\infty$ in this equality, we get $Lf(u)=0$ and so $L=0$ Setting $x\to-\infty$ in this equality, we get $lf(u)=0$ and so $l=0$ And so contradiction (since $f(x)$ is not the all zero constant function). Q.E.D. If $f(b+c)=0$ and $b+c\ne 0$ , then just choose $v=|b+c|$ . Q.E.D If $f(b+c)=0$ and $b+c=0$ , we get $c=-b$ and so $f(b)=f(c)=f(-b)=-f(b)$ and so $f(b)=f(c)=0$ with $b\ne c$ . So, since $f(x)$ is continuous, this would mean $f(x)$ constant, and so $f(x)=0$ $\forall x$ , impossible in this part of the proof. So $a\ne 0$ And so we got : $a>0$ $f(2a)=0$ and so $2a\in A$ and so $f(x+4a)=f(x)$ $\forall x$ $f(x)\ne 0$ $\forall x\in (0,2a)$ (since $2a=\inf(A)$ ) Q.E.D 4) $f(x)=b\sin(\frac{\pi x}{2a})$ ======================= If $f(x)$ is known over $[0,2a]$ , using $f(-x)=-f(x)$ implies knowlegde over $[-2a,+2a]$ Then $f(x+4a)=f(x)$ implis knowledge over $%Error. stem_md: In coordinate plane, a variable point  $M$ , starting from the origin  $O(0, 0)$ , moves on the line  $l$  with slope  $k$ , where  $k$  is an irrational number.**(i)** Prove that point  $O(0, 0)$  is the only rational point (namely, the coordinates of which are both rationals) on the line  $l.$ **(ii)** Prove that for any number  $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exist integers  $m, n$  such that the distance between  $l$  and the point  $(m, n)$  is less than  $\varepsilon.$
solution_md:
Suppose there exists a rational point  $(p, q)$  in that line and hence, the slope is  $k=\frac{q}{p}$  which is false as  $LHS$  is irrational, whereas  $RHS$  is rational.

Distance between  $(m, n)$  and  $l$  is  $\frac{|km-n|}{\sqrt{k^2+1}}<\varepsilon\Longleftrightarrow |km-n|<\varepsilon'$ , a constant

So, we need to find integers  $m, n$  such that  $km-n<\varepsilon'$ . This is true by Archimedian property.

[Archimedian property and corollaries.pdf](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/f/2/1fcd05a2c0a91a2e5f494650a0d6fa00c969cd)

\[(a^2 + ab + b^2)(b^2 + bc + c^2)(c^2 + ca + a^2) \geq (ab + bc + ca)^3.\]
When does the equality hold?
solution_md:
Let $a, b, c \in \mathbb R$ . Prove that \[(a^2 + ab + b^2)(b^2 + bc + c^2)(c^2 + ca + a^2) \geq (ab + bc + ca)^3.\] When does the equality hold?
This is also true: If $a,$ $b,$ $c$ are **real** numbers, then $3(a^2+ab+b^2)(b^2+bc+c^2)(c^2+ca+a^2) \ge (a+b+c)^2(ab+bc+ca)^2.$
$4\left(a^2+ab+b^2\right)\left(b^2+bc+c^2\right)=\left(2b^2+2ca+ab+bc\right)^2+3(ab-bc)^2$ , $4\left(c^2+ca+a^2\right)=3(a+c)^2+(c-a)^2$ $(a^2+ab+b^2)(b^2+bc+c^2)(c^2+ca+a^2)$ $\ge\frac{3}{4^2}\left(\left(2b^2+2ca+ab+bc\right)(a+c)+(ab-bc)(c-a)\right)^2$ $=3\left(\frac{ab^2+b^2c+c^2a+ca^2}{2}+abc\right)^2$ $3(a^2+ab+b^2)(b^2+bc+c^2)(c^2+ca+a^2)\ge\sum3\left(\frac{ab^2+b^2c+c^2a+ca^2}{2}+abc\right)^2$ $\ge\left(\sum\left(\frac{ab^2+b^2c+c^2a+ca^2}{2}+abc\right)\right)^2$ $=(a+b+c)^2(ab+bc+ca)^2$

Below is one of my proofs: First, we see that $(a^2+ab+b^2)(a^2+ac+c^2)=\frac{1}{4}[3a^2(a+b+c)^2+(2bc+ab+ac-a^2)^2].$ Now, using the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality, we have $\begin{aligned} a^2(a+b+c)^2+(2bc+ab+ac-a^2)^2& \ge \frac{[a(a+b+c)+(2bc+ab+ac-a^2)]^2}{2} &=2(ab+bc+ca)^2. \end{aligned}$ It follows that $(a^2+ab+b^2)(a^2+ac+c^2) \ge \frac{a^2(a+b+c)^2+(ab+bc+ca)^2}{2}.$ And since $b^2+bc+c^2 \ge \frac{3}{4} (b+c)^2,$ we get $\prod (a^2+ab+b^2) \ge \frac{3}{8}a^2(b+c)^2 \left( \sum a\right)^2 +\frac{3}{8} (b+c)^2 \left( \sum ab\right)^2.$ Adding this and its analogous inequalities, we get $3\prod (a^2+ab+b^2) \ge \frac{3}{8} \left[ \sum a^2(b+c)^2\right] \left( \sum a\right)^2 +\frac{3}{8}\left[ \sum (b+c)^2\right] \left( \sum ab\right)^2.$ On the other hand, the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality gives $\sum a^2(b+c)^2 \ge \frac{\left[ \sum a(b+c)\right]^2}{3} =\frac{4}{3} \left( \sum ab\right)^2,$ $\sum (b+c)^2 \ge \frac{\left[ \sum (b+c)\right]^2}{3} =\frac{4}{3} \left( \sum a\right)^2.$ So we have $\begin{aligned} 3\prod (a^2+ab+b^2) &\ge \frac{1}{2} \left( \sum ab\right)^2\left( \sum a\right)^2 +\frac{1}{2}\left( \sum a\right)^2\left( \sum ab\right)^2 &=\left( \sum a\right)^2\left(\sum ab\right)^2.\end{aligned}$ The proof is completed.

stem_md: Let  $L$  be a subset in the coordinate plane defined by  $L = \{(41x + 2y, 59x + 15y) | x, y \in \mathbb Z \}$ , where  $\mathbb Z$  is set of integers. Prove that for any parallelogram with center in the origin of coordinate and area  $1990$ , there exist at least two points of  $L$  located in it.
solution_md:
Consider the parallelogram  $(0,0),(41,2),(59,15),(18,13)$ , whose vertices lie in  $L$  and has area  $A=497$ . Call such a parallelogram  $P$ . Note that 1990 is slightly more than  $4\times 497$ . By using the points in  $L$ , we can make parallel cuts in the plane (parallel to sides of  $P$ ) to get a tessellation of  $P$ . (basically  $L$  is just a scaled lattice grid)

Lemma: for any figure of area more than  $A$ , we can translate it such that it will contain 2 points in  $L$ . 
Proof: chop up the entire plane into pieces along the cuts in the shape of  $P$  and stack them up. Then since the area of the figure is more than the area of  $P$ , there is a point on the stacked  $P$ 's where at least 2 parts of the figure overlap, and we are done.

Note that the Lemma is equivalent to for any figure of area more than  $A$ , there exist 2 points in the figure  $v_1,v_2$  such that  $v_1-v_2\in L$  (we take the points as vectors from origin). Back to the question, we replace the parallelogram by any convex figure  $F$  symmetric about the origin. Let  $F'$  be the image of  $F$  after homothety at  $O$  with ratio  $\frac12$ . Then the area of  $F'$  is more than  $A$ , so there are 2 distinct points  $v_1,v_2\in F'$  such that  $v_1-v_2\in L$ . Note that  $-v_2\in F'$  and  $2v_1,-2v_2\in F$ . Since  $F$  is convex,  $v_1-v_2\in F$ , so we have another point in  $L$  in  $F$ .

stem_md:
Function  $f(x, y): \mathbb N \times \mathbb N \to \mathbb Q$  satisfies the conditions:

(i)  $f(1, 1) =1$ ,

(ii)  $f(p + 1, q) + f(p, q + 1) = f(p, q)$  for all  $p, q \in  \mathbb N$ , and

(iii)  $qf(p + 1, q) = pf(p, q + 1)$  for all  $p, q \in  \mathbb N$ .

Find  $f(1990, 31).$
solution_md:
Function $f(x, y): \mathbb N \times \mathbb N \to \mathbb Q$ satisfies the conditions: *(i)* $f(1, 1) =1;$ *(ii)* $f(p + 1, q) + f(p, q + 1) = f(p, q)$ for all $p, q \in \mathbb N;$ *(iii)* $qf(p + 1, q) = pf(p, q + 1)$ for all $p, q \in \mathbb N$ Find $f(1990, 31).$
From (iii) we get $f(p+1,q)=\frac pqf(p,q+1)$ and induction gives $f(p,q)=\frac 1{\binom{p+q-2}{q-1}}f(1,p+q-1)$ Plugging this in (ii), we get $f(1,p+q)=\frac{p+q-1}{p+q}f(1,p+q-1)$ and so $f(1,n)=\frac 1n$ Setting this in previous line, we get $\boxed{f(p,q)=\frac {(p-1)!(q-1)!}{(p+q-1)!}}$ which indeed is a solution. So $f(1990,31)=\frac{1989!30!}{2020!}$

stem_md: Given function  $f(x) = \sin x + \sin \pi x$  and positive number  $d$ . Prove that there exists real number  $p$  such that  $|f(x + p) - f(x)| < d$  holds for all real numbers  $x$ , and the value of  $p$  can be arbitrarily large.
solution_md: This is my idea of the proof. Apply sum-product identities to  $f(x+p)-f(x)$  and obtain:  $2cos{\frac{2x+p}{2}}sin{\frac{p}{2}}+2cos{\frac{\pi(2x+p)}{2}}sin{\frac{\pi p}{2}}$ . We can show that we can arbitrarily minimize this sum by analizing the terms  $sin{\frac{p}{2}}$  and  $sin{\frac{\pi p}{2}}$ . We have to look for a  $p$  that satisfies both  $|p-2k|<\epsilon $  and  $|p-2\pi k|<\delta $  with  $h,k\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $\epsilon, \delta$  arbitrarily small reals. We can do this by Dirichlet's approximation theorem.

stem_md: Let  $m$  be an positive odd integer not divisible by  $3$ . Prove that  $\left[4^m -(2+\sqrt 2)^m\right]$  is divisible by  $112.$
solution_md:
Let $m$ be an positive odd integer not divisible by $3$ . Prove that $\left[4^m -(2+\sqrt 2)^m\right]$ is divisible by $112.$
Let the sequence $a_n$ defined as : $a_1=0$ $a_2=4$ $a_3=24$ $a_{n+3}=8a_{n+2}-18a_{n+1}+8a_n$ $\forall n>0$ It's easy to show that $a_n=4^n-(2+\sqrt 2)^n-(2-\sqrt 2)^n$ and since $1>(2-\sqrt 2)^n>0$ $\forall n>0$ and $a_n\in\mathbb Z$ $\forall n$ , we get : $\left\lfloor4^n-(2+\sqrt 2)^n\right\rfloor=a_n$ $\forall n>0$ Looking then at $a_n$ modulus $112$ , we get $\{0,4,24,8,$ and the repeated cycle $0,48,0,32,80,64\}$ Hence the required result.

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer.  $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$  are pairwise non-intersecting sets, and  $S_k $  has exactly  $k$  elements  $(k = 1, 2, \ldots, n)$ . Define  $S = S_1\cup S_2\cup\cdots \cup S_n$ . The function  $f: S \to S $  maps all elements in  $S_k$  to a fixed element of  $S_k$ ,  $k = 1, 2, \ldots, n$ . Find the number of functions  $g: S \to S$  satisfying  $f(g(f(x))) = f(x).$
solution_md:
Let  $x_k$  be the fixed element in  $S_k$  such that  $f: s_k \mapsto x_k$    $\forall s_k \in S_k$ ,  $(k=1,2,\dots,n)$ ;
let  $X={x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n}$ .
Hence  $f(x) \in X)$ .
So we have
\[ f(g(x_k))=x_k \]
follows that  $ g(x_k) \in S_k $ , then  $g(x_k)$  can assume  $k$  different values.
So the possible different  $g$  are :
\[ \prod_{i=1}^n i = n! \]
But in this way there are some elements of  $S$  that are not considered: all  $s \in S$  s.t.  $s \notin X$ .
Hence we have to count in how many ways it is possible to send an element  $a \in S-X$  into an arbitrary element  $b \in S$ ; in fact in the hypothesis the domain of  $g$  is  $S$ , but there are not indications about what  $g$  does out of  $X$ .
And so lets see the cardinality of  $S-X$  and  $S$ ;
the first is
\[ \sum_{i=1}^n i - n= \frac{n(n+1)}{2}-n=\frac{n(n-1)}{2} \]
the second is
\[ \sum_{i=1}^n i= \frac{n(n+1)}2 \]
And so when  $x \notin X$ , there are
\[ \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}2 = \frac{n^2(n-1)(n+1)}4 \] 
different  $g(x)$ .
Hence the value required by the thesis is
\[ n! \cdot \frac{n^2(n-1)(n+1)}4 = \frac{(n+1)!n^2(n-1)}4 \]
P.S. I think this exercise would have been posted in combinatorics.

stem_md:
Find the minimal value of the function 
\[\begin{array}{c}\ f(x) =\sqrt{15 - 12 \cos x} + \sqrt{4 -2 \sqrt 3 \sin x}+\sqrt{7-4\sqrt 3 \sin x} +\sqrt{10-4 \sqrt 3 \sin x - 6 \cos x}\end{array}\]
solution_md:
Find the minimal value of the function \[\begin{array}{c}\ f(x) =\sqrt{15 - 12 \cos x} + \sqrt{4 -2 \sqrt 3 \sin x}+\sqrt{7-4\sqrt 3 \sin x} +\sqrt{10-4 \sqrt 3 \sin x - 6 \cos x}\end{array}\]
By Minkowsky we obtain: $f(x)=\sqrt{(\sqrt3\sin x)^2+(2\sqrt3-\sqrt3\cos x)^2}+\sqrt{(\sqrt3\sin x-1)^2+(\sqrt3\cos x)^2}+$ $+\sqrt{(2-\sqrt3\sin x)^2+(\sqrt3\cos x)^2}+\sqrt{(2-\sqrt3\sin x)^2+(\sqrt3-\sqrt3\cos x)^2}\geq$ $\geq\sqrt{3^2+(3\sqrt3)^2}=6$ . Since $f\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=6$ , we see that $\min f=6$ .

solution_md:
Here we go.

The given inequality is equivalent to showing
\[
x^3y^2+ y^3z^2+z^3x^2 \ge x^3yz+xy^3z+xyz^3.
\]
Note that by the Muirhead (aka majorization) since  $[3,2,0] \succeq [3,1,1]$  we have that  $\sum_{{\rm sym}}x^3 y^2 \ge 2\sum x^3yz$ , where the  $\sum_{{\rm sym}}$  contains all six terms of degree  $(3,2,0)$ . Now, I claim
\[
x^3y^2+ y^3z^2+z^3x^2 \ge x^2y^3+y^2z^3+z^2x^3,
\] 
which will then yield the desired conclusion. 

I will prove this by factorization. We compute their difference to be
\[
(y-z)\left(x^3y + x^3 z +y^2z^2 -x^2y^2 -x^2yz -x^2z^2\right).
\]
Thus it suffices to show
\[
x^3y + x^3 z +y^2z^2 -x^2y^2 -x^2yz -x^2z^2\ge 0.
\]
We now factor this object further:
\[
x^3y + x^3 z +y^2z^2 -x^2y^2 -x^2yz -x^2z^2 = (x-z)\left(x^2y -y^2(x+z)+x^2z\right).
\]
Since  $x-z\ge 0$ , it finally boils down proving
\[
x^2y -y^2(x+z)+x^2z\ge 0 \Leftrightarrow xy(x-y)+z(x^2-y^2)\ge 0,
\]
which is evidently true. This concludes the proof.**Remark.** As easy at it appears in the retrospect, the solution above is not so easy to come up with. I had to experiment with different potential factorizations, while ``peeling" some terms and reducing the degree at each step.

stem_md: Let  $S, T$  be the circumcenter and centroid of triangle  $ABC$ , respectively.  $M$  is a point in the plane of triangle  $ABC$  such that  $90^\circ  \leq  \angle SMT < 180^\circ$ .  $A_1, B_1, C_1$  are the intersections of  $AM, BM, CM$  with the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$  respectively. Prove that  $MA_1 + MB_1 + MC_1 \geq MA + MB + MC.$
solution_md:
let use the notations  $ S=O,T=G $ .
then  $ MG^{2}+MO^{2} \leq OG^{2} $  and using Leibniz this is equivalent with  $ MA^{2}+MB^{2}+MC^{2} \leq 3R^{2}-3OM^{2} $ .
now we only have to use that  $ R^{2}-OM^{2}=AM*A_{1}M=BM*B_{1}M=CM*C_{1}M $  and the inequality  $ (x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2})(1/x+1/y+1/z) \geq x+y+z $ .

stem_md: Let  $S$  be the incenter of triangle  $ABC$ .  $A_1, B_1, C_1$  are the intersections of  $AS, BS, CS$  with the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$  respectively. Prove that  $SA_1 + SB_1 + SC_1 \geq SA + SB + SC.$
solution_md:
Let $S$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$ . $A_1, B_1, C_1$ are the intersections of $AS, BS, CS$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ respectively. Prove that $SA_1 + SB_1 + SC_1 \geq SA + SB + SC.$
First, we can get $ SA_1 = 2Rsin\frac{A}{2}$ , $SB_1 = 2Rsin\frac{B}{2}$ , $SC_1 = 2Rsin\frac{C}{2}$ Then $ SA+SB+SC = \sum\frac{SA.SA_1}{SA_1} = 2Rr\left(\frac{1}{SA_1}+\frac{1}{SB_1}+\frac{1}{SC_1}\right) $ $ = sin\frac{A}{2}sin\frac{B}{2}sin\frac{C}{2}\left(\frac{1}{sin\frac{A}{2}}+\frac{1}{sin\frac{B}{2}}+\frac{1}{sin\frac{C}{2}}\right) $ Then we need prove that : $ 2\left(sin\frac{A}{2}sin\frac{B}{2}+sin\frac{B}{2}sin\frac{C}{2}+sin\frac{C}{2}sin\frac{A}{2}\right) \le sin\frac{A}{2}+sin\frac{B}{2}+sin\frac{C}{2} $ This equality is true because $ sin\frac{A}{2} + sin\frac{B}{2} + sin\frac{C}{2} \le \frac{3}{2} $

stem_md:
Let  $a, b, c$  be the side lengths and  $P$  be area of a triangle, respectively. Prove that
\[(a^2+b^2+c^2-4\sqrt 3 P) (a^2+b^2+c^2) \geq 2 \left(a^2(b - c)^2 + b^2(c - a)^2 + c^2(a - b)^2\right).\]
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>By [Hadwiger-Finsler Inequality](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadwiger%E2%80%93Finsler_inequality), we have  $(a^2+b^2+c^2-4\sqrt{3}P)(a^2+b^2+c^2)\ge (a^2+b^2+c^2)((a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2)$ .

Now, it suffices to prove that  $(a^2+b^2+c^2)((a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2)\ge 2(a^2(b-c)^2+b^2(c-a)^2+c^2(a-b)^2)$ , which is equivalent to  $\sum a^2((c-a)^2+(a-b)^2)\ge \sum a^2(b-c)^2$ .

However, this is equivalent to  $2\sum a^2(a-b)(a-c)\ge 0$ , which is just Schur's Inequality.  $\blacksquare$</details>

Let  $\{ a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ . Prove that
\[\frac 12 +\frac 23 +\cdots+\frac{n-1}{n} \leq \frac{a_1}{a_2} + \frac{a_2}{a_3} +\cdots+\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}.\]
solution_md:
It seems quite simple. Do I miss something?

It is sufficient to prove that for  $\{ b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n\} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ , we have
\[\frac 12 +\frac 23 +\cdots+\frac{n-1}{n} \leq \frac{b_1}{2} + \frac{b_2}{3} +\cdots+\frac{b_{n-1}}{n}.\quad (*)\]<details><summary>(Why?</summary>We have  $\{ a_2, \ldots, a_n\} \subset \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ . Assume the worst case, i.e. we make the RHS of the original ineq smaller by increasing some of the denominators so that they compose the set  $ \{2, \ldots, n\}$ . We now apply a permutation to the fractions to have the denominators in ascending order and call the permuted numerators in this order  $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{n-1}$ . As each permutation is invertible, we are done if  $(*)$  is proved.</details>)

To prove  $ (*)$ , note that we have  $\{ b_1, \ldots, b_{n-1}\}\subset \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ . By reducing some of the  $b_i$ . we can assume the worst case  $\{ b_1, \ldots, b_{n-1}\}= \{1, 2, \ldots, {n-1}\}$ . So  $ (b_1, \ldots, b_{n-1})$  is a permutation  $\sigma$  of  $ (1, 2, \ldots, {n-1})$ , thus a succession of involutions. Now if  $a<b$  and  $i<j$ , we have trivially  $\frac ai+\frac bj<\frac bi+\frac aj$ , so the RHS increases.
Thus we only have to make sure that before applying an involution  $(a,b)$ ,  $a$  is left from  $b$ . This can be done by putting first the smallest of the  $b_i$ , i.e. the  $1$ , "in place" (if it is not already in the same position as on the LHS), by applying  $(1,\sigma^{-1}(1))$ , then  $2$  etc.  :oops:

Let  $\{b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_{n-1}\}=\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{n-1}\}$  and  $\{c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_{n-1}\}=\left\{\frac{1}{a_2},\frac{1}{a_3},\ldots,\frac{1}{a_n}\right\}$  be such that  $b_1<b_2<\cdots<b_{n-1}$  and  $c_1<c_2<\cdots<c_{n-1}$ , then by the **rearrangement inequality**, we have  $$ b_1c_{n-1}+b_2c_{n-2}+\cdots+b_{n-1}c_1\leq\frac{a_1}{a_2}+\frac{a_2}{a_3}+\cdots+\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n} $$  On the other hand, it is not difficult to see that  $k\leq b_k$  and  $\frac{1}{n-k+1}\leq c_k$  for all  $k\in\{1,2,\ldots,n-1\}$ , then  $$ \frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3}+\cdots+\frac{n-1}{n}\leq b_1c_{n-1}+b_2c_{n-2}+\cdots+b_{n-1}c_1 $$  Hence we conclude that  $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3}+\cdots+\frac{n-1}{n}\leq\frac{a_1}{a_2}+\frac{a_2}{a_3}+\cdots+\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_n}$ .

stem_md: For any permutation  $p$  of set  $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ , define  $d(p) = |p(1) - 1| + |p(2) - 2| + \ldots + |p(n) - n|$ . Denoted by  $i(p)$  the number of integer pairs  $(i, j)$  in permutation  $p$  such that  $1 \leqq < j \leq n$  and  $p(i) > p(j)$ . Find all the real numbers  $c$ , such that the inequality  $i(p) \leq c \cdot d(p)$  holds for any positive integer  $n$  and any permutation  $p.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Remark</summary>This proof got WAY longer than I thought it would. The reasoning moved rather quickly when I was drawing pictures, but it seems to drag on with words. Sorry...</details>

Let me re-state the problem, hopefully making it a bit more digestable and correcting what I imagine was a typo: For any permutation  $p$  of set  $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ , let us define  $d(p)$  and  $i(p)$  as follows.  $d(p) = |p(1) - 1| + |p(2) - 2| + \ldots + |p(n) - n|$  and  $i(p)$  is the number of integer pairs  $(i, j)$  such that  $i<j$  and  $p(i) > p(j)$ . Find the least upper bound for  $i(p)/d(p)$ , over all <u>non-identity</u> permutations over all  $n$ . 

Vision: I will be imagining a permutation as two columns, each with the numbers  $1$  to  $n$  in that order from top to bottom, with arrows pointing from elements of the first column to elements of the second column so as to create a bijection. Note that the quantity  $i(p)$  simply counts the number of intersections between arrows.

We will prove that, for a permutation of  $n>1$  elements, the maximum value of  $i(p)/d(p)$  is  $(2n-3)/(2n-2)$ . It can easily be verified that the permutation  $p = (1 \;n)$  gives this ratio, so clearly this is attainable for any  $n$ . Notice that this increases with  $n$ , and approaches 1. From this it will follow that the least upper bound for  $i(p)/d(p)$  is  $1$ .

<details><summary>Key Fact</summary>The following fact will come in handy. Imagine there are two portions of the permutation, say  $p_1$  and  $p_2$  that each contribute to the values of  $i(p)$  and  $d(p)$  in some predictable way, so that  $i(p) = i(p_1) + i(p_2)$  and  $d(p) = d(p_1) + d(p_2)$ . It is not hard to verify that the overall  $i(p):d(p)$  ratio is at most the maximum of the component ratios  $i(p_1):d(p_1)$  and  $i(p_2):d(p_2)$ .</details>

-----
Observation: Consider two arrows, say  $x: a_1 \to b_1$  and  $y: a_2 \to b_2$ . When we "swap" the two arrows, what we mean is that resulting arrows are  $x: a_1 \to b_2$  and  $y: a_2 \to b_1$ . We say that the two arrows have the "swapping property" if   $(1) \;a_1 < a_2 \leq b_1 < b_2$ , or  $(2)$  the same holds with the inequalities reversed. The motivation for this property is:  $(1)$  the arrows are non-intersecting,  $(2)$  they point in the same direction, and  $(3)$  when we swap them, neither changes direction. As a consequence, when we swap the two arrows,  $(1)$  the value of  $d(p)$  is invariant, and  $(2)$  the value of  $i(p)$  increases. 

<details><summary>Justification for (1)</summary>It becomes apparent when you draw it out. The swapping property ensures the direction of each arrow never changes from upwards to downwards or vice versa. Meanwhile, the change in  $d(p)$  caused by the change of  $x$  is equal and opposite to that caused by the change in of  $y$ .</details>

<details><summary>Justification for (2)</summary>Let us consider what happens to  $i(p)$ . First note that one intersection was added (between  $x$  and  $y$ , which used to be non-intersecting). For any other arrow  $z$ , we consider how the number of intersections between  $x$ ,  $y$ , and  $z$  changes. Notice that it is invariant, unless  $z$  lies strictly between the  $x$  and  $y$ , in which case, it creates an additional two intersections.</details>

Important takeaway: when we swap two arrows with the swapping property, the value of  $i(p)/d(p)$  necessarily increases.
-----
We use induction on  $n$  to prove that, for a permutation of  $n>1$  elements, the maximum value of  $i(p)/d(p)$  is  $(2n-3)/(2n-2)$ , as given by the permutation  $p = (1\;n)$ . This is obvious for  $n=2$ . 

Suppose  $p$  is a permutation on  $n$  elements which maximizes  $i(p)/d(p)$ . 

Claim 1: If  $m \geq p(n)$ , then  $p(m) \geq p(n)$ . 
Claim 2: if  $m \leq p(1)$  then  $p(m) \leq p(1)$ . 

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Claim 1: If  $m=n$  it is clearly true. Otherwise, assume we have some other  $m$  so that  $m \geq p(n)$  but  $p(m) < p(n)$ . Then the two arrows  $n\to p(n)$  and  $m\to p(m)$  have the swapping property, and swapping them necessarily increases  $i(p)/d(p)$ , which contradicts the assumption that  $p$  maximized this quantity.  Claim 2 is analagous.</details>

Let us take the Claim 1. This would implies the permutation can be partitioned into two independent components. The part  $p_1$  with order  $n_1$  acts on  $\{1, 2, \dots p(n) -1\}$  and the part  $p_2$  with order  $n_2$  acts on  $\{p(n) \dots n\}$ . 

Claim 3:  $p(n) =1$  

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Assume it doesn't. Then these two components are both non-empty, and smaller than  $p$  itself. They contribute to the  $i:d$  ratio independently, so we use the Key Fact. According to the inductive hypothesis, the maximum ratios they can contribute are  $(2n_1-3):(2n_1-2)$  and  $(2n_2-3):(2n_2-2)$ , respectively (it is also possible that at most one is the identity permutation, in which case it contributes  $0:0$ ). Either way,  $n_1$  and  $n_2$  are both smaller than  $n$ , and the cumulative  $i:d$  ratio must be smaller than  $(2n-3):(2n-2)$ . But we know a ratio of  $(2n-3):(2n-2)$  is attainable on a permutation of order  $n$ , so clearly  $p$  doesn't maximize the  $i:d$  ratio, which is a contradiction, as required.</details>

Claim 4:  $p(1) = n$ <details><summary>Proof</summary>Assume the opposite. If  $p(1) \neq n$ , then, according to Claim 2, we have all the elements  $\{1, 2, \dots p(1)\}$  being mapped to the elements  $\{2, \dots p(1)\}$ . The element  $1$  has already been taken since  $p(n) = 1$ , according to Claim 3. This is an impossibility.</details>

Claim 5: The permutation  $p$  is the identity on the elements  $\{2,  \dots n-1\}$ <details><summary>Proof</summary>Again use the Key Fact. We think about how the arrows  $x: p(1) \to n$  and  $y: p(n) \to 1$  contribute to  $i:d$  ratio. They necessarily contribute with the ratio  $(2n-3):(2n-2)$ . The rest of the permutation, ignoring  $x$  and  $y$  is a permutation on fewer than  $n$  elements, which cannot, according to the inductive hypothesis, attain this high of an  $i:d$  ratio. Hence, in order to maximize the overall ratio, we are forced to conclude that it contributes a ratio of  $0:0$  which makes it the identity permutation.</details>

It follows that the permutation  $ p = (1 \; n) $  gives the maximum value of  $i(p)/d(p) = (2n-3)/(2n-2)$ , which has least upper bound  $1$ .

candidates:
Let me also propose the most natural follow-up question: Find the greatest lower bound for the quantity  $i(p)/d(p)$ , over all non-identity permutations over all  $n$ . I claim it is  $1/2$ . First, to see that this is attainable, imagine a permutation  $p$  on  $n$  elements, for any  $n$ , such that  $p=(1 \; 2)$ . 

Definition 1: Let us say that a permutation is "special" if any two intersecting arrows point in opposite directions. <details><summary>Note</summary>By "direction," here I mean either up, down, or horizontal. We define horizontal to be the same as either up or down, and opposite to neither</details>

Say  $\pi$  is a special permutation of order  $n$ . We make a series of claims. Claim 4 is an arrival point, and points quickly to the finish line.

Claim 1: If y is an arrow  $m \to \pi(m)$  where  $\pi(m) > \pi(n)$ , then  $y$  is downwards pointing.
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Consider the arrow  $x: n \to \pi(n)$ . Clearly  $y$  must intersect  $x$ . But  $x$  points upwards. Since  $\pi$  is special,  $y$  must point downwards.</details>

Claim 2: Consider the following set,  $S(\pi)$ , of arrows:  $\{m \to \pi(m) \; | \; \pi(m) > \pi(n)\}$ . Then  $(1)$  these are precisely the arrows that intersect with  $n \to \pi(n)$ ,  $(2)$  there are  $n-\pi(n)$  of them, and  $(3)$  no two of them intersect each other, 
<details><summary>Proof</summary>$(1)$  They are precisely the arrows which originate from less than  $n$  and map to greater than  $\pi(n)$ . (2) This is the number of arrows that map to  $\{\pi(n) + 1 \dots n\}$ .  $(3)$  Claim 1 says they all point downwards. If any intersected,  $\pi$  wouldn't be special.</details>

Claim 3: If some arrow of the form  $x: k \to k+1$  exists in  $S(\pi)$ , then for all  $t \in \{k, k+1, \dots, n-1\}$ , the arrow  $t \to t+1$  is in  $S(\pi)$ . 
<details><summary>Proof</summary>No arrow originating from a value less than  $k$  can map to a value greater than  $k+1$ , since it would point in the same direction as  $x$  and intersect it. Hence we have a bijection between  $\{k, k+1, \dots, n-1\}$  and  $\{k+1, k+2, \dots, n\}$  which consists of arrows from  $S(\pi)$ , by definition of the set. They must not intersect, by Claim 2. Hence they all point downward by one.</details>

***Claim 4: The arrow  $a \to \pi(a)$  makes exactly  $|\pi(a)-(a)|$  intersections.
<details><summary>Proof</summary>We prove using an inductive method. Say we have a special permutation on  $n$  elements. We will perform some actions, and show that it is still special at every step. 

First, remove  $n$ ,  $\pi(n)$  and the arrow  $n \to \pi(n)$ . We only *removed* intersections, so it must still be special. 

Then, take all the arrows  $m \to \pi(m)$  in  $S(\pi)$ , and shift the endpoints of the arrows,  $p(m)$ , upwards by one, so as to fill the gap left by removing  $p(n)$ .  $\pi$  must still be special. 

Why? No intersections were created or destroyed in doing so. If the permutation is suddenly not special, it is because some arrows changed direction and caused some intersecting arrows to now point in the same direction. But the only arrows which changed were those in  $S(\pi)$ . These all originally pointed downward, and had their endpoints shifted up by one unit. So, if an arrow  $x \in S(\pi)$  changed direction,  $x$  must have gone from pointing downwards by one unit, to being horizontal. So if the permutation is not special, it must be caused by an intersection with the now horizontal arrow  $x$  in  $S(\pi)$ . But Claim 3 implies that all arrows below  $x$  would also have to be horizontal after this transformation, which means that  $x$  cannot have any intersections. Hence  $\pi$  must still be special.

The result is that  $\pi$  is now a special permutation of order  $n-1$ , so we apply the inductive hypothesis which says that the arrow  $a \to \pi(a)$  makes exactly  $|\pi(a)-(a)|$  intersections. What happens when we transform back to the original permutation? Take any arrow  $x \in S(\pi)$ . It is currently not pointing upward. As we transform back, the endpoint will shift down by one, causing  $|\pi(a)-(a)|$  to increase by one. Meanwhile, one intersection, the one with  $n \to \pi(n)$ , will be added. So for these arrows, Claim 4 is preserved. The arrow  $n \to \pi(n)$  now has  $n-\pi(n)$  intersections, one for each arrow in  $S(\pi)$ , according to Claim 2, so Claim 4 is preserved for this arrow as well. All other arrows are left unaffected. Hence, by inductive reasoning, Claim 4 applies to all special permutations.</details>

Claim 5:  $i(\pi) = 1/2 \times d(\pi)$ . 
<details><summary>Proof</summary>If we go through each arrow, and count the intersections it makes, then the total count, according to Claim 4, will be precisely the quantity  $d(\pi)$ . However, each intersection got counted twice. Hence the actual number of intersections between arrows, given by  $i(\pi)$ , must be half this amount.  $\Rightarrow i(\pi) = 1/2 \times d(\pi)$ .</details>

Claim 6: If  $p$  is a non-identity permutation on  $n$  elements which minimizes  $i(p)/d(p)$ , then  $p$  is special.
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Imagine it is not, so there exist two intersecting arrows that point in the same direction. Then, we can swap them. As a result, neither changes direction,  $d(p)$  is invariant, and  $i(p)$  necessarily decreases. Overall, the quantity  $i(p)/d(p)$  decreases contradicting the assumption that it was being minimized. Hence, the claim must be true.</details>

Conclusion: If  $p$  is a non-identity permutation on  $n$  elements which minimizes  $i(p)/d(p)$ , then  $i(p)/d(p)$  is  $1/2$ .

Over this post and the last one, we see that  $\displaystyle \frac{1}{2} \leq \frac{i(p)}{d(p)} < 1$  over all non-identity permutation, over all  $n$ . Moreover, this is the smallest interval that contains this ratio.

stem_md: $AB, AC$  are two chords of the circle centered at  $O$ . The diameter, which is perpendicular to  $BC$ , intersects  $AB, AC$  at  $F, G$  respectively ( $F$  is in the circle). The tangent from  $G$  tangents the circle at  $T$ . Prove that  $F$  is the projection of  $T$  on  $OG. $

stem_md: Given a triangle  $ ABC$ . Let  $ G$ ,  $ I$ ,  $ H$  be the centroid, the incenter and the orthocenter of triangle  $ ABC$ , respectively. Prove that  $ \angle GIH > 90^{\circ}$ .
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Note that  $\overrightarrow{IG}\cdot\overrightarrow{IH}=|\overrightarrow{IG}|\cdot|\overrightarrow{IH}|\cdot\cos{\angle{GIH}}.$  Thus, if  $\angle{GIH}>90^{\circ},$  then  $\cos{\angle{GIH}}<0,$  which means that  $\overrightarrow{IG}\cdot\overrightarrow{IH}<0.$  Now,   $$ \overrightarrow{IG}\cdot\overrightarrow{IH}=(\overrightarrow{G}-\overrightarrow{I})(\overrightarrow{H}-\overrightarrow{I})=\overrightarrow{G}\cdot\overrightarrow{H}-\overrightarrow{I}\cdot(\overrightarrow{H}+\overrightarrow{G})+\overrightarrow{I}\cdot\overrightarrow{I}. $$   Let the circumcenter of triangle  $ABC$  be the origin. This means that  $\overrightarrow{G}=\frac{\overrightarrow{A}+\overrightarrow{B}+\overrightarrow{C}}{3},\overrightarrow{H}=\overrightarrow{A}+\overrightarrow{B}+\overrightarrow{C},$  and  $\overrightarrow{I}=\frac{a\cdot\overrightarrow{A}+b\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+c\cdot\overrightarrow{C}}{a+b+c}.$  Setting the circumradius to  $R,$  we find that   $$ \overrightarrow{G}\cdot\overrightarrow{H}=\left(\frac{\overrightarrow{A}+\overrightarrow{B}+\overrightarrow{C}}{3}\right)\cdot(\overrightarrow{A}+\overrightarrow{B}+\overrightarrow{C})= $$    $$ \frac{1}{3}\left(\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{A}+\overrightarrow{B}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+\overrightarrow{C}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}+2\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+2\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}+2\overrightarrow{B}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}\right)= $$    $$ \frac{1}{3}\left(3R^2+2R^2\left(\frac{2R^2-a^2}{2R^2}+\frac{2R^2-b^2}{2R^2}+\frac{2R^2-c^2}{2R^2}\right)\right)= $$    $$ \frac{1}{3}\left(9R^2-(a^2+b^2+c^2)\right). $$   Also,   $$ \overrightarrow{I}\cdot(\overrightarrow{H}+\overrightarrow{G})=\frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{a\cdot\overrightarrow{A}+b\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+c\cdot\overrightarrow{C}}{a+b+c}\right)\cdot(\overrightarrow{A}+\overrightarrow{B}+\overrightarrow{C})= $$    $$ \frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{a\cdot\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{A}+b\cdot\overrightarrow{B}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+c\cdot\overrightarrow{C}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}+(a+b)\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+(a+c)\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}+(b+c)\overrightarrow{B}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}}{a+b+c}\right)= $$    $$ \frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{(a+b+c)R^2+R^2\left((a+b)\left(\frac{2R^2-c^2}{2R^2}\right)+(a+c)\left(\frac{2R^2-b^2}{2R^2}\right)+(b+c)\left(\frac{2R^2-a^2}{2R^2}\right)\right)}{a+b+c}\right)= $$    $$ \frac{4}{3}\left(3R^2-\frac{a^2b+ab^2+ac^2+a^2c+b^2c+bc^2}{2(a+b+c)}\right). $$   In addition,   $$ \overrightarrow{I}\cdot\overrightarrow{I}=\left(\frac{a\cdot\overrightarrow{A}+b\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+c\cdot\overrightarrow{C}}{a+b+c}\right)\left(\frac{a\cdot\overrightarrow{A}+b\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+c\cdot\overrightarrow{C}}{a+b+c}\right)= $$    $$ \frac{a^2\cdot\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{A}+b^2\cdot\overrightarrow{B}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+c^2\cdot\overrightarrow{C}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}+2ab\cdot\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}+2ac\cdot\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}+2bc\cdot\overrightarrow{B}\cdot\overrightarrow{C}}{(a+b+c)^2}= $$    $$ \frac{R^2(a^2+b^2+c^2)+2R^2\left(ab\cdot\frac{2R^2-c^2}{2R^2}+ac\cdot\frac{2R^2-b^2}{2R^2}+bc\cdot\frac{2R^2-a^2}{2R^2}\right)}{(a+b+c)^2}= $$    $$ \frac{R^2(a^2+b^2+c^2+2ab+2ac+2bc)-(abc^2+ab^2c+a^2bc)}{(a+b+c)^2}= $$    $$ R^2-\frac{abc}{a+b+c}. $$   This means that   $$ \overrightarrow{IG}\cdot\overrightarrow{IH}=(\overrightarrow{G}-\overrightarrow{I})(\overrightarrow{H}-\overrightarrow{I})=\overrightarrow{G}\cdot\overrightarrow{H}-\overrightarrow{I}\cdot(\overrightarrow{H}+\overrightarrow{G})+\overrightarrow{I}\cdot\overrightarrow{I}= $$    $$ \frac{1}{3}(9R^2-(a^2+b^2+c^2))-\frac{4}{3}\left(3R^2-\frac{a^2b+ab^2+ac^2+a^2c+b^2c+bc^2}{2(a+b+c)}\right)+\left(R^2-\frac{abc}{a+b+c}\right)= $$    $$ -\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{3}+\frac{2(a^2b+ab^2+ac^2+a^2c+b^2c+bc^2)}{3(a+b+c)}-\frac{abc}{a+b+c}= $$    $$ -\frac{a^3+b^3+c^3+3abc-a^2b-ab^2-a^2c-ac^2-b^2c-bc^2}{3(a+b+c)}. $$   From Schur's inequality,   $$ a^3+b^3+c^3+3abc-a^2b-ab^2-a^2c-ac^2-b^2c-bc^2>0. $$   Now, since  $a,b,c$  are the sidelengths of a triangle,  $a,b,c>0\Leftrightarrow3(a+b+c)>0.$  Thus,   $$ -\frac{a^3+b^3+c^3+3abc-a^2b-ab^2-a^2c-ac^2-b^2c-bc^2}{3(a+b+c)}<0, $$   which implies that  $\angle{GIH}>90^{\circ},$  as desired.</details>

Thus,  $ BC \equal{} CA$ .

stem_md: The integer  $ 9$  can be written as a sum of two consecutive integers:  $ 9 \equal{} 4\plus{}5.$  Moreover, it can be written as a sum of (more than one) consecutive positive integers in exactly two ways:  $ 9 \equal{} 4\plus{}5 \equal{} 2\plus{}3\plus{}4.$  Is there an integer that can be written as a sum of  $ 1990$  consecutive integers and that can be written as a sum of (more than one) consecutive positive integers in exactly  $ 1990$  ways?
solution_md:
Yes.
From  $n=(x+1)+\dots+(x+1990)=1990x+1989\cdot 995$  we get  $n$  - odd and  $n$  is a multiple of  $995$ .
Suppose  $n=(x_{i}+1)+\dots+(x_{i}+k_{i})$ , for  $i=\overline{1,1990}$  and one of the  $k_{i}$ 's is 1990. Also  $k_{i}>1$ .
Then  $2n=k_{i}(2x_{i}+k_{i}+1)$ . For any  $k_{i}|n$ ,  $k_{i}<\sqrt{n}$  there is an integer  $x_{i}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{n}{d}-k_{i}-1\right)$ .
So  $2n$  has exactly  $1990$  divisors which are  $>1$  and  $<\sqrt{n}$ , which means that  $2n$  has  $2\cdot1991=2\cdot11\cdot181$  divisors.
Since  $2n$  has already  $3$  prime divisors:  $2,5,199$  we conclude that these are the only prime divisors of  $2n$ . Now since  $n$  is odd, it is clear that  $n$  must be  $5^{10}\cdot199^{180}$  or  $5^{180}\cdot199^{10}$ . So, such  $n$  exists, but these are the only values  $n$  can take.

By the first condition we get  $n=x+(x+1)+\cdots+(x+1989)=995(2x+1989) \Rightarrow 5\mid n,199 \mid n$  and  $n$  is odd.

By the second condition there exists  $1990$  pairs of  $(j,k)$  such that  $n=j+(j+1)+\cdots+(j+k)$ ,or  $2n=(k+1)(k+2j)$ .It is also easy to see that  $k+1<k+2j$  so  $\frac{d(2n)}{2}-1=1990 \Rightarrow d(2n)=3982$ .Now it is natural to set  $2n=2\times 199^{y_1} \times 5^{y_2} \times {p_1}^{y_3} \times \cdots {p_m}^{y_m}$ .Then  $3982=2\times 11\times 181=d(2n)=2(y_1+1)(y_2+1)\cdots(y_m+1)$ .We also know that  $y_1,y_2 \ge 1$ .This forces us to conclude that either  $y_1+1=11,y_2+1=181$  or  $y_1+1=181,y_2+1=11$  and the rest  $y_i=0$ Thus  $(y_1,y_2)=(10,180),(180,10)$  and the numbers  $5^{180}\times199^{10}$  and  $5^{10}\times199^{180}$  satisfy our conditions.So the answer to the problem is:Oh,Yes!

Proof (sketch):

The first condition implies  $n \equiv 995$  (mod 1990). So 5 and 199 appear in  $n$ 's prime factorization. Also note that n has to be odd.

If n can be decomposed into an even number 2k, then  $n \equiv k$  (mod 2k). If n can be decomposed into an odd number, d, of consecutive integers, then d  $\mid$  n. We can combine these two statements to get an iff for the number of numbers in which odd n can be decomposed: All divisors of 2n work.

Also note that  $\sqrt{2n}$  provides the upper bound of divisors. This is convenient, since it just divides the divisors of 2n by 2.

So we just need an n that prime factors 5 and 199 with 1991 divisors. This gives us the two solutions  $5^{10} * 199^{180}$  and  $5^{180} * 199^{10}$ .

stem_md: Let S be a 1990-element set and P be a set of 100-ary sequences  $(a_1,a_2,...,a_{100})$  ,where  $a_i's$  are distinct elements of S.An ordered pair (x,y) of elements of S is said to *appear* in  $(a_1,a_2,...,a_{100})$  if  $x=a_i$  and  $y=a_j$  for some i,j with  $1\leq i<j\leq 100$ .Assume that every ordered pair (x,y) of elements of S appears in at most one member in P.Show that  $|P|\leq 800$ .
solution_md:
Any 100-aray sequence  $(a_1;a_2;...;a_{100})$  has exactly  ${100\choose 2}$  pair  $(a_i;a_j)$  with  $1\le i<j\le 100$ 

But any two 100-ary sequences  $(a_1;a_2;...;a_{100}) ;(b_1;...;b_{100})$  we have  $(a_i;a_j)\neq (b_k;b_l)$   $\forall 1\le i<j\le 100; 1\le k,l\le 100.$  ( because any pair  $(x;y)$  appears in at most one member in S).

Therefore: let m be the number of members of P, we have: $m{100\choose 2}\le 2.{1990\choose 2}$ .  $\Rightarrow$   $m \frac{100.99}{2}\le 2\frac{1990.1989}{2}$ .Thus,  $m\le 800$ .

stem_md: Assume that the set of all positive integers is decomposed into  $ r$  (disjoint) subsets  $ A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \ldots \cup A_r \equal{} \mathbb{N}.$  Prove that one of them, say  $ A_i,$  has the following property: There exists a positive  $ m$  such that for any  $ k$  one can find numbers  $ a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$  in  $ A_i$  with  $ 0 < a_{j \plus{} 1} \minus{} a_j \leq m,$   $ (1 \leq j \leq k \minus{} 1)$ .
solution_md:
Call a sequence of  $n$  consecutive integers an  $n$ -string. Call a subset  $A_i$  *bad* if it does not satisfy the property: namely, that for any  $m$ , there exists a  $k$ , such that in any  $k$  sequential elements of  $A_i$ , at least one adjacent pair differs by more than  $m$ . You can verify the following consequence: for any  $m$ , there exists a  $p$  (namely  $p=mk$ ) such that any  $p$ -string contains an  $m$ -string with no elements from  $A_i$ . 

Now assume all  $A_2$  through  $A_r$  are bad. We claim  $A_1$  is good: namely, we prove that for any  $k$ , we can find a  $k$ -string contained in  $A_1$  (the case where  $m=1$  ). 

Given any  $k$ , define the numbers  $p_1,p_2, ... p_r$  as follows:  $p_1=k$ , and for  $i>1$ ,  $p_i$  is the number such that any  $p_i$ -string contains a  $p_{i-1}$ -string with no elements from  $A_i$ . The existence of these numbers is ensured by: (1) the existence of  $p_1$ , (2) the badness of  $A_2$  through  $A_r$ , and (3) the consequence of badness described earlier. 

It follows that any  $p_r$ -string contains a  $p_{r-1}$ -string with no elements from  $A_{r}$ , and this string contains a  $p_{r-2}$ -string with no elements from  $A_{r-1}$  or  $A_r$ , and this string contains ... etc. .... and this string contains a  $p_1$ -string with no elements from any of  $A_2$  through  $A_r$ .
