Call a set  $A \subset {\mathbb N}$  *good* if it has the desired property, i.e. there is an  $m$  such that for every  $k$  there are  $a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{k} \in A$  s.t.  $0<a_{i+1}-a_{i} \leq m$ , for  $i=1,2,...,k-1$ . Call a sequence  $x$ -bounded if it is strictly increasing and the difference between any two consecutive numbers is at most  $x$ .
**Lemma**. I'll prove that if  $A,B \subset {\mathbb N}$  such that  $A \cap B =\emptyset$  and  $A \cup B$  is good, then at least one of  $A$  and  $B$  is good. 

For any  $k$ , take an  $m$ -bounded sequnce  $c_{1},c_{2},...,c_{k} \in A \cup B$  and let  $l_{k}$  be the largest number for which there is a  $j$  such that all  $c_{j}$ ,  $c_{j+1}$ , ...,  $c_{j+l_{k}-1}$  belong to the same set ( $A$  or  $B$ ). If the sequence  $l_{k}$  is unbounded, then we are done, so suppose it is bounded and take  $L>l_{k},\forall k$ . In any sequence  $m$ -bounded sequence from  $A \cup B$ , the two subsequences formed from numbers belonging to the same set are  $(L+1)m$ -bounded, so at least one set must contain arbitrarily long  $(L+1)m$ -bounded sequences.

Back to the problem, let  $A_{1} \cup A_{2} \cup ... \cup A_{n}$  be a partition of the set of positive integers. If  $A_{1}$  is not good, then  $A_{2} \cup A_{3} \cup ... \cup A_{n}$  is good. If  $A_{2}$  is not good, then  $A_{3} \cup ... \cup A_{n}$  is good etc. In the end, you get that if  $A_{n-1}$  is not good, then  $A_{n}$  is good.

Solution by [Severius](http://www.mathlinks.ro/profile.php?mode=viewprofile&u=6798):

For  $ r \equal{} 2$ , if some subset contains arbitrarily long blocks of consecutive numbers, we're done with  $ m \equal{} 1$ . Otherwise they have maximal block lengths  $ M_1, M_2$ , so that any block of consecutive numbers in the same subset is of length at most  $ M$  for some fixed  $ M$ , and any two consecutive elements of a subset differ by no more than  $ M \plus{} 1$ . So we're done with  $ m \equal{} M \plus{} 1$ .

Now suppose the problem is true for  $ r$ , and take it for  $ r \plus{} 1$ . Among the  $ r \plus{} 1$  subsets, imagine that two of them are the same and apply the induction hypothesis. If the resulting good subset is one of the singles, we're done; otherwise, it must be the "double" subset, say, the union of  $ A$  and  $ B$ . For each  $ k$  we take a sequence  $ a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_k$  contained in  $ A \cup B$  and with  $ \minus{} m \leq a_{i \plus{} 1} \minus{} a_i \leq m$ , and we consider the collection of these sequences. If among them there are arbitrarily long subsequences of consecutive elements  $ a_{i \plus{} 1}, a_{i \plus{} 2}, ..., a_{i \plus{} d}$  in the same subset, we're done. Otherwise, as above, the maximal length of such a block is bounded by some fixed  $ M$ , and in a sequence  $ a_1 < a_2 < ... < a_k$ , for any element  $ a_i$ , the smallest  $ j > i$  such that  $ a_j$  is in the same subset as  $ a_i$  satisfies  $ j \leq i \plus{} M \plus{} 1$ , so it is easy to see that we are done.

stem_md: Prove that  $\frac{5^{125}-1}{5^{25}-1}$  is a composite number.
solution_md:
Let  $ x\equal{}5^{25}$  , then 

 $ 5^{125}\minus{}1$ 
 $ \equal{}x^{5}\minus{}1$ 
 $ \equal{}(x\minus{}1)(x^{4}\plus{}x^{3}\plus{}x^{2}\plus{}x\plus{}1)$ 
 $ \equal{}(x^{4}\plus{}9x^{2}\plus{}1\plus{}6x^{3}\plus{}6x\plus{}2x^{2}\minus{}5x^{3}\minus{}10x^{2}\minus{}5x)(x\minus{}1)$ 
 $ \equal{}((x^{2}\plus{}3x\plus{}1)^{2}\minus{}5x(x\plus{}1)^{2})(x\minus{}1)$ 
 $ \equal{}((x^{2}\plus{}3x\plus{}1)^{2}\minus{}(5^{13}(x\plus{}1)^{2})(x\minus{}1)$ 
 $ \equal{}(x^{2}\plus{}3x\plus{}1\plus{}5^{13}(x\plus{}1))(x^{2}\plus{}3x\plus{}1\minus{}5^{13}(x\plus{}1))(x\minus{}1)$ 



Which implies that  $ \frac {5^{125} \minus{} 1}{5^{25} \minus{} 1}$  is a composite number!

Two circles  $ \Omega_{1}$  and  $ \Omega_{2}$  are externally tangent to each other at a point  $ I$ , and both of these circles are tangent to a third circle  $ \Omega$  which encloses the two circles  $ \Omega_{1}$  and  $ \Omega_{2}$ .
The common tangent to the two circles  $ \Omega_{1}$  and  $ \Omega_{2}$  at the point  $ I$  meets the circle  $ \Omega$  at a point  $ A$ . One common tangent to the circles  $ \Omega_{1}$  and  $ \Omega_{2}$  which doesn't pass through  $ I$  meets the circle  $ \Omega$  at the points  $ B$  and  $ C$  such that the points  $ A$  and  $ I$  lie on the same side of the line  $ BC$ .
Prove that the point  $ I$  is the incenter of triangle  $ ABC$ .

*Alternative formulation.* Two circles touch externally at a point  $ I$ . The two circles lie inside a large circle and both touch it. The chord  $ BC$  of the large circle touches both smaller circles (not at  $ I$ ). The common tangent to the two smaller circles at the point  $ I$  meets the large circle at a point  $ A$ , where the points  $ A$  and  $ I$  are on the same side of the chord  $ BC$ . Show that the point  $ I$  is the incenter of triangle  $ ABC$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The following lemma solves the problem.**Lemma 1:** In triangle  $ABC$ ,  $D$  is an arbitrary point on segment  $BC$ . Circle  $\omega$  is tangent to  $(ABC)$  and segments  $BD$ ,  $AD$  at  $X$ ,  $E$ ,  $F$ . Show that the incenter of triangle  $ABC$  lies on line  $EF$ .**Proof:** Let  $Z\not\equiv A$  be the second intersection of line  $AD$  with  $(ABC)$ . Furthermore, let  $M$ ,  $Y$  be the midpoints of arcs  $BC$ ,  $ZA$ . Finally, let  $I=AM\cap EF$ . It suffices to show that  $I$  is the incenter of triangle  $ABC$ , or equivalently, that  $MI=MB$ .

Since the tangent to  $(ABC)$  at  $Y$  is parallel to the tangent to  $\omega$  at  $F$ , it follows that the homothety centered at  $X$  that sends  $\omega$  to  $(ABC)$  also sends  $F$  to  $Y$ , i.e.  $Y\in XF$ . Similarly,  $M\in XE$ . Now since  $\angle MBC=\angle MXC=\angle MXB$ , it follows that  $MB$  is tangent to  $(BEX)$ , whence  $ME\cdot MX=MB^2$ . Similarly,  $YF\cdot YX=YA^2$ . Dividing yields  $\dfrac{ME}{YF}\cdot\dfrac{MX}{YX}=\dfrac{MB^2}{YA^2}$ . Since  $\triangle XEF\sim\triangle XMY$ , it follows that  $\dfrac{ME}{YF}=\dfrac{MX}{YX}$ . Therefore,  $\dfrac{MX^2}{YX^2}=\dfrac{MB^2}{YA^2}$ , which rearranges as  $\dfrac{MX}{MB}=\dfrac{YX}{YA}$ . From  $ME\cdot MX=MB^2$  we deduce that  $\dfrac{MX}{MB}=\dfrac{MB}{ME}$ . Therefore,  $\dfrac{MB}{ME}=\dfrac{YX}{YA}$ . Angle chasing yields  $\triangle YXA\sim\triangle MIE$ , whence  $\dfrac{YX}{YA}=\dfrac{MI}{ME}$ . It follows that  $\dfrac{MB}{ME}=\dfrac{MI}{ME}$  and consequently  $MB=MI$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Let  $D$ ,  $E$  be the tangency points of  $\Omega_1$ ,  $\Omega_2$  with  $BC$ . By Lemma  $1$ ,  $I=DI\cap EI$  is the incenter of triangle  $ABC$ .  $\blacksquare$</details>

Consider the inversion with pole  $I$  which invariates  $\Omega$ . We can see that  $\omega$  is a ircle passing through  $I$  and tangent to  $d_1,d_2$ , so its radius is the same as that of  $\Omega$ . We have  $\{B',C'\}=\omega\cap \Omega$ . I think it's pretty clear now why  $A$  is the symmetric of  $I$  wrt  $B'C'$ , so  $A'=$  the other point of intersection of  $IA,\Omega$  is the orthocenter of  $IB'C'$  (or equivalently,  $I$  is the orthocenter of  $A'B'C'$ , Q.E.D.).

*Solution, second version:* Let's first observe that if I is the incenter of ABC then, by an inversion of pole I, A, B, C have images A', B', C' s.t. I is the orthocenter of A'B'C' and vice-versa (just look at the case of an inversion of pole H and power HA*HD where D is the foot of the height HA: the images of A, B, C are D, E, F, the feet of the heights of ABC and H is the incenter of DEF).

Now, in our original problem, let's consider an inversion of center I and power -k^2 (k is a length; negative means that the image of a point and that point are on opposite sides of I). Our new configuration is this:

*(i)* its side lengths are  $ 1, 2, 3, \ldots, 1992$  in some order;

Nice problem !
My solutionLet $ \{a_i\}_{i\equal{}1}^n$ the $ n$ ordered sides of such a polygon ( $ \{a_i\}$ is a permutation of $ 1,2,...,n$ ). Let R the radius of the circle about which the polygon is circumscribed and $ O$ its center. 1) **This situation is impossible if $ n\equal{}2\pmod 4$ (and so for example for $ n\equal{}1990$ )** : Let $ A_1,...,A_n$ the n vertices ( $ A_{n\plus{}1}\equal{}A_1$ ) with $ A_kA_{k\plus{}1}\equal{}a_k$ . Let $ \Delta_i$ the distance between $ A_i$ and the contact (tangent) between the circle and the side $ A_iA_{i\plus{}1}$ . solution_md:
Let $ f(x)$ be a polynomial with rational coefficients and $ \alpha$ be a real number such that \[ \alpha^3 \minus{} \alpha \equal{} [f(\alpha)]^3 \minus{} f(\alpha) \equal{} 33^{1992}. \] Prove that for each $ n \geq 1,$ \[ \left [ f^{n}(\alpha) \right]^3 \minus{} f^{n}(\alpha) \equal{} 33^{1992}, \] where $ f^{n}(x) \equal{} f(f(\cdots f(x))),$ and $ n$ is a positive integer.
Since the equation $ x^3 \minus{}x \minus{} c \equal{} 0$ has only one real root for every $ c > \frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}$ , $ \alpha$ is the unique real root of $ x^3\minus{}x\minus{}33^{1992} \equal{} 0$ . Hence $ f^n(\alpha) \equal{} f(\alpha) \equal{} \alpha$ ,as desired

stem_md:
Let  $ f, g$  and  $ a$  be polynomials with real coefficients,  $ f$  and  $ g$  in one variable and  $ a$  in two variables. Suppose

\[ f(x) \minus{} f(y) \equal{} a(x, y)(g(x) \minus{} g(y)) \forall x,y \in \mathbb{R}\]

Prove that there exists a polynomial  $ h$  with  $ f(x) \equal{} h(g(x)) \text{ } \forall x \in \mathbb{R}.$
solution_md:
Let $ f, g$ and $ a$ be polynomials with real coefficients, $ f$ and $ g$ in one variable and $ a$ in two variables. Suppose \[ f(x) \minus{} f(y) \equal{} a(x, y)(g(x) \minus{} g(y)) \forall x,y \in \mathbb{R}\] Prove that there exists a polynomial $ h$ with $ f(x) \equal{} h(g(x)) \text{ } \forall x \in \mathbb{R}.$
**Lemma 1**: If $f(x) = x^m$ and $g(x) = x^n$ satisfy the equation, then $m$ must be a power of $n$ . *Proof:* Let $c(x) = b(x,1)$ . We have that $c(x) = \frac{x^m - 1}{x^n - 1}$ for all $x$ , so the polynomial $x^n - 1$ divides the polynomial $x^m - 1$ . Hence, if $\omega$ is a primitive $n$ th root of unity, $\omega^n - 1 = \omega^m - 1 = 0$ , whence $n | m$ . $\blacksquare$ **Lemma 2**: $\deg g$ divides $\deg f$ . *Proof:* Because we may scale $a(x,y)$ , we may suppose without loss of generality that $f$ and $g$ are monic. Let $\deg f = m$ and $\deg g = n$ . Let $b(x,y)$ be the sum of the monomials in $a(x,y)$ with degree $m-n$ . Because the degree of $a(x,y)$ is $m-n$ , the only monomials with degree $m$ that can be obtained by multiplying $a(x,y)$ by $g(x) - g(y)$ are obtained by multiplying $b(x,y)$ with $x^n - y^n$ . Equating the terms with degree $m$ on both sides of the original equation, we find that $x^m - y^m = b(x,y) (x^n - y^n)$ . By lemma 1, it follows that $n$ divides $m$ . $\blacksquare$ For a fixed polynomial $g$ , we perform strong induction on the degree of $f$ . The base case, $\deg f = \deg g$ , is obvious since $a(x,y)$ must be constant. Suppose now that the result is true for all polynomials with degree less than $\deg f$ . By lemma 2, $n \deg g = \deg f$ for some positive integer $n$ . By the division algorithm, we can find some real $k$ and some polynomial $r(x)$ with degree less than $\deg f$ such that $f(x) = k g(x)^n + r(x)$ . Hence, we have $f(x) - f(y) = k(g(x)^n - g(y)^n) - (r(x) - r(y))$ . Because $g(x) - g(y)$ divides $f(x) - f(y)$ and $g(x)^n - g(y)^n$ , it must divide $r(x) - r(y)$ as well, so by the inductive hypothesis $r(x) = h_0(g(x))$ for some polynomial $h_0$ . Setting $h(x) = h_0(x) + kx^n$ , we find that $h(g(x)) = h_0(g(x)) + k g(x)^n = f(x)$ , so we are done.
How is the last "hence" proven?

Here's a solution for part (c). 

Let  $k$  be a sufficiently large positive integer, and  $a > 2^k \cdot 10^{10^{10^{10}}}$  be an even larger positive integer. stem_md:
Let  $ \lfloor x \rfloor$  denote the greatest integer less than or equal to  $ x.$  Pick any  $ x_1$  in  $ [0, 1)$  and define the sequence  $ x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots$  by  $ x_{n\plus{}1} \equal{} 0$  if  $ x_n \equal{} 0$  and  $ x_{n\plus{}1} \equal{} \frac{1}{x_n} \minus{} \left \lfloor \frac{1}{x_n} \right \rfloor$  otherwise. Prove that

\[ x_1 \plus{} x_2 \plus{} \ldots \plus{} x_n < \frac{F_1}{F_2} \plus{} \frac{F_2}{F_3} \plus{} \ldots \plus{} \frac{F_n}{F_{n\plus{}1}},\]

where  $ F_1 \equal{} F_2 \equal{} 1$  and  $ F_{n\plus{}2} \equal{} F_{n\plus{}1} \plus{} F_n$  for  $ n \geq 1.$
solution_md:
Let  $[a_0; a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n, \cdots]$  be the continued fraction representation of  $x_1$ , in other words  $$ x_1 = a_0 + \frac{1}{a_1 + \frac{1}{a_2 + \frac{1}{a_3 + \cdots}}}, $$  where  $a_0 = 0$  and  $a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n > 1.$  

Then, in terms of continued fraction representations, we wish to prove that  $[0; a_1, a_2, \cdots] + [0; a_2, a_3, \cdots] + [0; a_3, a_4, \cdots] + \cdots + [0, a_n, \cdots] < \frac{F_1}{F_2} + \frac{F_2}{F_3} + \cdots + \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}.$  

Since we clearly have  $[0; a_1, a_2, \cdots] < [0; a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n], [0; a_2, a_3, \cdots] < [0; a_2, a_3, \cdots, a_n], \cdots$ , we can just show that  $$ [0;a_1, a_2, \cdots a_n] + [0; a_2, a_3, \cdots, a_n] + \cdots + [0; a_n] \le \frac{F_1}{F_2} + \frac{F_2}{F_3} + \cdots + \frac{F_n}{F_{n+1}}. $$  Observe that the RHS is the same as the LHS when all  $a_i$ 's are one, and so let us just show that the LHS is maximized when all  $a_i$ 's are one. We will prove this via strong induction on  $i$ , with our hypothesis being that  $a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_i$  must all be one in any "maximal" choice of  $a_i$ 's. 

For  $i=1$ , it is immediate, since  $a_1$  has no influence on any of the terms but  $[0; a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n]$  and it's clear that  $a_1 = 1$  maximizes  $[0; a_1, \cdots, a_n].$  

Let's now suppose that it holds for  $i \le t.$  In this way, we have that  $a_1 = a_2 = \cdots = a_t = 1.$  Let us show that  $a_{t+1} = 1$  in any maximal configuration. Clearly,  $a_{t+1}$  is independent of  $[0; a_{t+2}, \cdots, a_n], [0, a_{t+3}, \cdots, a_n], \cdots$ . Hence, we can let  $q = [0; a_{t+2}, \cdots, a_n]$  and pick the optimal  $a_{t+1}$  in these conditions. Viewing this as a function in terms of  $x = a_{t+1}+q$ , the relevant quantity (not including later stuff not influenced by  $a_{t+1}$ ) is precisely:  $$ \frac{1}{x} + \sum_{j=1}^{t} \frac{F_jx + F_{j-1}}{F_{j+1}x + F_j}. $$  We now make the spectacular observation that:  $$ \frac{F_jx + F_{j-1}}{F_{j+1}x + F_j} = \frac{F_j}{F_{j+1}} + \frac{F_{j+1}F_{j-1} - F_j^2}{F_{j+1} (F_{j+1}x + F_j)}, $$  and so hence if we plug this into the expression we actually just need to maximize:  $$ \frac1x + \sum_{j=1}^{t} \frac{(-1)^j}{F_{j+1} (F_{j+1}x + F_j)} = \frac{1}{x(x+1)} + \sum_{j=2}^{t} \frac{(-1)^j}{F_{j+1} (F_{j+1}x + F_j)}. \qquad (1) $$  Keeping in mind that  $x$  is positive, it's obvious that any fraction of the form  $\frac{\alpha}{\beta x^2 + \gamma x + \delta}$  is maximized when  $x$  is minimized, and similarly for fractions of the form  $\frac{\alpha}{\beta x + \gamma}$ . Now, it just remains to partition the sum in  $(1)$  into functions of these form. Indeed,  $\frac{1}{x(x+1)}$  is of this form, and so is  $\frac{1}{F_{j+1}(F_{j+1} x + F_j)} - \frac{1}{F_{j+2} (F_{j+2} x+ F_{j+1})}$  for any  $j$  even. Finally, if  $t$  is even, then we will need a final piece which is  $\frac{1}{F_{t+1} (F_{t+1}x + F_t)},$  which is also maximized as  $x$  is minimized.

In conclusion, it's clear that  $x$  should be minimized to maximize the sum in  $(1)$ , so since  $x = a_{t+1} + q$ , we have that  $a_{t+1} = 1$  in any maximal choice of  $a_i$ 's. The induction is complete. $\square$

stem_md:
For any positive integer  $ x$  define  $ g(x)$  as greatest odd divisor of  $ x,$  and

\[ f(x) \equal{} \begin{cases} \frac {x}{2} \plus{} \frac {x}{g(x)} & \text{if \ \(x\) is even}, 
 2^{\frac {x \plus{} 1}{2}} & \text{if \ \(x\) is odd}. \end{cases}
\]

Construct the sequence  $ x_1 \equal{} 1, x_{n \plus{} 1} \equal{} f(x_n).$  Show that the number 1992 appears in this sequence, determine  the least  $ n$  such that  $ x_n \equal{} 1992,$  and determine whether  $ n$  is unique.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Observation 1:
Say  $ x_n \equal{} (2k\plus{}1)2^p$  where  $ p$  is positive.
Then,  $ x_{n\plus{}1} \equal{} (2k\plus{}1)2^{p\minus{}1} \plus{} 2^p \equal{} (2k\plus{}1)2^{p\minus{}1} \plus{} 2(2^{p\minus{}1}) \equal{} (2k\plus{}3)2^{p\minus{}1}$ Observation 2:
From repeated use of Observation 1, we can see that \[ x_n \equal{} 2^p \implies x_{n\plus{}k} \equal{} (2k\plus{}1)2^{p\minus{}k}\] given  $ p \ge k$ .

Observation 3:
It follows that if there exist  $ n_1$  such that  $ x_{n_1} \equal{} 2^p$ , then there exist  $ n_2 \equal{} n_1\plus{}p$  such that  $ x_{n_2} \equal{} (2p\plus{}1)$ .
Since  $ 2p\plus{}1$  is odd,  $ x_{n_2\plus{}1} \equal{} 2^\frac{2p\plus{}1\plus{}1}{2} \equal{} 2^{p\plus{}1}$ .
Thus \[ x_{n} \equal{} 2^p \implies x_{n\plus{}p\plus{}1} \equal{} 2^{p\plus{}1}\]

Observation 4:
Since  $ x_1 \equal{} 1 \equal{} 2^0$  is in the sequence, it follows  $ 2^p$  is in the sequence for any  $ p$ , which in turn implies  $ (2k\plus{}1)2^{p\minus{}k}$  is in the sequence for any given  $ p \ge k$ .

In fact,  $ 1992 \equal{} (2*124 \plus{} 1)2^{127\minus{}124}$ , so  $ x_1 \equal{} 2^0$  so,  $ x_{1\plus{}(1)\plus{}(2)\plus{}...(127)}\equal{}2^{127}$  so,  $ x_{1\plus{}(1)\plus{}...(127)\plus{}124} \equal{} (2*124 \plus{} 1)2^{127\minus{}124} \equal{} 1992$ It's not hard to see that  $ n \equal{} 1 \plus{} 1... \plus{} 124 \equal{} 8253$  is the smallest and the only value such that  $ x_n \equal{} 1992$</details>

Any comments on correctness or how I could word it better are welcome.

Nice pattern finding problem. The following two claims are the key to the problem:

Claim: For all nonnegative integers  $n,$  we have that  $x_{\frac{n^2+n+2}{2}} = 2^n$ .

Claim: Call a *block* the numbers from  $x_i$  to  $x_k$ , including  $x_i$  and excluding  $x_k,$  such that  $x_i$  and  $x_k$  are the consecutive powers of two of the sequence which have the form given in the first claim. We claim that between two adjacent blocks, the only thing that happens is the numbers in the previous block get multiplied by  $2$ , and there is one extra odd number at the end, which is just the next odd number after the previous odd number in the first block.

Both of these claims are easily provable by induction by just listing out the terms.

From here it is easy to find the index at which 1992 appears, and because 1992 has a unique prime factorization, it is also unique. :)

stem_md:
Let  $a, b, c$  be positive real numbers and  $p, q, r$  complex numbers. Let  $S$  be the set of all solutions  $(x, y, z)$  in  $\mathbb C$  of the system of simultaneous equations
\[ax + by + cz = p,\]\[ax2 + by2 + cz2 = q,\]\[ax3 + bx3 + cx3 = r.\]
Prove that  $S$  has at most six elements.
solution_md:
The thesis follow simply looking the degree of the system: since there are three equation of degree 1,2,3 respectively, we can calculate the degree of the system multiplying the degrees of the three equation, so  $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 6$  , so there are at most 6 triads  $(x;y;z)$  that are solution of the system.
Moreover, we would have to ensure that two equation are equivalent (e.g.  $y= 2x+1$  is the same of  $2y=4x+2$ ) in that case there would be infinitely many solution, but since there aren't two equation of the same degree we can be sure that there isn't a pair of equivalent equations.

stem_md: Let  $m$  be a positive integer and  $x_0, y_0$  integers such that  $x_0, y_0$  are relatively prime,  $y_0$  divides  $x_0^2+m$ , and  $x_0$  divides  $y_0^2+m$ . Prove that there exist positive integers  $x$  and  $y$  such that  $x$  and  $y$  are relatively prime,  $y$  divides  $x^2 + m$ ,  $x$  divides  $y^2 + m$ , and  $x + y \leq m+ 1.$
solution_md:
We have  $x_0y_0$  divide  $x_0^2 + y_0^2 + m$ . Without loss of generality assume that  $x_0<y_0$  (the case  $x_0=y_0=1$  is trivial).
It is easy to see that  $\gcd(x_0,y_0)=1$  implies that  $\gcd(x_0,m)=\gcd(y_0,m)=1$ .

Let  $f(a,b) = \frac{a^2+b^2+m}{ab}$  so that  $f(x_0,y_0)$  is an integer. It is easy to check that  $f(a,b)=f(a,b')$  where  $b' = \frac{a^2+m}{b}.$ Since  $\gcd(b'b,a)=\gcd(a^2+m,a)=\gcd(m,a)=1$ , we have  $\gcd(b',a)=1$ .
Moreover, if  $m < ab - a^2 = a(b-a)$  then  $b'<a$ ; and if  $m < b^2 - a^2 = (b+a)(b-a)$  then  $b'<b$ . Starting with  $b=y_0$  and  $a=x_0$ , we construct a decreasing sequence:
\[y_0 > x_0 > y'_0 > x'_0 > \dots > y > x\]
such that  $f(y_0,x_0) = f(x_0,y'_0) = \dots = f(y,x)$  is the same integer, and the terminal terms are such that  $x(y-x)\leq m$ .
If  $(y+x)(y-x) \leq m$  then  $y+x\leq m$  and we are done.
If  $(y+x)(y-x) > m$  then we further define  $y' = \frac{x^2+m}{y} < y$  and consider two cases:
i) if  $y'=x$  then since  $\gcd(y',x)=1$ , we have  $x=y'=1$  and thus  $x+y'=2\leq m+1$ .
ii) if  $y'>x$  then  $(y'+x)(y'-x)\leq m$  (since other wise we would have  $y<y'$ , a contradiction) and thus  $y'+x \leq m$ .

stem_md: Let  $I,H,O$  be the incenter, centroid, and circumcenter of the nonisosceles triangle  $ABC$ . Prove that  $AI \parallel HO$  if and only if  $\angle BAC =120^{\circ}$ .
solution_md:
Let  $A = a^2, B = b^2, C = c^2$ , and let  $M = -bc$  be the midpoint of arc  $BC$ . Then  $AI \parallel HO$  is equivalent to 
\[
	\frac{a^2 + bc}{a^2+b^2+c^2} \in \mathbb{R} \iff
	(a^2+bc)\overline{(a^2+b^2+c^2)} = \overline{(a^2+b+c)}(a^2+b^2+c^2)
\]
which simplifies as
\[
	a^2\overline{b}^2 + a^2\overline{c}^2 + \overline{a}^2bc = 
	b^2\overline{a}^2 + c^2\overline{a}^2 + a^2\overline{bc} \iff
	a^2 \overline{(b^2 + c^2 - bc)} = 
	\overline{a}^2 (b^2 + c^2 - bc)
\]
Now,  $b^2 + c^2 - bc$  is the reflection of the major arc midpoint  $N$  over line  $BC$ , which has magnitude either  $1$  or  $0$ . The first case implies that  $BC$  is a diameter of the circle, and  $A = H$ , so  $AI \parallel HO$  implies that  $ABC$  is isoceles. As such,  $b^2 + c^2 - bc = 0$ , and thus  $\angle BNC = \angle BOC \implies \angle BNC = 120^\circ$  as desired.

stem_md:
Let  $\phi(n,m), m \neq 1$ , be the number of positive integers less than or equal to  $n$  that are coprime with  $m.$  Clearly,  $\phi(m,m) = \phi(m)$ , where  $\phi(m)$  is Euler’s phi function. Find all integers  $m$  that satisfy the following inequality:
\[\frac{\phi(n,m)}{n} \geq \frac{\phi(m)}{m}\]
for every positive integer  $n.$
solution_md:
The inequality holds for every positive integer  $n$  if and only if  $m$  is a power of a prime.  

For  $m = p^a$  with  $p$  prime and  $a \geq 1$ , it's easy to see that the inequality holds for every positive integer  $n$ , since  $\phi(n,m) = n - \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p} \right \rfloor$ , so that  $\frac{\phi(n,m)}{n} = \frac{n - \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p} \right \rfloor}{n} \geq \frac{n - \frac{n}{p}}{n} = 1 - \frac{1}{p} = \frac{\phi(m)}{m}$ .

Suppose now  $m$  has more than  $1$  distinct prime factors, say  $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_r$  and  $r > 1$ .  

Take  $n = p_1p_2 \cdots p_r - p_1$ .  Then  $\phi(n,m) = \phi(n,p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r) = \phi(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r) - (p_1 - 1)$  because  $p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r - i$  for  $0 < i < p_1$  (that's  $p_1 - 1$  such  $i$ 's) are all relatively prime to  $m$  (or equivalently relatively prime to  $p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r$ ).

Also,  $\frac{\phi(m)}{m} = \frac{\phi(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r)}{p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r}$ , and we have  $\frac{\phi(n,m)}{n} = \frac{\phi(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r) - (p_1 - 1)}{p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r - p_1}$ , so  $\frac{\phi(n,m)}{n} < \frac{\phi(m)}{m}$  follows since this is the inequality  $\frac{\phi(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r) - (p_1 - 1)}{p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r - p_1} < \frac{\phi(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r)}{p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r}$  and this is equivalent to  $-(p_1 - 1)p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r < -p_1 \phi(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r) = -p_1 (p_1 - 1)(p_2 - 1)\cdots(p_r - 1)$ , which is in turn equivalent to $p_2 \cdots p_r > (p_2 - 1)\cdots(p_r - 1)$  and this is clearly true.

stem_md: An *Egyptian number* is a positive integer that can be expressed as a sum of positive integers, not necessarily distinct, such that the sum of their reciprocals is  $1$ . For example,  $32 = 2 + 3 + 9 + 18$  is Egyptian because  $\frac 12 +\frac 13 +\frac 19 +\frac{1}{18}=1$  . Prove that all integers greater than  $23$  are *Egyptian*.
solution_md:
An *Egyptian number* is a positive integer that can be expressed as a sum of positive integers, not necessarily distinct, such that the sum of their reciprocals is $1$ . For example, $32 = 2 + 3 + 9 + 18$ is Egyptian because $\frac 12 +\frac 13 +\frac 19 +\frac{1}{18}=1$ . Prove that all integers greater than $23$ are *Egyptian*.
Let $A$ be the set of egyptian numbers. If $1=\sum\frac 1{a_k}$ , then : $1=\sum\frac 1{2a_k}+\frac 12$ $1=\sum\frac 1{2a_k}+\frac 14+\frac 14$ $1=\sum\frac 1{2a_k}+\frac 13+\frac 16$ $1=\sum\frac 1{3a_k}+\frac 13+\frac 13$ $1=\sum\frac 1{3a_k}+\frac 12+\frac 16$ So $n\in A$ $\implies$ $\{2n+2,2n+8,2n+9,3n+6,3n+8\}\subset A$ $1=\frac 11$ and so $1\in A$ . Applying the five above rules, we get : $\implies$ $\{1,4,9,10,11\}\subset A$ $\implies$ $\{1,4,9,10,11,16,17,18,$ $20,22,24,26,27,28,29,30,$ $31,33,35,36,38,39,41\}\subset A$ $\implies$ $\{1,4,9,10,11,16,17,18,$ $20,22,24,26,27,28,29,30,$ $31,33,34,35,36,38,39,40,41,42,43$ $,44,45,46,48,49,50,52,53,54\}\subset A$ $(5,5,5,5,5)\implies 25\in A$ $(2,3,9,18)\implies 32\in A$ $(4,4,4,5,20)\implies 37\in A$ $(4,4,6,6,9,18)\implies 47\in A$ $(4,4,5,6,12,20)\implies 51\in A$ $(6,6,6,6,6,10,15)\implies 55\in A$ So all positive integers in $[24,55]$ are in $A$ Using then the rules $n\to 2n+8$ and $n\to 2n+9$ , we get that all positive integers in $[24,119]$ are in $A$ And it's then easy to show with induction that any positive integer $>23$ is in $A$ Q.E.D.

stem_md:
Find all rational solutions of
\[a^2 + c^2 + 17(b^2 + d^2) = 21,\]\[ab + cd = 2.\]
solution_md:
Multiply the second equation by  $2\sqrt{17}$  and add to the first equation.  This gives  $(a+\sqrt{17}b)^2+(c+\sqrt{17}d)^2=21+4\sqrt{17}=(2+\sqrt{17})^2$ .  Realizing that as long as all 4 variables are rational, then by expanding and taking the rational part of both sides, we get the first equation, and by subtracting that out, we get the second.  So this equation replaces both old equations, as long as all four variables are rational.  Note also that this means that  $a=2, b=1, c=d=0$  is a solution.  If  $a=2$  and  $b=1$ , then  $c$  and  $d$  must equal 0.

Let  $e=a-2$  and  $f=b-1$ .  Then the equation becomes  $(e+\sqrt{17}f+(2+\sqrt{17}))^2+(c+\sqrt{17}d)^2=(e+\sqrt{17}f)^2+2(2+\sqrt{17})(e+\sqrt{17}f)+(2+\sqrt{17})^2+(c+\sqrt{17}d)^2=(2+\sqrt{17})^2$ or, by letting  $x=e+\sqrt{17}f$  and  $y=c+\sqrt{17}d$ ,   $x^2+(4+2\sqrt{17})x+y^2=0$ .  Now by the above, if  $x=0$ , then  $y=0$ , so suppose  $x\neq0$ .  Let  $\frac{y}{x}=k$ .  Define  $r, s\in\mathbb{Q}$  as  $k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{y\overline{x}}{x\overline{x}}=r+\sqrt{17}s$ .  Then  $x^2+(4+2\sqrt{17})x+k^2x^2=0$ .  Since  $x\neq0$ , we can divide by it and get  $(k^2+1)x=-4-2\sqrt{17}$ , so  $x=\frac{-4-2\sqrt{17}}{k^2+1}$ .

We should rationalize the denominator.  Letting  $k=r+\sqrt{17}s$  and expanding, we get  $x=\frac{-4-2\sqrt{17}}{(1+r^2+17s^2)+\sqrt{17}(2rs)}=\frac{(-4-2\sqrt{17})(1+r^2+17s^2-2\sqrt{17}rs)}{(1+r^2+17s^2+2\sqrt{17}rs)(1+r^2+17s^2-2\sqrt{17}rs)}$  $=\frac{(68rs-68s^2-4r^2-4)+\sqrt{17}(8rs-34s^2-2r^2-2)}{(1+r^2+17s^2)^2-17(2rs)^2}$ .

So  $a=\frac{(68rs-68s^2-4r^2-4)+2((1+r^2+17s^2)^2-17(2rs)^2)}{(1+r^2+17s^2)^2-17(2rs)^2}$  $=\frac{2((r^2-17s^2)^2+34rs-1)}{(r^2-17s^2)+34s^2+2r^2+1}$  $b=\frac{8rs-34s^2-2r^2-2+(1+r^2+17s^2)^2-17(2rs)^2}{(1+r^2+17s^2)^2-17(2rs)^2}$  $=\frac{(r^2-17s^2)^2+8rs-1}{(r^2-17s^2)^2+34s^2+2r^2+1}$  $y=kx=(r+\sqrt{17}s)(\frac{(68rs-68s^2-4r^2-4)+\sqrt{17}(8rs-34s^2-2r^2-2)}{(1+r^2+17s^2)^2-17(2rs)^2})$  $=\frac{(34r^2s+68rs^2-578s^3-4r^3-4r-34s)+\sqrt{17}(4r^2s+34rs^2-68s^3-2r^3-2r-4s)}{(r^2-17s^2)^2+34s^2+2r^2+1}$  $c=\frac{34r^2s+68rs^2-578s^3-4r^3-4r-34s}{(r^2-17s^2)^2+34s^2+2r^2+1}$  $=\frac{(-2r^2+34s^2)(2r-17s)-4r-34s}{(r^2-17s^2)^2+34s^2+2r^2+1}$  $d=\frac{4r^2s+34rs^2-68s^3-2r^3-2r-4s}{(r^2-17s^2)^2+34s^2+2r^2+1}$  $=\frac{(-2r^2+34s^2)(r-2s)-2r-4s}{(r^2-17s^2)^2+34s^2+2r^2+1}$ These parametric equations describe all solutions to the two equations given.

Let  $p, q$ , and  $r$  be the angles of a triangle, and let  $a = \sin2p, b = \sin2q$ , and  $c = \sin2r$ . If  $s = \frac{(a + b + c)}2$ , show that
\[s(s - a)(s - b)(s -c) \geq 0.\]
When does equality hold?
solution_md:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle for which denote $m=\sin2A$ , $n= \sin2B$ and $p= \sin2C$ . Show that $s(s - m)(s - n)(s -p) \geq 0$ , where $2s=m+n+p$ . When does equality hold ?
**Proof.** Prove easily that $\boxed{\alpha +\beta+\gamma=\pi\implies\sin 2\alpha +\sin 2\beta+\sin 2\gamma=4\sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma}$ . Therefore, $\left\|\begin{array}{ccc} A+B+C=\pi & \implies & 2s=\sin 2A+\sin 2B+\sin 2C=4\sin A\sin B\sin C \left(\frac {\pi}{2}-B\right)+\left(\frac {\pi}{2}-C\right)+(\pi -A)=\pi & \implies & 2(s-m)=\sin 2B+\sin 2C-\sin 2A=4\cos B\cos C\sin A \left(\frac {\pi}{2}-C\right)+\left(\frac {\pi}{2}-A\right)+(\pi -B)=\pi & \implies & 2(s-n)=\sin 2C+\sin 2A-\sin 2B=4\cos C\cos A\sin B \left(\frac {\pi}{2}-A\right)+\left(\frac {\pi}{2}-B\right)+(\pi -C)=\pi & \implies & 2(s-p)=\sin 2A+\sin 2B-\sin 2C=4\cos A\cos B\sin C\end{array}\right\|\ \bigodot\implies$ $16s(s-m)(s-n)(s-p)=$ $4\cdot\left[\prod (2\sin A\cos A)\right]^2=$ $4\cdot \prod\sin ^22A\ge 0$ . The equality is hold iff $\frac {\pi}{2}\in \left\{A,B,C\right\}$ .

If none of  $p, q, r$  is  $\ge 90^\circ$ , then  $a, b, c$  are the sides of a triangle with circumradius  $\frac{1}{2}$  and angles  $180^\circ - 2p, 180^\circ - 2q, 180^\circ - 2r$ , and hence the inequality holds true.

Otherwise, suppose  $p \ge 90^\circ$ . Then  $-a, b, c$  are the sides of a triangle with circumradius  $\frac{1}{2}$  and angles  $2p - 180^\circ, 2q, 2r$ . Note that  $s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$  is an even function of  $a, b, c$ , so the inequality follows in this case too.

Edit: Equality holds if such a triangle becomes degenerate. That is, when one of  $p, q, r$  is  $90^\circ$ .

Sol:<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Let  $p, q, r$  be the angles of a triangle, so  $p,q,r \in (0, \pi)$  and  $p+q+r=\pi$ .
Let  $a = \sin 2p$ ,  $b = \sin 2q$ ,  $c = \sin 2r$ .
Let  $s = \frac{a+b+c}{2}$ . We wish to show that  $s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) \ge 0$  and determine when equality holds.

We utilize the trigonometric identity for angles  $x,y,z$  such that  $x+y+z=\pi$ :  $$  \sin 2x + \sin 2y + \sin 2z = 4\sin x \sin y \sin z  $$  Applying this identity to the angles  $p,q,r$ :  $$  a+b+c = \sin 2p + \sin 2q + \sin 2r = 4\sin p \sin q \sin r  $$  Thus, the semi-perimeter  $s$  is:  $$  s = \frac{a+b+c}{2} = 2\sin p \sin q \sin r  $$  Since  $p,q,r \in (0,\pi)$ , it follows that  $\sin p > 0, \sin q > 0, \sin r > 0$ , which implies  $s > 0$ .

Next, we express the terms  $s-a, s-b, s-c$ .
\begin{align*} s-a &= 2\sin p \sin q \sin r - \sin 2p  &= 2\sin p \sin q \sin r - 2\sin p \cos p  &= 2\sin p (\sin q \sin r - \cos p)\end{align*}
Since  $p+q+r=\pi$ , we have  $p=\pi-(q+r)$ , so  $\cos p = \cos(\pi-(q+r)) = -\cos(q+r)$ .
Therefore,  $\sin q \sin r - \cos p = \sin q \sin r + \cos(q+r)$ .
Using the identity  $\cos(q+r) = \cos q \cos r - \sin q \sin r$ , we get:  $$  \sin q \sin r - \cos p = \sin q \sin r + \cos q \cos r - \sin q \sin r = \cos q \cos r  $$  Thus,  $$  s-a = 2\sin p \cos q \cos r  $$  By symmetry, we also have:  $$  s-b = 2\cos p \sin q \cos r  $$    $$  s-c = 2\cos p \cos q \sin r  $$  Now, we compute the product  $P = s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$ :
\begin{align*} P &= (2\sin p \sin q \sin r) \cdot (2\sin p \cos q \cos r) \cdot (2\cos p \sin q \cos r) \cdot (2\cos p \cos q \sin r)  &= 16 (\sin^2 p \cos^2 p) (\sin^2 q \cos^2 q) (\sin^2 r \cos^2 r) \end{align*}
Using the identity  $\sin x \cos x = \frac{1}{2}\sin 2x$ , we have  $(\sin x \cos x)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\sin^2 2x$ .
\begin{align*} P &= 16 \left(\frac{\sin 2p}{2}\right)^2 \left(\frac{\sin 2q}{2}\right)^2 \left(\frac{\sin 2r}{2}\right)^2  &= 16 \left(\frac{\sin^2 2p}{4}\right) \left(\frac{\sin^2 2q}{4}\right) \left(\frac{\sin^2 2r}{4}\right)  &= 16 \cdot \frac{1}{64} (\sin^2 2p \sin^2 2q \sin^2 2r)  &= \frac{1}{4} (\sin 2p \sin 2q \sin 2r)^2 \end{align*}
Substituting  $a=\sin 2p, b=\sin 2q, c=\sin 2r$ :  $$  P = \frac{1}{4} (abc)^2  $$  Since  $a,b,c$  are values of sine functions, they are real numbers. Therefore,  $(abc)^2 \ge 0$ .
It follows that  $s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) = \frac{1}{4}(abc)^2 \ge 0$ .

Equality holds if and only if  $P=0$ , which means  $\frac{1}{4}(abc)^2 = 0$ , implying  $abc=0$ . This requires that at least one of  $a,b,c$  must be zero. If  $a=\sin 2p = 0$ , since  $p \in (0,\pi)$  (and thus  $2p \in (0,2\pi)$ ), it must be that  $2p=\pi$ , so  $p=\pi/2$ . Similarly,  $b=0$  implies  $q=\pi/2$ , and  $c=0$  implies  $r=\pi/2$ . Therefore, equality holds if and only if the triangle with angles  $p,q,r$  is a right-angled triangle.</details>

stem_md: Suppose that n numbers  $x_1, x_2, . . . , x_n$  are chosen randomly from the set  $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ . Prove that the probability that  $x_1^2+ x_2^2 +\cdots+ x_n^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 5$  is at least  $\frac 15.$
solution_md:
Here is an algebraic solution. 

Note that in modulo  $5$ ,  $x_i^2\in\{0,1,-1\}$ . Moreover, if  $x_i$  is chosen uniformly at random from  $\{1,\dots,5\}$ , it follows 
\[
\mathbb{P}(x_i^2\equiv 1\pmod{5})=\mathbb{P}(x_i^2\equiv -1\pmod{5}) = \frac{2}{5} \quad \text{ and } \quad\mathbb{P}(x_i^2\equiv 0\pmod{5}) = 1/5.
\] 
Let  $S_n\triangleq \sum_{1\le i\le n}x_i^2$ , and let  $p_n \triangleq\mathbb{P}(S_n\equiv 0\pmod{5})$ ,  $q_n \triangleq\mathbb{P}(S_n\equiv 1\pmod{5})$ , and  $r_n\triangleq \mathbb{P}(S_n\equiv 2\pmod{5})$ . **Key Observation.** We now make the key observation: if  $(x_i:1\le i\le n)$  is such that  $S_n\equiv 1\pmod{5}$ , then  $(2x_i :1\le i\le n)$  is such that  $\sum_{1\le i\le n}(2x_i)^2\equiv -1\pmod{5}$  (here, we consider this vectors reduced modulo  $5$ ). Notice, moreover, that these vectors are distinct: if  $(x_i :1\le i\le n)=(2x_i:1\le i\le n)$  (coordinate-wise, modulo  $5$ ), then  $x_i\equiv 0\pmod{5}$ , which is not possible, since the sum is assumed to be non-zero. Thus,  $\mathbb{P}(S_n\equiv -1\pmod{5})=q_n$ , as well. Similarly,  $\mathbb{P}(S_n\equiv -2\pmod{5})=r_n$ , too. 

Now, observe the following recursions: applying the law of total probability with respect to  $x_n$ , we deduce $p_n = \frac15 p_{n-1} + \frac45 q_{n-1}$ ,  $q_n = \frac25 p_{n-1} +\frac15 q_{n-1}+ \frac25 r_{n-1}$ ; and  $r_n = \frac25 q_{n-1}+ \frac35 r_{n-1} $ . With this, we arrive at the expression 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}p_n  q_n  r_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac15 & \frac45 & 0  \frac25 &\frac15 &\frac25  0 &\frac25 &\frac35\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p_{n-1}  q_{n-1}  r_{n-1} \end{pmatrix},
\]
with the initial condition  $(p_1,q_1,r_1) = (1/5,2/5,0)$ . solution_md:
Given two positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ , suppose that a mapping $f : \mathbb R^+ \to \mathbb R^+$ satisfies the functional equation \[f(f(x)) + af(x) = b(a + b)x.\] Prove that there exists a unique solution of this equation.
$a+2b>0$ and we get thru simple induction : $f^{[n]}(x)=\frac{((a+b)x+f(x))b^n+(bx-f(x))(-a-b)^n}{a+2b}$ If, for some $x$ , $f(x)-bx\ne 0$ , we get that, for some $n$ great enough, $f^{[n]}(x)<0$ , which is impossible. Hence the unique solution : $f(x)=bx$ which indeed is a solution.

stem_md:
Integers  $a_1, a_2, . . . , a_n$  satisfy  $|a_k| = 1$  and
\[ \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_ka_{k+1}a_{k+2}a_{k+3} = 2,\]
where  $a_{n+j} = a_j$ . Prove that  $n \neq 1992.$
solution_md:
Define  $b_k=a_ka_{k+1}a_{k+2}a_{k+3}$ . We begin with  $a_i = 1$ , for all  $i$ , and change  $1$ 's to  $-1$ 's wherever needed ( $b_i=1, \forall i$  at start). When we change  $a_m$  from  $1$  to  $-1$ , it negates each of the values of  $b_{m-3}, b_{m-2}, b_{m-1},$  and  $b_{m}$ , and affects nothing else. When this happens, the number of  $b_i$ 's which are  $-1$  changes by an even number. Hence the number of  $b_i$ 's which are  $-1$  is always even.

Now suppose  $4 | n$ . If  $\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i = 2$ , then exactly  $\frac{n}{2}+1$  of the  $b_i$ 's must be  $1$ , and  $\frac{n}{2}-1$  of the  $b_i$ 's must be  $-1$ . But  $\frac{n}{2}-1$  is odd: a contradiction.  $\Rightarrow 4 \nmid n \Rightarrow n \neq 1992$ .

stem_md: Prove that there exist  $78$  lines in the plane such that they have exactly  $1992$  points of intersection.
solution_md: You can partition the set of lines in  $1$  set of  $45$  lines,  $7$  sets of  $3$  lines and  $12$  sets of  $1$  line, where each set is made of parallel lines that are not parallel to those of other sets and in general position (no triple intersections, achieved for example by choosing them recursively avoiding the pre-existing intersections). The way to count the intersections of such sets of lines with multiplicity  $s_1+\dots + s_n=78$  is   $$ \frac 1 2 \sum_{i=1}^n s_i(78-s_i)=39\sum_{i=1}^n s_i-\frac 1 2\sum_{i=1}^n s_i^2=39\cdot 78-\frac 1 2(45^2+7\cdot 3^2+12\cdot 1^2)=1992 $$  and the proof is finished.

stem_md: Fibonacci numbers are defined as follows:  $F_0 = F_1 = 1, F_{n+2} = F_{n+1}+F_n, n \geq 0$ . Let  $a_n$  be the number of words that consist of  $n$  letters  $0$  or  $1$  and contain no two letters  $1$  at distance two from each other. Express  $a_n$  in terms of Fibonacci numbers.
solution_md:
Let's first define $B_n$ as the set of 0-1-sequences of length $n$ that don't have two *consecutive* 1's. Let $b_n:=|B_n|$ . I claim that $b_n=F_{n+1}$ . To prove this, observe $b_1=1,b_2=2$ and $b_n=b_{n-1}+b_{n-2}$ because there is a bijection $B_n\to B_{n-1}\cup B_{n-2}$ : if a sequence of $B_n$ ends with a 0, cut the 0 off to get one of $B_{n-1}$ ; if a sequence of $B_n$ ends with a 1, it must end with 01. Cut the 01 off to get one of $B_{n-2}$ . Inversely, we can add 0 and 01 respectively to each sequence of $B_{n-1}$ and $B_{n-2}$ . Now for obtaining the sequences counted in $a_n$ , we can intersparse two of the $B_k$ sequences. For even $n=2k$ , we have $a_n=2b_k=2F_{k+1}$ , for odd $n=2k-1$ , we have $a_n=b_k+b_{k-1}=F_{k+1}+F_{k}=F_{k+2}$ . :)
@ amparvardiNormally the Fibonacci numbers are defined $F_0=F_1=1$ . That gives nicer formulas.
In the last bit, don't you mean: For even $n=2k$ , we have $a_n={b_k}^2={F_{k+1}}^2$ , for odd $n=2k-1$ , we have $a_n=b_k \times b_{k-1}=F_{k+1} \times F_{k}$ . When intersparsing sequences, if there are $A$ of the first kind, and $B$ of the second, then there are $A \times B$ possible results. On a side note, recursive formula for $a_n$ is $a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-3} + a_{n-4}$ .

stem_md: Let  $X$  and  $Y$  be two sets of points in the plane and  $M$  be a set of segments connecting points from  $X$  and  $Y$  . Let  $k$  be a natural number. Prove that the segments from  $M$  can be painted using  $k$  colors in such a way that for any point  $x \in X \cup Y$  and two colors  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$   $(\alpha \neq \beta)$ , the difference between the number of  $\alpha$ -colored segments and the number of  $\beta$ -colored segments originating in  $X$  is less than or equal to  $1$ .
solution_md:
It is from IMO Longlist 1992, problem 20.

Let  $G$  be the bipartite graph corresponding to  $M$ . We fix  $k$  and use induction on the number of edges of  $G$ . Base of induction is trivial. Assume we have a graph  $G$  and the assertion is true for graphs with fewer edges.
Take an arbitrary edge  $ab \in E(G)$  and let  $G' = G - ab$ . Then edges of  $G'$  can be colored in  $k$  colors complying the problem's statement. It is easy to see that there exist two colors  $\alpha$  and  $\beta$ , so that if we color  $ab$  with  $\alpha$ , the vertex  $a$  will comply with the requirement and if we color  $ab$  with  $\beta$ , the vertex  $b$  will comply with the requirement. If  $\alpha=\beta$ , we color  $ab$  with this color and we are done, so assume  $\alpha \neq \beta$ . This means that  $a$  is incident with a  $\beta$ -edge (in  $G'$ ), because if not, we can color  $ab$  with  $\beta$  and are done.
Now, extend this edge to a maximal walk  $W$  which edges are colored  $\beta$  and  $\alpha$  alternately. This walk may not be a path, because it may pass  through some vertices many times, but it has two properties:
(i)  $W$  can not end in  $b$ .
(ii) if  $W$  ends in  $z$  then it passes along all edges incident to  $z$ , which are colored with  $\alpha$  or  $\beta$ .
Both (i), (ii) are straightforward, e.g. (i):  $W$  can not enter in  $b$  with  $\alpha$ , because this will imply that there exists odd cycle in  $G$ , which contradicts that  $G$  is bipartite. If  $W$  enter in  $b$  with  $\beta$ , there should exist edge with color  $\alpha$  for  $W$  to leave  $b$ , because otherwise coloring  $ab$  with  $\beta$  wouldn't comply the requirement with respect to the vertex  $b$ .

Now (the essential part), we recolor all edges of  $W$  swapping  $\alpha$  with  $\beta$ . It is easy to see that the new coloring still satisfies the requirement, but now we can color  $ab$  with  $\beta$  and so the extended coloring of  $G$  still be OK.    


<u>**Comment**</u>. This statement can be viewed as some generalization of the following:**Theorem (König 1916).**Every bipartite graph  $G$  satisfies  $\chi'(G)=\Delta(G)$ , 
where  $\chi'(G)$  is the min number of colors neded for edge coloring of  $G$ ,  $\Delta(G)$  is the max degree of vertices of  $G$ .
(e.g. see R. Diestel, "Graph Theory").

The above proof uses the same technique (with a little modification), used to prove the König's result.

stem_md: *(a)* Show that there exists exactly one function  $ f : \mathbb Q^+ \to \mathbb Q^+$  satisfying the following conditions:**(i)** if  $0 < q < \frac 12$ , then  $f(q)=1+f \left( \frac{q}{1-2q} \right);$ **(ii)** if  $1 < q \leq 2$ , then  $f(q) = 1+f(q + 1);$ **(iii)**  $f(q)f(1/q) = 1$  for all  $q \in \mathbb Q^+.$ *(b)* Find the smallest rational number  $q \in \mathbb Q^+$  such that  $f(q) = \frac{19}{92}.$
solution_md:
Let  $T_1=(0,\frac 13), T_2=\{\frac 13\}, T_3=(\frac 13,\frac 12)$ , $T_4=(\frac 12,1), T_5=\{1\}, T_6=(1,2]$ , $T_7=(2,3), T_8=\{3\}, T_9=(3,\infty)$ and  $g_1(x)=\frac{x}{1-2x}, g_2(x)=x-1, g_3(x)=\frac{1}{x}.$ Then your condition is
1)  $f(g_1(x))=g_2^{-1}(f(x)), x\in (0,\frac 12)$ ,

stem_md:
***(a)*** Show that the set  $\mathbb N$  of all positive integers can be partitioned into three disjoint subsets  $A, B$ , and  $C$  satisfying the following conditions:
\[A^2 = A, B^2 = C, C^2 = B,\] \[AB = B, AC = C, BC = A,\]
where  $HK$  stands for  $\{hk | h \in H, k \in K\}$  for any two subsets  $H, K$  of  $\mathbb N$ , and  $H^2$  denotes  $HH.$ ***(b)*** Show that for every such partition of  $\mathbb N$ ,  $\min\{n \in N | n \in A \text{  and  } n + 1 \in A\}$  is less than or equal to  $77.$
solution_md:
a.  If we let  $p_n$  be the number of primes, not necessarily distinct, in  $n$ 's prime decomposition, then we can put all the  $n's$  so that  $p_n\equiv0\mod 3$  in  $A$ , all the  $n's$  so that  $p_n\equiv1\mod3$  in  $B$  and all the rest in  $C$ .  If we multiply any two numbers in  $B$ , the number of primes add to become  $2\mod3$ , so the product is in  $C$ , and same for all the other subsets.

b.  Suppose we have a division so that there is no  $n$  in  $A$  so that both  $n+1$  is also in  $A$  and  $n\leq77$ .  We use the notation  $P(n)$  to mean that not both  $n$  and  $n+1$  are in  $A$ .  

The primes are the only numbers we are worried about, because once we have placed them, every other number is the product of some primes and hence is in a specified subset.

First note that whichever subset  $n$  is in,  $n^3$  is in  $A$ .   $P(8)$  gives that  $3$  is not in  $A$ , so suppose it is in  $B$ , WLOG.  Now  $P(7)$  gives that 7 isn't in  $A$ , and  $P(63)$  shows that 7 is not in  $B$ , so 7 is in  $C$ .  Then  $P(27)$  gives that 2 is not in  $C$  and  $P(1)$  gives that 2 isn't in  $A$ , so it is in  $B$ .  So far we have that  $A:\{\}$ ,  $B:\{2, 3\}$ ,  $C:\{7\}$ . $P(20)$  shows that 5 isn't in  $B$ , and  $P(14)$  shows that 5 isn't in  $C$ .  So 5 is in  $A$ .   $P(11)$ : 11 not in  $A$ ,  $P(21)$ : 11 not in C, so 11 is in  $B$ .  So  $A:\{5\}$ ,  $B:\{2, 3, 11\}$ ,  $C:\{7\}$ Now here's where the contradiction happens.   $P(64)$  shows that 13 can't be in  $A$ ,  $P(39)$  shows that 13 can't be in  $C$ , and  $P(77)$  shows that 13 can't be in  $B$ , contradiction.  So the assumption was wrong, and part b is true.

stem_md:
Let  $a, b, c$  be integers. Prove that there are integers  $p_1, q_1, r_1, p_2, q_2, r_2$  such that
\[a = q_1r_2 - q_2r_1, b = r_1p_2 - r_2p_1, c = p_1q_2 - p_2q_1.\]
solution_md:
Consider the linear system  $\left\{\begin{array}{l} p_1 x + q_1 y = r_1  p_2 x + q_2 y = r_2 \end{array}\right.$ Then,  $x$  and  $y$  can be found with Cramer's rule as
\[x = \frac{\begin{vmatrix}r_1 & q_1  r_2 & q_2 \end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix}p_1 & q_1  p_2 & q_2 \end{vmatrix}} = \frac{r_1 q_2 - q_1 r_2}{p_1 q_2 - q_1 p_2}\]
\[y = \frac{\begin{vmatrix}p_1 & r_1  p_2 & r_2 \end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix}p_1 & q_1  p_2 & q_2 \end{vmatrix}} = \frac{p_1 r_2 - r_1 p_2}{p_1 q_2 - q_1 p_2}\]

And where  $x = \frac{-a}{c}$ ,  $y = \frac{-b}{c}$ , $a = q_1 r_2 - q_2 r_1$ ,  $b = r_1 p_2 - r_2 p_1$ ,  $c = p_1 q_2 - p_2 q_1$ .

stem_md:
Let  $n \geq 2$  be an integer. Find the minimum  $k$  for which there exists a partition of  $\{1, 2, . . . , k\}$  into  $n$  subsets  $X_1,X_2, \cdots , X_n$  such that the following condition holds:
for any  $i, j, 1 \leq i < j \leq n$ , there exist  $x_i \in X_1, x_j \in X_2$  such that  $|x_i - x_j | = 1.$
solution_md:
We use the following theorem:
An undirected multigraph contains an Eulerian path (= a path which visits every edge exactly once) if and only if the number of odd-degree vertices is at most  $2$ .

Note the bijection between partitions of  $\{1, 2, ..., k\}$  and paths  $P$  of length  $k - 1$  in the graph  $K_n$ , where  $i \in X_m \iff P(i)=m $ .
The condition (**ocha**'s) translates to the following: every edge of  $K_n$  is visited at least once.

Thus the problem is equivalent to the problem of finding an Eulerian multigraph with vertices  $\{1, 2, ..., n\}$  which contains  $K_n$  and has  $|E|$  minimized.
For odd  $n$ ,  $K_n$  works, so  $k = {n \choose 2} + 1$ .
For even  $n$ , there are  $n$  vertices of odd degree in  $K_n$ , but we want only two to let it contain an Eulerian path. So we add  $\frac{n}{2}-1$  edges  $\{1, 2\}, \{3, 4\}, ..., \{n-3, n-2\}$  and  $k = {n \choose 2} + \frac{n}{2}$ .

stem_md: The colonizers of a spherical planet have decided to build  $N$  towns, each having area  $1/1000$  of the total area of the planet. They also decided that any two points belonging to different towns will have different latitude and different longitude. What is the maximal value of  $N$ ?
solution_md:
Suppose the maximum and minimum latitude of some town is given by points  $\ell_M$  and  $\ell_m$ , then no other town can intersect the band of width  $w=|\ell_M\ell_m|$ . The surface area of this band is proportional to it's width, i.e.  $A = 2\pi r w$ , where  $r$  is the radius of the planet. If the most easterly and westerly points of the town subtend an angle  $\theta$  with the center of the sphere, then they chop the latitudinal band into an area of  $\frac{\theta}{2\pi}A = r \theta w$ . Now the town must be completely within this square(ish) area and no town can enter the latitudinal or longitudinal bands that define the town. 

Let  $\{w_i\}_{i=1}^N$  be the widths of longitudinal bands made by the towns, and let  $\{\theta_i\}_{i=1}^N$  be angles which represent width of the longitudinal bands of the towns. Then  $\sum_i w_i \le 2r$  and  $\sum_i \theta_i \le 2\pi$  and the area of town  $i$  is at most  $A_i = r \theta_i w_i = \frac{4\pi r^2}{1000}$ So by Cauchy-Schwarz:   $2r \cdot 2 \pi \ge \left(\sum_i w_i \right)\left(\sum_i \theta_i \right) \ge \left(\sum_i\sqrt{ w_i \theta_i}\right)^2 = \left(N \sqrt{\frac{4\pi r}{1000}}\right)^2$ Therefore  $N \le \sqrt{1000}$  so  $\max(N) = 31$

stem_md:
Find the number of positive integers  $n$  satisfying  $\phi(n) | n$  such that
\[\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \left( \left[ \frac nm \right] - \left[\frac{n-1}{m} \right]  \right) =  1992\]
What is the largest number among them? As usual,  $\phi(n)$  is the number of positive integers less than or equal to  $n$  and relatively prime to  $n.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>$\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(\lfloor \frac{n}{m} \rfloor-\lfloor \frac{n-1}{m} \rfloor)=1992$  is the same as having  $n$  having  $1992$  positive factors (because the number of times we get +1 is the number of times  $m|n$  and the other times we get +0).  

Also, we have  $\phi(n)|n$  therefore  $n(1-\frac{1}{p_1})(1-\frac{1}{p_2})\cdots (1-\frac{1}{p_k})|n$  for  $p_1, p_2, \cdots p_k$  being the prime divisors of  $n$ .  Therefore  $\frac{p_1*p_2*\cdots p_k}{(p_1-1)(p_2-1)\cdots (p_k-1)}$  is an integer.  Note that if we have two odd prime divisors, there will be at least two factors of  $2$  in the denominator and at most one factor of  $2$  in the numerator, so this isn't an integer.  If we have one odd prime divisor and  $2$ , then we get:   $\frac{2p}{p-1}$  being an integer.  This gives  $\gcd(2p, p-1)=p-1$  or  $\gcd(2, p-1)=p-1$ .  Therefore  $2\ge p-1$  or  $3\ge p$  so therefore the only prime divisor that can go with  $2$  as a divisor is  $3$ .  

Also, obviously  $2^a$  works, so we have two cases:   $2^b*3^c$ .   $2^a$  has  $a+1$  prime divisors therefore  $a+1=1992$  and  $a=1991$ .  The other possibility gives  $(b+1)(c+1)=1992$ .  
 
Note that  $2^{1991}$  is greater than the maximum for  $2^b*3^c$  which is  $3^{995}*2$  since this gives the largest sum which you need and the most powers of  $3$  which you need to get the highest sum.   $2^{1991}>3^{995}*2$  since  $2^{1990}>3^{995}$  from  $2^{1990}=4^{995}$ .  Therefore, the largest solution is  $\boxed{2^{1991}}$  and the number of solutions is 1+(number of non-negative solutions to (b+1)(c+1)=1992)-2(for b=0 and c=0 cases) and since  $1992=2^3*3*83$  which has  $4*2*2=16$  divisors, we get  $16+1-2=\boxed{15}$  solutions.</details>

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer. Prove that the number of ways to express  $n$  as a sum of distinct positive integers (up to order) and the number of ways to express  $n$  as a sum of odd positive integers (up to order) are the same.
solution_md:
Let us define an " $m$ -power of  $2$ " to be a positive integer of the form  $m \times 2^k$ , where  $m$  is odd. Notice that the positive integers are partitioned by sets of this form, i.e. for every positive integer  $x$ , there is exactly one value of  $m$  such that  $x$  is an  $m$ -power of  $2$ . 

Now let us note that any sum which consists only of an odd integer  $m$  can be written as the sum of <u>distinct</u>  $m$ -powers of 2. For example,  $5+5+5+5+5+5+5 = 5\times (1+1+1+1+1+1+1) = 5\times (2^2 + 2^1 + 2^0) = (5\times 2^2) + (5\times 2^1) + (5\times 2^0)$ . 

This allows us to convert from a sum of only odd integers to a sum of distinct positive integers, as follows. For every  $m$  that appears in the sum of odd integers, collect all values of  $m$  together, and express these as the sum of distinct  $m$ -powers of 2. This ensures that the result consists of distinct positive integers, since the  $m$ -powers of 2 don't intersect with the  $n$ -powers of 2, when  $m$  and  $n$  differ, and the  $m$ -powers of 2 themselves are all distinct. 

It is not hard to see that this process is reversible. If you have a sum of distinct positive integers, then for every odd  $m$ , collect all the  $m$ -powers of 2 together (every positive integer will be in exactly one such collection), and express these instead as a sum of copies of  $m$ . This process is uniquely defined, and is the inverse of the previous process.

The existence of this invertible function shows that we have a bijection between the sums of positive odd integers and the sums of distinct positive integers. The problem statement follows.

Let  $n$  be written as sum of distinct natural numbers in  $a(n)$  ways and as odd natural numbers in  $b(n)$  ways.

Consider the generating functions  $A(x)=\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a(n)x^n$  and  $B(x)=\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b(n)x^n$ .

We need to prove that  $A(x)$  and  $B(x)$  are identically equal.

But we have  $A(x)=(1+x)(1+x^2)(1+x^3)\cdots$ Note that this is so because any  $x^n$  in the expansion is got by multiplying some  $1s$  and  $x^{k_i}$ s for different and distinct  $k_i$ s which is just partitioning  $n$  in to  $k_i$ s. So, the coefficient of  $x^n$  is the number of such partitions $=a(n)$  from definition.

Now, we claim that  $B(x)=(1+x+x^{1+1}+\cdots)(1+x^3+x^{3+3}+\cdots)\cdots$ By similar reasoning, we have the result.

And hence $A(x)=\prod(1+x^i)=\prod\frac{1-x^{2i}}{1-x^i}$ Note that all terms in numerator gets cancelled and only terms of the form  $(1-x^{2k+1})$  are present in the denominator.

So, we have  $A(x)=\prod\frac{1}{1-x^{2k+1}}=\prod(1+x^{2k+1}+x^{(2k+1)+(2k+1)}+\cdots)=B(x)$  as required.

stem_md:
Find all the functions  $f : \mathbb R^+ \to \mathbb R$  satisfying the identity
\[f(x)f(y)=y^{\alpha}f\left(\frac x2 \right) + x^{\beta} f\left(\frac y2 \right) \qquad \forall x,y \in \mathbb R^+\]
Where  $\alpha,\beta$  are given real numbers.
solution_md:
$x\to y$  give $f(x)f(y)=x^{\alpha}f(\frac{y}{2})+y^{\beta}f(\frac{x}{2}).$ Therefore  $(x^{\alpha}-x^{\beta})f(\frac{y}{2})=(y^{\alpha}-y^{\beta})f(\frac{x}{2})$  or
\[\frac{f(y)}{(2y)^{\alpha}-(2y)^{\beta}}=\frac{f(x)}{(2x)^{\alpha}-(2x)^{\beta}}\]
or  $f(x)=C[(2x)^{\alpha}-(2x)^{\beta}].$  $f(x)f(y)=C^2[(2x)^{\alpha}-(2x)^{\beta}][(2y)^{\alpha}-(2y)^{\beta}]=Cy^{\alpha}(x^{\alpha}-x^{\beta})+Cx^{\beta}(y^{\alpha}-y^{\beta}).$ Therefore if  $\alpha\not =\beta$  $C^2*2^{2\alpha}=C$ , $-C^22^{\alpha +\beta}=0$  or  $f(x)=0$  for all  $x$ .
If  $\alpha=\beta$ , then for  $g(y)=2^{\alpha}y^{-\alpha}f(y)$  we get  $g(x)g(y)=g(\frac{x}{2})+g(\frac{y}{2})$ or  $g(y)=2.$

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be an integer  $> 1$ . In a circular arrangement of  $n$  lamps  $L_0, \cdots, L_{n-1}$ , each one of which can be either ON or OFF, we start with the situation that all lamps are ON, and then carry out a sequence of steps,  $Step_0, Step_1, \cdots$ . If  $L_{j-1}$  ( $j$  is taken mod n) is ON, then  $Step_j$  changes the status of  $L_j$  (it goes from ON to OFF or from OFF to ON) but does not change the status of any of the other lamps. If  $L_{j-1}$  is OFF, then  $Step_j$  does not change anything at all. Show that:

*(a)* There is a positive integer  $M(n)$  such that after  $M(n)$  steps all lamps are ON again.

*(b)* If  $n$  has the form  $2^k$ , then all lamps are ON after  $n^2 - 1$  steps.

*(c)*If  $n$  has the form  $2^k +1$ , then all lamps are ON after  $n^2 -n+1$  steps.
solution_md:
Contrary to the problem statement, we begin at  $L_1$  and  $Step_1$ , without loss of generality. First some definitions: A *loop* is a series of  $n$  steps performed. The *current position* is the position of the lamp about to be acted upon. The *configuration* of the lamps is their appearance <u>taken relative to the current position.</u> $(a)$  Viewing each configuration relative to the current position, it is evident that the transition, which takes one configuration to the next, is an invertible function on the set of all configurations (a finite set). What we have therefore is a permutation, which must be composed of finite length cycles. In other words, any configuration will return to itself in a finite number of steps. The problem statement follows. $(b)$  We will work through the problem in loops, starting each at  $L_1$ . The problem statement equivalently states that after  $n-1$  loops, the only lamp lit is  $L_0$ . This is what we prove. 

Let us imagine the lamps in a row, moving left to right from  $L_0$  to  $L_{n-1}$ . Define the range as the index of the lit lamp furthest right (initially  $n-1$ ). Suppose that at some stage, there are an even number of lamps lit, including  $L_0$ , and label them  $A_0$ ,  $A_1$ ,  $A_2$ ,  $…$  starting with  $L_0$ . Then the result of one loop is that all the lamps between  $A_{2i}$  and  $A_{2i+1}$  are turned on, while  $A_{2i+1}$  is turned off. Note that the even number of lit lamps ensures that the influence of the first is contained (doesn’t continue past the last, and doesn’t propagate back to the beginning). After one loop,  $L_0$  is still lit, and the range decreased by  $1$ . Since the range decreases by one after every loop, it suffices to show that the number of lit lamps is always even until one is left (from which follows that only  $L_0$  is lit after  $n-1$  loops). This is trivial for  $n=2$ . For  $n\geq4$ , we use inductive reasoning. 

For if we divide the row of lamps into two equal parts, and apply the inductive hypothesis to each half, they will have an even number of lit lamps (and thus remain independent of one another) until one is left in each half, necessarily the first. During the process, the whole, composed of two identical halves, must contain an even number of lamps lit. After the next loop, only the first half of the lamps are lit, which must be an even number since  $n\geq4$ , and applying the inductive hypothesis to this first half, we know an even number must be lit until only one is left, as required.  $(c)$  Consider a circle of  $n=2^k+1$  lamps ( $n-$ circle), and one of  $m=2^k$  lamps ( $m$ -circle). Notice that the configuration of the  $n$ -circle after  $n+2$  steps corresponds precisely with that of the  $m$ -circle after  $m$  steps. The unlit lamps  $L_0$  and  $L_1$  in the  $n$ -circle act as one single unit, corresponding with the unlit lamp  $L_{m-1}$  in the  $m$ -circle. From part  $(b)$ , we know that in the  $m$ -circle, all lamps are lit after one step less than  $m$  loops. The same must be true in the  $n$ -circle, with the exception of the two extra steps in the first loop. The total number of steps in the  $n$ -circle is  $mn-1+2=n^2-n+1$ .

stem_md: A directed graph (any two distinct vertices joined by at most one directed line) has the following property: If  $x, u,$  and  $v$  are three distinct vertices such that  $x \to u$  and  $x \to v$ , then  $u \to w$  and  $v \to w$  for some vertex  $w$ . Suppose that  $x \to u \to y \to\cdots \to z$  is a path of length  $n$ , that cannot be extended to the right (no arrow goes away from  $z$ ). Prove that every path beginning at  $x$  arrives after  $n$  steps at  $z.$
solution_md:
If  $V$  is a set of vertices, let the function  $f(V)$  be defined as the set of all vertices which have an edge directed towards some vertex in  $V$ .
Now, define  $A_0 = \{z\}$  and  $A_{i+1} = f(A_i)$  for all  $i\geq 0$ . Note that  $x \in A_n$ . It may be in more  $A_i$  since we do not assume that these  $A_i$  are disjoint. **Claim**: All edges originating in  $A_{i+1}$  end in  $A_i$ .
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Induction on  $i$ . 
Base case (by contradiction):  $i=0$ . Suppose that not all edges from  $A_1$  end in  $A_0$ . Then there exists  $a \in A_1$  and  $b \notin A_0$  such that  $a \to b$  and  $a \to z$ . But this would imply that some edge leaves  $z$ , contrary to the problem statement. Hence all edges originating in  $A_1$  end in  $A_0$ . 
Inductive step (by contradiction): Assume all edges from  $A_{k+1}$  end in  $A_k$ . Suppose not all edges from  $A_{k+2}$  end in  $A_{k+1}$ . Then there exists  $a \in A_{k+2}, b \in A_{k+1}$ , and  $c \notin A_{k+1}$  such that  $a \to b$  and  $a \to c$ . Then there exists  $d$  such that  $b \to d$  and  $c \to d$ . Vertex  $d$  cannot be in  $A_k$ , since that would imply  $c \in A_{k+1}$ , contrary to our set up. Meanwhile,  $b \in A_{k+1}$ ,  $d \notin A_k$ , and  $b \to d$ . This contradicts the inductive hypothesis that all edges from  $A_{k+1}$  end in  $A_k$ , which completes the proof by contradiction.</details>**Claim**:  $z$  is not part of any  $A_i$  except for  $A_0$ . 
<details><summary>Proof</summary>If  $i>0$ ,  $A_i$  is defined as the set of all points which have an edge directed towards  $A_{i-1}$ . But we know  $z$  has no edges directed away from it, so  $z \notin A_i$ .</details>**Claim**: If  $v \in A_i$ , every path from  $v$  to  $z$  has length  $i$ .
<details><summary>Proof</summary>Induction on  $i$ . 
Base case:  $i=0$ . Vertex  $z$  is alone in  $A_0$ , and every path from  $z$  to itself has length  $0$ , since there are no edges leaving  $z$ .
Inductive step: Assume that if  $v \in A_k$ , for some  $k \geq 0$ , then every path from  $v$  to  $z$  has length  $k$ . Consider a path from  $w \in A_{k+1}$  to  $z$ . First, since  $k+1>0$ , we know  $z \notin A_{k+1}$  and therefore  $w \neq z$ . Hence this path must have at lease one edge, the first originating in  $A_{k+1}$ . By earlier claim, this must end in  $A_k$ , and by the inductive hypothesis, every path from a vertex in  $A_k$  to  $z$  has length  $k$ . Therefore, every path from  $w \in A_{k+1}$  to  $z$  must have length  $k+1$ , completing our proof by induction.</details>**Conclusion**: Since  $x \in A_n$ , every path from  $x$  to  $z$  has length  $n$ . 

<details><summary>Remark</summary>Although not necessary for the proof, it is noteworthy that the last claim implies all  $A_i$  are disjoint.</details>

stem_md:
For positive numbers  $a, b, c$  define  $A = \frac{(a + b + c)}{3}$ ,  $G = \sqrt[3]{abc}$ ,  $H = \frac{3}{(a^{-1} + b^{-1} + c^{-1})}.$  Prove that
\[ \left( \frac AG \right)^3 \geq \frac 14 + \frac 34 \cdot  \frac AH.\]
solution_md:
It is trivial by  $uvw$  method.

It's equal to: $\frac{u^3}{w^3} \ge \frac{1}{4}+\frac{3uv^2}{4w^3}$ , or  $f(w^3)=Aw^3+B \le 0$ . Linear funciton  $f(w^3)$  reaches maximum when  $w^3$  reaches extremal value, so we need to prove just cases when  $c\rightarrow 0$ , and  $b=c=1$ 1.st case  $c\rightarrow 0$  is obvious since we have: $\frac{u}{w^3}(u^2-\frac{3}{4}v^2) \ge \frac{1}{4}$ When  $c\rightarrow 0$ ,  $LHS \rightarrow \infty$ .

2.nd case  $b=c=1$ : $\frac{(a+2)^3}{27a} \ge \frac{1}{4}+\frac{(a+2)(2a+1)}{12a}$  $\Leftrightarrow$   $2(a-1)^2(2a+7) \ge 0$  what is true since  $a>0$ .

We have equality for  $a=b=c=1$ . ;)

Let a regular  $7$ -gon  $A_0A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$  be inscribed in a circle. Prove that for any two points  $P, Q$  on the arc  $A_0A_6$  the following equality holds:
\[\sum_{i=0}^6 (-1)^{i} PA_i = \sum_{i=0}^6 (-1)^{i} QA_i .\]
solution_md:
We claim:  $\displaystyle \sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i \sin\left(\frac{\pi i}{7}\right) = \sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i \cos\left(\frac{\pi i}{7}\right) =0$  
<details><summary>Proof</summary>First,  $\displaystyle \sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i \sin\left(\frac{\pi i}{7}\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{6} (-1)^i \sin\left(\frac{\pi i}{7}\right) = 0$  (Note: since every term  $\displaystyle (-1)^i \sin\left(\frac{\pi i}{7}\right)$  cancels with  $\displaystyle (-1)^{7-i} \sin\left(\frac{\pi(7-i)}{7}\right)$ Second,  $\displaystyle \sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i \cos\left(\frac{\pi i}{7}\right)=\cos(0) + \sum_{i=1}^{3} 2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i}{7}\right) - \sum_{i=1}^{6} \cos\left(\frac{\pi i}{7}\right)=\cos(0) +  \sum_{i=1}^{3} 2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i}{7}\right)$  (Note: since every term  $\displaystyle \cos\left(\frac{\pi i}{7}\right)$  cancels with  $\displaystyle \cos\left(\frac{\pi(7-i)}{7}\right))$  $= \cos(0) +  \sum_{i=1}^{6} \cos\left(\frac{2\pi i}{7}\right)$    (Note: since  $\displaystyle \cos\left(\frac{2\pi i}{7}\right) = \cos\left(\frac{2\pi (7-i)}{7}\right)$  ) $=\sum_{i=0}^{6} \cos\left(\frac{2\pi i}{7}\right)=0$  (by the symmetry of 7 equally spaced points around a circle)</details>
Now suppose  $A_i$  is represented by the complex number  $cis\left(\frac{2\pi i}{7}\right)$  and  $P$  by the number  $cis (\theta)$ . It is well known that  $|cis(b) - cis(a)| = 2\sin\left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)$ . Hence,
  $\displaystyle \sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i PA_i = \sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i | cis(2\pi i/7) - cis (\theta) | = \sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i \times 2\sin(\pi i/7 - \theta/2) = 2\cos(\theta/2)\sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i \sin(\pi i/7) - 2\sin(\theta/2)\sum_{i=0}^{6} (-1)^i \cos(\pi i/7) = 2\cos(\theta/2) \times 0 - 2\sin(\theta/2) \times 0 = 0 $

stem_md: Let  $c_1, \cdots, c_n  \ (n \geq  2)$  be real numbers such that  $0 \leq \sum c_i \leq n$ . Prove that there exist integers  $k_1, \cdots , k_n$  such that  $\sum k_i=0$  and  $1-n \leq c_i + nk_i \leq n$  for every  $i = 1, \cdots , n.$
solution_md:
For all  $i$  the maximal integer  $k_i$  that satisfies the inequality is  $k_i^\ast=\left\lfloor\frac{n-c_i}{n}\right\rfloor$ . $\sum k_i^\ast = \sum \frac{n-c_i}{n} - \sum \left\{\frac{-c_i}{n}\right\} > (n-1) -n$ , therefore  $\sum k_i^\ast \geq 0$ .
For all  $i$  the minimal integer  $k_i$  that satisfies the inequality is  $k_{i\ast}=\left\lceil\frac{1-n-c_i}{n}\right\rceil$ . $\sum k_{i\ast} = -\sum \left\lfloor\frac{n-1+c_i}{n}\right\rfloor = -\sum \frac{n-1+c_i}{n} + \sum \left\{\frac{c_i-1}{n}\right\} < -(n-1) + n$ , therefore  $\sum k_{i\ast} \leq 0$ .
Clearly  $\sum k_i = K$  can be achieved for all integers  $\sum k_{i\ast} \leq K \leq \sum k_i^\ast$ , the proof of the statement follows.

stem_md:
Let two circles  $A$  and  $B$  with unequal radii  $r$  and  $R$ , respectively, be tangent internally at the point  $A_0$ . If there exists a sequence of distinct circles  $(C_n)$  such that each circle is tangent to both  $A$  and  $B$ , and each circle  $C_{n+1}$  touches circle  $C_{n}$  at the point  $A_n$ , prove that 
\[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |A_{n+1}A_n| < \frac{4 \pi Rr}{R+r}.\]
solution_md: Let  $M,N$  be the antipodes of  $A_0$  in  $\mathcal{A}$  and  $\mathcal{B},$  respectively. The inversion through pole  $A_0$  with power  $\overline{A_0M} \cdot \overline{A_0N}=4R \cdot r$  transforms  $\mathcal{A}$  and  $\mathcal{B}$  into two lines  $a,b$  perpendicular to  $A_0N$  through  $N,M,$  respectively and the Pappus chain   $C_n$  into a chain of congruent circles  $U_n$  tangent to each other and tangent to the parallels  $a,b.$  Hence, contact points of  $U_n$  lie on the midline  $\ell$  of  $a,b$   $\Longrightarrow$  Points  $A_n$  are concyclic on a circle  $\mathcal{C}$  with radius  $\varrho,$   i.e. the inverse image of  $\ell.$  If  $L$  is the midpoint of  $MN,$  we have  $\overline{A_0M} \cdot \overline{A_0N}=4R \cdot r=2\varrho \cdot A_0L=2\varrho \cdot  (R+r) \Longrightarrow \varrho=\frac{2Rr}{R+r}$ Since  $A_0A_1A_2...A_n$  is inscribed in  $\mathcal{C},$  then its perimeter  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|A_{n}A_{n+1}|$  is less than  $\mathcal{C}$  's  $\Longrightarrow 2\pi \cdot \varrho=\frac{4\pi Rr}{R+r} > \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|A_{n}A_{n+1}|$

stem_md: Let  $P_1(x, y)$  and  $P_2(x, y)$  be two relatively prime polynomials with complex coefficients. Let  $Q(x, y)$  and  $R(x, y)$  be polynomials with complex coefficients and each of degree not exceeding  $d$ . Prove that there exist two integers  $A_1, A_2$  not simultaneously zero with  $|A_i| \leq d + 1 \  (i = 1, 2)$  and such that the polynomial  $A_1P_1(x, y) + A_2P_2(x, y)$  is coprime to  $Q(x, y)$  and  $R(x, y).$
solution_md:
This problem, when translated, becomes an easy combinatorial one.
Let   $ Q(x,y)=S_1(x,y)S_2(x,y)\ldots S_i(x,y)$   $ R(x,y)=S_{i+1}(x,y)S_{i+2}(x,y)\ldots S_m(x,y)$ , 
where  $m \leq 2d$  and  $S_j(x,y),\,j=1,2,\ldots,m $  are irreducible polynomials over  $\mathbb{C}[x,y]$ .
In order to prove the assertion, let assume on the contrary that for each  $(k,\ell),\, -d-1 \leq k,\,\ell \leq d+1 $ ,  $k P_1(x,y) + \ell P_2(x,y)$  is not coprime with  $Q$  or  $R$ , i.e. 

(1)  $\forall (k,\ell),\, -d-1 \leq k,\ell \leq d+1, \, (k,\ell) \neq (0,0) \,\, \Rightarrow $  $ k P_1(x,y) + \ell P_2(x,y)=S_{r(k,\ell)}(x,y)T_{k,\ell}(x,y),\, 1 \leq r(k,\ell) \leq m$ . **Proposition 1**. Lattice points  $(k,\ell),\, -d-1 \leq k,\ell \leq d+1,\, (k,\ell) \neq (0,0)$  are colored with  $2d$  colors. Then, there exist two lattice points  $(k_1,\ell_1), \, (k_2,\ell_2)$  colored with the same color and linear independent (as vectors).**Proof**. There are  $ (2d+3)^2-1$  lattice points, colored with  $2d$  collors, so there are at least  $2d+6$  of them with the same color. It is impossible all of them to belong to the same line through the origin, because each line through the origin contains at most  $2d+2$  such points. Thus, there are two non collinear lattice points with the same color.  $\square$ Now, using (1) we color each  $(k,\ell)$  with color  $r(k,\ell)$  and apply Proposition 1, which implies there exist non collinear  $(k_j,\ell_j),\, j=1,2$  such that: $ k_1 P_1(x,y)+ \ell_1 P_2(x,y) = S_r(x,y) T_{k_1,\ell_1}(x,y)$ . $ k_2 P_1(x,y)+ \ell_2 P_2(x,y) = S_r(x,y) T_{k_2,\ell_2}(x,y)$ .

This yields  $P_1(x,y)= S_r(x,y)T'(x,y),\, P_2(x,y)=S_r(x,y)T''(x,y)$ , which contradics that  $P_1$  and  $P_2$  are relatively prime.

solution_md:
The question asks to find the number of ways of making such a list of preferences. We abbreviate courses by the first letter. Parantheses indicate the same level of preference, and the symbol   $\Leftrightarrow$  indicates interchangeability between different levels of preference. 

We begin by considering the possible listings of  $H, P, B, G,$  with the only requirement that  $H>G$  and  $P>B$ . These can be split into either  $2, 3$  or  $4$  levels of preferences. 
For  $2$  preferences, there is only  $1$  case:  $[(HP)(BG)]$ For  $3$  preferences, there are  $6$  cases:  $[H \Leftrightarrow P,(BG)]$   $[(HP),G \Leftrightarrow B]$    $[H, (PG), B]$  and  $[P, (BH), G]$  
For  $4$  preferences, there are  $6$  cases:  $[H \Leftrightarrow P, G \Leftrightarrow B]$   $[P,B,H,G]$  and  $[H,G,P,B]$  

Whenever there are  $n$  different levels preferences for these four subjects, the remaining two (Music and Math) can be placed in  $4n-2$  ways. Hence we have  $(1 \times 6) + (6 \times 10) + (6 \times 14) = 150$  ways.

stem_md: Let  $\{A_n | n = 1, 2, \cdots \} $  be a set of points in the plane such that for each  $n$ , the disk with center  $A_n$  and radius  $2^n$  contains no other point  $A_j$  . For any given positive real numbers  $a < b$  and  $R$ , show that there is a subset  $G$  of the plane satisfying:**(i)** the area of  $G$  is greater than or equal to  $R$ ;**(ii)**for each point  $P$  in  $G$ ,  $a < \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{|A_nP|} <b.$
solution_md:
We choose point  $P$  distance  $k$  from  $A_n$ , where  $k<2^{n-1}$ . Then we have \[\frac{1}{k}<\sum^{\infty}{\frac{1}{A_nP}}<\frac{1}{k}+\sum^{n-1}{\frac{1}{2^n-k}}+\sum_{n+1}{\frac{1}{2^i-k}}<\frac{1}{k}+\sum^{n-1}{\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}}+\sum_{n+1}{\frac{1}{2^{i-1}}}=\frac{1}{k}+\frac{n-1}{2^{n-1}}+\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}=\frac{1}{k}+\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}\]
So now we choose  $n$  such that  $\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}<b-a$ , and a range of values  $k$  such that  $\frac{1}{k}>a$  and  $\frac{1}{k}+\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}<b$ . So now we have rings of radius the range of  $k$  surrounding  $A_n,A_{n+1},...$ , each ring of same finite area. Now we choose  $G$  to be all those rings, which can be of arbitrary large area, and every point in it satisfies (ii).

stem_md: Let  $S = \{\frac{\pi^n}{1992^m} | m,n \in \mathbb Z \}.$  Show that every real number  $x \geq 0$  is an accumulation point of  $S.$
solution_md:
Consider the set  $T$  consisting of  $n\log_{1992}\pi-m$ .  $\log{1992}\pi$  is irrational, since if  $\log{1992}\pi=\frac{a}{b}$  for some integers  $a,b$  then  $\pi^b=1992^a$ , which would imply  $\pi$  was algebraic. Since it is transcendental, we have the desired contradiction.

By suitable choice of  $m$ , we know that  $T$  contains the fractional part of  $n(\log{1992}\pi)$  for each integer  $n$ . Since  $\log{1992}\pi$  is irrational, we can either state, or use an easy application of pigeonhole, to show that every  $x$  in  $[0,1]$  is an accumulation point of  $T$ . By adding multiples of  $m$ , we therefore have that every real  $x$  being an accumulation point of  $T$ .  $S$  is then formed by taking  $e$  to the power of every element in  $T$ . It is not hard to show that the image of a point under this operation retains it's accumulation property, so therefore for all positive  $x$ ,  $x$  is an accumulation point. Then, since arbitrarily small positive values of  $x$  are accumulation points, we also have  $x=0$  as an accumulation point, and we thus have the desired result.

Cheers,

Rofler

stem_md:
A sequence  $\{an\}$  of positive integers is defined by 
\[a_n=\left[ n +\sqrt n + \frac 12 \right] , \qquad \forall n \in \mathbb N\]
Determine the positive integers that occur in the sequence.
solution_md:
A sequence $\{an\}$ of positive integers is defined by \[a_n=\left[ n +\sqrt n + \frac 12 \right] , \qquad \forall n \in \mathbb N\] Determine the positive integers that occur in the sequence.
It's immediate to check that $m^2+k+1> (m^2-m+k)+\sqrt{m^2-m+k}+\frac 12 \ge m^2+k$ $\forall$ positive integers $m,k$ such that $1\le k\le 2m$ So $a_{m^2-m+k}=m^2+k$ $\forall$ positive integers $m,k$ such that $1\le k\le 2m$ and so **any non square positive integer may be reached**. On the other hand, the equation $p^2+1>n+\sqrt n+\frac 12\ge p^2$ may be written : $p^2+\frac 34>(\sqrt n+\frac 12)^2\ge p^2-\frac 14$ $\iff$ $\sqrt{p^2+\frac 34}-\frac 12>\sqrt n\ge \sqrt{p^2-\frac 14}-\frac 12$ $\iff$ $p^2+1-\sqrt{p^2+\frac 34}>n\ge p^2-\sqrt{p^2-\frac 14}$ which is impossible since $p^2-p+1>p^2+1-\sqrt{p^2+\frac 34}$ and $p^2-\sqrt{p^2-\frac 14}>p^2-p$ And so **no perfect square may be reached**. Hence the answer : the set of values of the sequence $\{a_n\}$ is exactly the set of all non perfect square positive integers.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/International Contests/IMO Longlists/1992 IMO Longlists/364945.json

stem_md: Given any triangle  $ABC$  and any positive integer  $n$ , we say that  $n$  is a *decomposable* number for triangle  $ABC$  if there exists a decomposition of the triangle  $ABC$  into  $n$  subtriangles with each subtriangle similar to   $\triangle ABC$ . Determine the positive integers that are decomposable numbers for every triangle.
solution_md:
Let the triangle side be 1. 

Normally "similar" for triangles means "having the same angles". In that case, any even number  $n=2k,k\ge 2$  will do trivially: take one triangle of side  $\frac{k-1}k$ , and a 'double' row of small ones of side  $\frac 1k$ .  

From  $n=4$ , we further get  $n=7,10,...$ , by subdividing successively one of the triangles into four smaller ones. Likewise 
from  $n=6$ , we get  $n=9,12,...$  and
from  $n=8$ , we get  $n=11,14,...$ .

The only missing values are thus  $n=2,3,5$ . It is easy to see that those are not feasible.

Let  $F_n$  be the nth Fibonacci number, defined by  $F_1 = F_2 = 1$  and  $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$  for  $n > 2$ . Let  $A_0, A_1, A_2,\cdots$  be a sequence of points on a circle of radius  $1$  such that the minor arc from  $A_{k-1}$  to  $A_k$  runs clockwise and such that
\[\mu(A_{k-1}A_k)=\frac{4F_{2k+1}}{F_{2k+1}^2+1}\]
for  $k \geq 1$ , where  $\mu(XY )$  denotes the radian measure of the arc  $XY$  in the clockwise direction. What is the limit of the radian measure of arc  $A_0A_n$  as  $n$  approaches infinity?
solution_md:
If I get it right, we are essentially looking for  $A:=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{F_{2k+1}}{F_{2k+1}^2+1}$ . 
Let  $S:=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac1{F_{2k+1}}$ . 
Now we have $A=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{F_{2k+1}}{F_{2k-1}F_{2k+3}}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \left(\frac1 {F_{2k-1}}-\frac{F_{2k+2}}{F_{2k-1}F_{2k+3}}\right)$  (*) 

and also $A=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\left(\frac2 {F_{2k+3}} +\frac{F_{2k-2}}{F_{2k-1}F_{2k+3}}\right)$  (**)

Adding  $\frac13$ (*) and  $\frac23$ (**) and using  $F_{2k-1}=\frac{F_{2k+2}-2F_{2k-2}}3 $ , we can simplify the denominators and find $A=\frac{1+S}3+4\frac{S-1}3-(S-1)=\frac23S$ . Sadly, it seems impossible though to give a closed form expression for  $S$  using only elementary functions.

stem_md: Given a graph with  $n$  vertices and a positive integer  $m$  that is less than  $ n$ , prove that the graph contains a set of  $m+1$  vertices in which the difference between the largest degree of any vertex in the set and the smallest degree of any vertex in the set is at most  $m-1.$
solution_md: We approach the problem by using a double induction. First, we induct on $n$ . For $n=2$ we have $m=1$ , and the graph $G$ has at most one edge. In any case, we can always take the whole vertex set as the required subset. Now assume the statement holds for $n=s-1 \geqslant 2$ , and consider a graph $G$ with $s$ vertices. Fixing $n$ , we proceed with a reverse induction on the number of edges $E$ of $G$ , where $0 \leqslant E \leqslant \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ . For $E=\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$ the claim is obvious, since $G$ is then a complete graph and the degrees of any two vertices are equal, so the difference is $0 \leqslant m-1$ . Now assume the claim holds for $E=k \geqslant 1$ , and consider a graph $G$ with $E=k-1$ edges.**Case 1.** $m=n-1$ . If $G$ has no vertex of degree $n-1$ , then taking the whole vertex set works. Otherwise, if there exists a vertex of degree $n-1$ , then again taking all vertices works, since every other vertex has degree at least $1$ (being adjacent to that vertex).**Case 2.** $m2.1.** $n$ is even. Add a perfect matching to $G$ . Then apply the second induction hypothesis. Since every degree increases by $1$ , the desired subset follows.**2.2.** $n$ is odd. Let $w$ be a vertex of minimum degree. Add a perfect matching to $G-w$ , and apply the second induction hypothesis on this new graph. If the resulting subset lies entirely in $G-w$ , we are done. Otherwise, when transferring back to $G$ , the degrees of vertices in the subset decrease by $1$ (except for $w$ , which is already the minimum-degree vertex), so the condition is still satisfied. Thus both induction steps are complete, and the problem is proved. $\square$

candidates: Isn't it a simple consequence of the [Erdős–Gallai Theorem](http://mathworld.wolfram.com/GraphicSequence.html)?

Proof :

Assume that we have counterexample for pair  $(n, m)$  with maximal  $m$  while  $n$  is fixed. Let  $G$  be graph with such pair and let  $d_1\leq d_2\leq\ldots\leq d_n$  be set of orders of elements from  $G$ . Then easy to see that  $d_{m+i}-d_i\geq m, d_{2m+i}-d_{m+i}\geq m, \ldots, d_{lm+i}-d_{(l-1)m+i}\geq m$ . So  $d_{lm+i} - d_i\geq m$  for every  $i$  and  $l : lm+1\leq n$ . So if  $n<2m$  we have that pair  $(n, 2m)$  gives us counterexample with larger  $m$ . So we have that  $n\leq 2m$ .

If  $n = 2m$  we have that  $d_{m+1}-d_1\geq m, d_{m+2}-d_{2}\geq m, \ldots, d_{2m}-d_{m}\geq m$ , so  $(d_{m+1}+\ldots + d_{2m}) - (d_1 + \ldots + d_m)\geq m^2$  and so induced graph on vertices  $v_{m+1}, \ldots, v_{2m}$  must have  $\geq \frac{m^2}{2}$  edges which can't be true.

If  $n< 2m$ , then consider graph  $G':=G\setminus v_m$  and use induction hypothesis to it. So there exists vertices  $v_i, v_{i+1}, \ldots, v_{j}$  in induced graph  $G'$  formed set of  $m$  vertices in which the difference between the largest degree of any vertex in the set and the smallest degree of any vertex in the set is at most  $m-2$ . So we have that  $d_{j} - d_i\leq m-1$  (because we need to add  $v_m$  and edges from it to get graph  $G$ ). From  $n<2m$  we get that  $m\in [i, j]$ , so  $j-i= m+1$  and we get contradiction.  $\Box$
