We trivially see  $h'=0$  and  $p'=\frac{b+c}{a}$ similarly  $q'=\frac{c+a}{b},r'=\frac{a+b}{c}$ Now notice:  $$ |p'+1|=|q'+1|=|r'+1|=|a+b+c| $$  So  $o'=-1$  and because  $h'=0$  it's left to prove  $g'$  is a real number which is true since:  $$ p'+q'+r'=\frac{a^2b+a^2c+b^2a+b^2c+c^2a+c^2b}{abc}\in \mathbb{R}~~\blacksquare $$

Let  $A_B$  be the reflection of  $A$  over the  $B$ -altitude, and define  $A_C,B_A,B_C,C_A,C_B$  similarly. Let  $A_BB_A\cap A_CC_A=A'$  and define  $B',C'$  similarly.

Notice  $\measuredangle BA_CC=-\measuredangle BAC=\measuredangle BHC,$  so  $(BHC)$  passes through  $A_C,$  and by symmetry  $A_B.$  Next, since  $AB\cdot AA_C=AC\cdot AA_B,$  we get  $A$  lies on the radical axis of  $(C_ABA_C)$  and  $(B_ACA_B),$  but pairs  $B,B_A$  and  $C,C_A$  share a midpoint, which is the foot of the altitude from  $A,$  and thus the radical axis is line  $AH.$ In particular we have  $(C_ABA_C)$  and  $(B_ACA_B)$  are congruent, so  $\measuredangle A'A_CA=\measuredangle C_AA_CB=\measuredangle B_AA_BC=\measuredangle A'A_BA,$  so  $A,A',A_B,A_C$  are concyclic. By definition we have  $AH=A_BH=A_CH,$  so  $AH=A'H.$  Also  $\measuredangle C'A'B'=\measuredangle A_CA'A_B=\measuredangle A_CAA_B=\measuredangle BAC,$  so by symmetry we have  $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle A'B'C',$  oppositely oriented.

Next reflect  $\triangle A'B'C'$  over the perpendicular bisector of  $AA',$  which passes thorugh  $H.$  If  $B',C'$  are sent to  $D,E$  then  $\triangle ADE\sim\triangle ABC,$  similarly oriented. We also have  $HB=HB'=HD$  and  $HC=HC'=HE.$ Now, letting  $M,N$  be midpoints of  $BD,CE$  we get  $BD\perp MH,CE\perp NH.$  Now if  $P=BD\cap CE,$  then by spiral similarity we have  $(ADEP),(ABCP)$  cyclic, and by Gliding Principle, also  $(AMNP).$  But the right angles give  $(PMHN)$  is cyclic with diameter  $HP.$  Since  $AH\perp BC$  we must then have  $AP\parallel BC,$  and since  $APBC$  is cyclic we get that it is an isosceles trapezoid.

Now we want to show that  $H$  lies on the Euler line of  $\triangle ADE,$  because reflecting back gives the desired result. Call  $O,O'$  the circumcenters of  $\triangle ABC$  and  $\triangle ADE,$  and call  $H'$  the orthocenter of  $\triangle ADE.$  Now if  $HO\cap H'O'=X\ne H,$  we would have  $A,O,O',X$  cyclic by spiral similarity. Thus it suffices to show  $A,O,O',H$  are cyclic. Since  $O,O'$  lie on the perpendicular bisector of  $AP,$  it suffices to show  $AO'OH$  is an isosceles trapezoid.

Now let  $O''$  be the midpoint of  $PH$  and thus the circumcenter of  $\triangle AMN.$  There is a spiral similarity at  $A$  sending  $\triangle BCO$  to  $\triangle MNO''$  to  $\triangle DEO',$  so there is a spiral similarity at  $A$  sending  $BMD$  to  $OO''O'$  to  $CNE,$  so by Gliding Principle  $O''$  is the midpoint of  $OO'.$  Thus the perpendicular bisectors of  $AH$  and  $OO'$  are parallel and both pass through  $O'',$  so we are done.

For points  $P$  and  $Q$ , let  $P_Q$  be the reflection of  $P$  over  $QH$ . Then define  $A' = \overline{C_AA_C} \cap \overline{B_AA_B}$  and define  $B'$ ,  $C'$  similarly. Clearly this is the triangle that we care about.

Now, taking a homothety at  $A$  with scale factor  $\frac 12$ , we find that  $A_CA_B$  is antiparallel to  $BC$ , whence  $A_CBA_BC$  is cyclic. More particularly this means that  $\triangle AC_AB_A \sim^+ \triangle AA_CA_B$ , so  $A$  is the spiral center taking  $C_AB_A$  to  $A_CA_B$ . In particularly it follows that  $AA_CA'A_B$  is cyclic. Moreover since we have reflections over  $BH$  and  $CH$ , we conclude that  $A'H = AH$ .

Let  $H'$  and  $O'$  be the orthocenter and circumcenter respectively of  $A'B'C'$ .

From similar triangles we have
\[ \frac{A'H'}{B'H'} = \frac{AH}{BH} = \frac{A'H}{B'H} \]
and similar, so  $H'$  lies on the  $H$ -apollonian circles of  $\triangle HA'B'$ ,  $\triangle HB'C'$ , and  $\triangle HC'A'$ .

But then it is well known that these apollonian circles are orthogonal to  $(A'B'C')$  by say, inversion. Particularly these three circles stay fixed, and  $H$  must be the inverse of  $H'$  with respect to  $(A'B'C')$ . We are done.

I had a terrible time solving this problem because I thought it was going to be harder than it was. The crux is to introduce  $K$  the isogonal conjugate of the point of infinity along the Euler line;  $T = KH \cap (ABC)$  actually lies on the circumcircle of  $\mathcal{T}$ . This can be proven with a terrible amount of angle chasing because  $T$  lies on  $(AHP)$ ,  $(BHQ)$ ,  $(CHR)$  as well (where  $P$ ,  $Q$ ,  $R$  are the vertices of  $\mathcal{T}$ ). This allows one to do inversion at  $H$  and it turns out that the orthocenter of  $\mathcal{T}$ , which is  $PH_A \cap QH_B \cap RH_C$ , maps to the center of the image under inversion of the circumcircle of  $\mathcal{T}$ .

This problem is an extension to the Isreal problem [https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/u1035145h3212242p31098325](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/u1035145h3212242p31098325). The triangle obtained by the reflections of circumcenters over altitudes shifted by the vector  $\overrightarrow{OX}$  will give you the triangle formed by the three lines  $\ell_a$ ,  $\ell_b$ ,  $\ell_c$ . Noticing this will give you the desired synthetic solution.

Notice that  $H$  is the circumcenter of  $AA_BA_C$  and so  $HA'=HA=2r(ABC)\cos \angle A$ .

Since  $H'A'=2r(A'B'C')\cos \angle A'$  we must have $\frac{HA'}{H'A'}=\frac{r(ABC)}{r(A'B'C')}$  as  $\angle A = \angle A'$  by aforementioned concyclicity. This expression is symmetric in  $A'$ ,  $B'$ ,  $C'$  then by Apollonius circles  $H$  and  $H'$  are inversive pairs in  $(A'B'C')$ , i.e.  $HH'$  passes through the circumcenter  $O'$  of  $\mathcal{T}$ .

<details><summary>Two hybrid solutions</summary>Let  $P_q$  denote the reflection of  $P$  in  $QH$  and let the new triangle be  $\triangle A'B'C'$  with Euler line  $O'H'$ . It's easy to see that  $A_b, A_c \in (BHC)$ , so  $\triangle AA_bA_c \sim \triangle AB_aC_a$ . Thus, by spiral similarity  $\triangle AA_bB_a \sim \triangle AA_cC_a$  and  $AA_bA_cA'$  is cyclic with circumcenter  $H$ . This implies that  $AB_aC_aA'$  is cyclic and that  $\triangle A'B'C' \sim \triangle ABC$ . Moreover, it's easy to see that  $B'C'=B_cC_b$  as  $HB'=HB_c$  and  $HC'=HC_b$ . This implies by law of sines that  $\triangle A'B'C'$ ,  $\triangle AB_cC_b$  and the other two analogous triangles have the same circumradius (denote it by  $R'$ ). Now, we present two hybrid ways to finish the solution, where the first one motivates the second. $\textit{Approach 1.}$  We will use the classic trick to deal with a line passing through a circumcenter by reflecting a point on the circumcircle in this line. Let  $(AA_bA_c) \cap (A'B'C')=A"$ ; notice that  $HA=HA"$ , so it suffices to show that  $H'A"=H'A'$ . We notice that  $AA" \parallel B_aC_a$ , so instead redefine  $A"$  as the intersection of the line through  $A$  parallel to  $B_aC_a$  with  $(AA_bA_c)$ . Since  $HB'=HB_c$ ,  $HC'=HC_b$  and  $HA=HA"$ ,  $AB_cB'A"$  and  $AC_bC'A"$  are isosceles trapezoids. This means that  $\triangle AB_cC_b$  and  $\triangle A"B'C'$  are congruent, which implies that  $A" \in (A'B'C')$ . 

Now that we have a lot of equal segments, we can calculate  $H'A"$  via law of cosines in  $\triangle H'A"C$ . Let  $\angle AB_cC_b=\varphi$ . Indeed, observe that  $A'H'=2R'\cos \alpha$ ,  $C'H'=2R'\cos \gamma$ ,  $A"C'=AC_b=2R'\sin \varphi$  and  $\angle H'C'A"=90^{\circ}-\beta+\alpha-\varphi$ , so we want   $$ (2R'\cos \alpha)^2=(2R'\cos \gamma)^2+(2R'\sin \varphi)^2-2\cdot 2R'\cos \alpha \cdot 2R'\sin \varphi \cdot \sin (\beta+\varphi-\alpha). $$   Now we can divide by  $4R'^2$  and we can express with the sides of  $\triangle ABC$   $\sin \varphi, \cos \varphi$  by law of sines and cosines in  $\triangle AB_cC_b$ . Then we can plug them in the above expression and this eventually finishes the problem, though the amount of bash is brutal. Instead, we will use synthetic progress from here in Approach 2 to minimize the amount of bash. $\textit{Approach 2.}$  We will again introduce the line through  $A$  parallel to  $B_aC_a$ , but this time for all three vertices. Notice that if the lines for  $A,B$  meet at  $X$ , then  $\angle AXB=\angle A'C'B'=\angle ACB$ , so the three lines meet at a point  $X \in (ABC).$  We now conjecture that  $X \in (A'B'C')$ , which leads to  $\triangle ABC \cup \{X\} \sim \triangle A'B'C' \cup \{X\}$  and  $A'X \parallel BC$  by simple angle chasing. This motivates us to redefine  $X$  as the intersection of the lines through  $A'$  parallel to  $BC$  and the two analogous ones - they are concurrent since the intersection of any two of them lies on  $(A'B'C')$  (the angle chase proving this is similar to the one for  $ABC$ ). We want to show that  $X \in (ABC)$ , so consider the intersections of these lines with  $(ABC)$  - call them  $A_2,B_2,C_2$ . We have that  $\angle B_2XC_2=\angle BAC$  and we want to show that  $\angle B_2XC_2=\angle B_2A_2C_2$ , so it suffices to show that  $\triangle A_2B_2C_2$  and  $\triangle ABC$  are congruent. Thus,  $HA_2=HA$  and  $OA_2=OA$ , so  $A,A_2$  are reflections in  $OH$ . This finally implies that  $X \in (ABC)$ . As we said before,  $\angle A'XB'=\angle ACB=\angle AXB$ , so indeed  $\triangle ABC \cup \{X\} \sim \triangle A'B'C' \cup \{X\}$ .

The last one implies that  $\angle XO'H'=\angle XOH$ , so we need  $\angle XOH=\angle XO'H$ . Thus, proving that  $OHO'X$  is a parallelogram will finish the problem. We have that  $\angle O'XA'=\angle OXA=\angle AA_2X-90^{\circ}=\angle (OH, BC)$ , so  $OH \parallel O'X$ . We are only left to show that  $R'=OH$  - this can be done by showing  $B_cC_b=2OH \sin \alpha$ , which can be calculated via law of cosines in  $\triangle AB_cC_b$  by using  $OH^2=9R^2-(a^2+b^2+c^2)$  (and this length bash is by far much better than the one in Approach 1). Let  $A_B$  and  $A_C$  be the reflections of  $A$  over  $BH$  and  $CH$ , and define  $B_A$ ,  $B_C$ ,  $C_A$ ,  $C_B$  similarly. Then  $\triangle AC_BB_C$  is the reflection of  $\triangle ABC$  over  $AH$ , so they are inversely similar. Also,  $\measuredangle CA_BA = \measuredangle ABC = \measuredangle AA_CB$ , so  $BA_CCA_B$  is cyclic, and hence  $\triangle AA_CA_B$  and  $\triangle ABC$  are also inversely similar. Therefore,  $\triangle AC_BB_C \stackrel{+}{\sim} \triangle AA_BA_C$ , so  $A$  is the Miquel point of quadrilateral  $A_BC_BB_CA_C$ . In particular,  $A, A', A_B, A_C$  are concyclic, and  $\measuredangle B'A'C' = -\measuredangle BAC$ . Since  $H$  is the circumcenter of  $\triangle A'A_BA_C$ , it also follows that  $HA = HA' = HA_B = HA_C$ . Repeating this for other vertices, we see that  $\triangle ABC$  and  $\triangle A'B'C'$  are inversely similar.

Let  $H'$  be the orthocenter of  $\triangle A'B'C'$ . Let  $M', N', P'$  be the midpoints, and let  $D'$ ,  $E'$ ,  $F'$  (resp.  $X$ ,  $Y$ ,  $Z$ ) be the feet of perpendiculars from  $H'$  (resp.  $H$ ) onto the sides  $B'C', C'A'$  and  $A'B'$ . To show the collinearity, it then suffices to show that
\[ \frac{M'X}{M'D'} = \frac{N'Y}{N'E'} = \frac{P'Z}{P'F'}, \]
in the directed sense. We will show the second equality, using complex numbers to avoid dealing with config issues. Since  $HC_B = HC'$ ,  $Y$  is the midpoint of  $C_BC'$ , so  $A'C_B = 2N'Y$ , and similarly,  $A'B_C = 2P'Z$ . Therefore,
\[ \frac{y - n'}{z - p'} = \frac{c_b - a'}{b_c - a'}. \]

Similarly,  $\ell_{B}\parallel SB$  and  $\ell_{C}\parallel SC$ .**Proof.** Notice that
\begin{align*}\angle\left(OH, BC\right)&=\angle SCB+\angle H_ASC
&=\angle SCB+\left(90^{\circ}-\angle ACB\right),
\end{align*}
therefore
\begin{align*}\angle\left(SA, BC\right)&=\angle ASC-\angle SCB
&=\angle ABC-\left(\angle\left(OH, BC\right)+\angle ACB-90^{\circ}\right)
&=\angle AHO+\angle HAO
&=180^{\circ}-\angle AOH,
\end{align*}
so it remains to show that  $\angle\left(\ell_{A}, BC\right)=180^{\circ}-\angle AOH$ . To this extent, we invert around  $A$  with power  $AH\cdot AD$ . Then  $B_C$  maps to  $U$ , the intersection of  $DE$  and  $AB$  (by harmonic bundles). Similarly,  $C_B$  maps to  $V$ , the intersection of  $DF$  and  $AC$ . Also due to harmonic bundles,  $UV, EF$  and  $BC$  concur at a point  $S$  and (because  $AO\perp EF$ ) we find that  $$ \angle\left(\ell_{A}, BC\right)=\angle ESU=90^{\circ}-\angle\left(AO, UV\right). $$  However it is well-known that  $OH\perp UV$  (since  $UV$  is simply the orthic axis of  $\triangle ABC$ ), therefore  $$ 90^{\circ}-\angle\left(AO, UV\right)=90^{\circ}-\angle\left(OH, EF\right)=180^{\circ}-\angle AOH, $$  as desired. Our proof is complete.

Because of our lemma, it immediately follows that  $\triangle SBC\simeq\triangle XC_AB_A$ . Furthermore,  $SXB_AC$  is a parallelogram and so  $SX\parallel BC$ . Similarly,  $SY\parallel AC$  and  $SZ\parallel AB$ . We consequently have the following**Claim.**  $\triangle XYZ\cup S\simeq\triangle ABC\cup S$ .**Proof.** Clear by the above.

Let  $H'$  and  $O'$  be the orthocenter and circumcenter of  $\triangle XYZ$  respectively. We will show that  $O', H', H$  are collinear on a line parallel to  $SO$ . To this extent, we make two separate claims (the second of which is pretty enlightening).**Claim.**  $O'H'\parallel SO.$ **Proof.** We wish to show that  $\angle\left(O'H', BC\right)=\angle\left(SO, BC\right)$ . This follows by angle chasing (freely using the very first lemma and the subsequent claim). Notice that   $$ \angle\left(O'H', BC\right)=180^{\circ}-\angle\left(\ell_{A}, BC\right)-\left(180^{\circ}-\angle\left(O'H', \ell_{A}\right)\right) $$  or equivalently  $$ \angle\left(O'H', BC\right)=180^{\circ}-\angle\left(\ell_{A}, BC\right)-\left(180^{\circ}-\angle\left(OH, BC\right)\right). $$  However  $\angle\left(\ell_{A}, BC\right)=\angle\left(SA, BC\right)$ , so the desired reduces to showing that  $$ \angle\left(OH, BC\right)=\angle\left(SA, BC\right)+\angle\left(SO, BC\right)=\angle ASO. $$  But  $\angle ASO=90^{\circ}-\angle SCA$  and  $\angle\left(OH, BC\right)=90^{\circ}-\angle AHO$ , so we simply wish to prove that  $\angle SCA=\angle AHO$ . But since  $\angle\left(SA, BC\right)=180^{\circ}-\angle AOH$ , it follows that  $$ \angle SAB+\left(180^{\circ}-\angle ABC\right)=\angle AOH, $$  so 
\begin{align*}\angle SAB&=\left(\angle ABC-\angle HAO\right)-\angle AOH
&=\angle ACB-\angle AOH,
\end{align*}
which reduces to the desired.**Claim.**  $SO'HO$  is a parallelogram.**Proof.** We start by showing that  $SO'\parallel OH$ . This is an angle chasing argument similar to the above. We wish to show that  $\angle\left(SO', BC\right)=\angle\left(OH, BC\right)$ . But notice that
\begin{align*}\angle\left(SO', BC\right)&=\angle\left(SO', \ell_{A}\right)+\angle\left(\ell_{A}, BC\right)
&=\angle\left(SO, BC\right)+\left(180^{\circ}-\angle AOH\right)
\end{align*}
Due to the evaluation of  $\angle SAB=\angle SCB$  provided in the previous claim, we have
\begin{align*}\angle\left(SO, BC\right)&=180^{\circ}-\angle SBC-\angle BSO
&=\angle SAC-\left(90^{\circ}-\angle SCB\right)
&=2\angle SCB+\angle BAC-90^{\circ}
&=2\left(\angle ACB-\angle AHO\right)+\angle BAC-90^{\circ}
&=90^{\circ}-\left(\angle ABC-\angle ACB\right)-2\angle AHO
&=90^{\circ}-\angle HAO-2\angle AHO
&=\angle AOH-\angle AHO-90^{\circ}
\end{align*}
Because  $\angle\left(OH, BC\right)=90^{\circ}-\angle AHO$ , the desired follows readily.

Finally, we show that  $SO'=OH$ . Recalling that  $\triangle XYZ\cup S\simeq\triangle ABC\cup S$  and denoting the circumradius of  $\triangle ABC$  by  $R$ , we have  $$ \frac{SO'}{R}=\frac{XS}{SA}=\frac{B_AC}{SA}, $$  so it suffices to show that  $$ \frac{OH}{R}=\frac{B_AC}{SA}. $$  However by the law of sines  $SA=2R\sin{\angle SCA}=2R\sin{\angle AHO}$  (as computed previously). Moreover, also by the law of sines   $$ \frac{OH}{R}=\frac{\sin{\left(B-C\right)}}{\sin{\angle AHO}}, $$  so it remains to show that  $$ B_AC=2R\sin{\left(B-C\right)}. $$  But
\begin{align*}B_AC&=CD-BD
&=AC\cos{C}-AB\cos{B}
&=2R\left(\sin{B}\cos{C}-\sin{C}\cos{B}\right)
&=2R\sin{\left(B-C\right)}.
\end{align*}
The claim is proven.

stem_md:
Let \(\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) be the set of all positive integers. Determine all subsets \(\mathcal{S}\) of \(\{2^{0},2^{1},2^{2},\ldots\}\) for which there exists a function \(f\colon\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) such that
\[\mathcal{S}=\{f(a+b)-f(a)-f(b)\mid a,b\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\}.\]
*Pitchayut Saengrungkongka, Thailand*
solution_md:
Beautiful problem! In my opinion this weird function condition has a strong combinatorical flavor, which makes this problem elegant. This is my favorite ISL Algebra problem so far :coolspeak: I also like the fact that the construction part is simple but not trivial, where only about $2$ out of $27$ contestants got the construction in Indonesia TST. I found the construction but did not get any progress on the bounding part at the TST, but I believe I have found a solution after doing it for a long time after the TST, I hope this is valid :)**Answer:** Non-empty $\boxed{ | \mathcal{S} | \le 2}$ **Construction:** Let a nonempty $|\mathcal{S}|\le 2$ . Let $\mathcal{S} = \{2^m,2^k\}$ for nonnegative integers $m,k$ . (If $|\mathcal{S}|=1$ , we let $m=k$ ) Define a function $f :\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ as follows: $$ f(x) = x + \left\lfloor \frac{x}{2} \right\rfloor 2^m + \left\lfloor \frac{x-1}{2} \right\rfloor 2^k. $$ Observe that for each $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} $ , we have \begin{align*} f(a+b)- &f(a) -f(b) &= \left( \left\lfloor \frac{a+b}{2} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{a}{2} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{b}{2} \right\rfloor \right)2^m &+ \left( \left\lfloor \frac{a+b-1}{2} \right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \frac{a-1}{2} \right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \frac{b-1}{2} \right\rfloor\right) 2^k \end{align*} Observe that $\left\lfloor \dfrac{x}{2} \right\rfloor+\left\lfloor \dfrac{x-1}{2} \right\rfloor = x-1$ , so $$ \left( \left\lfloor \frac{a+b}{2} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{a}{2} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{b}{2} \right\rfloor \right) + \left( \left\lfloor \frac{a+b-1}{2} \right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \frac{a-1}{2} \right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \frac{b-1}{2} \right\rfloor\right) = 1. $$ Moreover, observe that \begin{align*} \left\lfloor \frac{a+b}{2} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{a}{2} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{b}{2} \right\rfloor &= \left\lfloor \left\{\frac{a}{2} \right\} + \left\{\frac{b}{2} \right\} \right\rfloor \in \{0,1\} \left\lfloor \frac{a+b-1}{2} \right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \frac{a-1}{2} \right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \frac{b-1}{2} \right\rfloor &= 1 - \left\lfloor \left\{\frac{a}{2} \right\} + \left\{\frac{b}{2} \right\} \right\rfloor \in \{0,1\} \end{align*} Hence, they both are nonnegative integers whose sum to $1$ . Hence, \[ f(a+b)-f(a)-f(b) \in \{2^m,2^k\}= \mathcal{S}. \] For the pair $(a,b)$ that generates $2^m,2^k$ , take \begin{align*} (a,b)=(1,1) \implies f(2)-f(1)-f(1) &= (2x+2^m)-x-x = 2^m (a,b)=(2,1)\implies f(3)-f(2)-f(1) &= (3x+2^m+2^k)-(2x+2^m)-x = 2^k \end{align*} Hence, it's proven that $$ \{f(a+b)-f(a)-f(b) \mid a,b\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \} = \{2^m,2^k\} = \mathcal{S}. $$ Hence, any nonempty set $|\mathcal{S}|\le 2$ satisfies. **Necessity:** We will prove that $|\mathcal{S}|\le 2$ . Assume there exist a function $f:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that \[ \{ f(a+b)-f(a)-f(b) \mid a,b\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \}=\mathcal{S}\subseteq \{2^0,2^1,2^2,\ldots\}.\] We will show that $|\mathcal{S}|\le 2$ . Throughout this solution, let $\{\}$ denote multiset. Let $A:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to \mathcal{S}$ be a function such that \[A(x,y) = f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y) \text{ for every } x,y \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \] **Lemma:** If $2^a+2^b=2^c+2^d$ , then $\{a,b\}=\{c,d\}$ for nonnegative integers $a,b,c,d$ .
ProofIf $a=b$ , then $2^{a+1}=2^c+2^d$ . If $c\ne d$ , then $2^c+2^d$ is divisible by some odd prime, contradiction. So, $a=b=c=d$ . Now, assume $a\ne b$ and $c\ne d$ , hence $\text{min}\{a,b\}=\nu_2(2^a+2^b)=\nu_2(2^c+2^d)=\text{min}\{c,d\}$ . From $\text{min}\{a,b\}=\text{min}\{c,d\}$ , it also follows that $2^{\text{max}\{a,b\}}=2^{\text{max}\{c,d\}}$ , So $\{a,b\}=\{c,d\}$ proven
The main claim is as follows: **Claim:** $\{ A(1,1) , A(2,1) , A(3,1), \ldots \}$ has at most $2$ distinct elements **Proof:** We will prove the statement:if $A(n,1) \not\in \{ A(1,1), A(2,1), \ldots, A(n-1,1) \}$ , then $A(1,1)=A(2,1)=\ldots = A(n-1,1)$ . Let $A(1,1)=2^a$ . Let $A(n,1)=2^b$ such that $A(1,1),A(2,1),\ldots,A(n-1,1)\ne 2^b$ . From \begin{align*} f(n+2)-f(n)-f(1)-f(1) = A(n,1)+A(n+1,1) &= A(n,2)+A(1,1) \implies 2^b + A(n+1,1) &= A(n,2) + 2^a \end{align*} hence $A(n,2) = 2^b$ . Now, for $x\ge 2$ , observe that \[ A(x-1,y+1) + A(y,1) = A(x,y) + A(x-1, 1)\] if $y\le n-1$ and $x\ge 2$ with $A(x,y)=2^b$ , observe that from lemma, $2^b = A(x,y)\in \{ A(x-1,y+1), A(y,1)\}$ . Since $y\le n-1$ , then $A(y,1)\ne 2^b$ . Hence, $A(x-1,y+1)=2^b$ . Applying it repeatedly \begin{align*} 2^b &= A(n,2) = A(n-1, 3) = \cdots = A(3, n-1) = A(2, n) 2^b &= A(n,1) = A(n-1, 2) = \cdots = A(3, n-2) = A(2, n-1) \end{align*} Which implies \begin{align*} f(n)+f(2) &= f(n-1)+f(3) = \cdots = f(3)+f(n-1) = f(2)+f(n) f(n)+f(1) &= f(n-1)+f(2) = \cdots = f(3)+f(n-2) = f(2)+f(n-1) \end{align*} substracting, we get \begin{align*} &f(2)-f(1) = f(3)-f(2)=\cdots = f(n)-f(n-1) \implies &f(2)-f(1)-f(1) = f(3)-f(2)-f(1) = \cdots = f(n)-f(n-1)-f(1) \implies &A(1,1) = A(2,1) = \cdots = A(n-1,1) \end{align*} Hence, it is proven that if $A(n,1)\ne A(1,1), A(2,1),\ldots , A(n-1,1)$ , then $A(1,1)=A(2,1)=\cdots = A(n-1,1)$ . Therefore, $ \{ A(1,1) , A(2,1) , A(3,1), \ldots \}$ only has at most $2$ distinct elements. Claim proven $\square$ By claim, let set $\{ A(1,1) , A(2,1) , A(3,1), \ldots \} \subseteq \{2^a , 2^b\}$ . Recall from earlier that $$ A(x-1,y+1) + A(y,1) = A(x,y) + A(x-1, 1). $$ If $A(x,y) \in \{2^a, 2^b\}$ , observe that $A(x-1,y+1)\in \{2^a, 2^b\}$ . Take $y=1$ , since $A(x,1)\in \{2^a, 2^b\}$ , inductively we obtain $A(x,1), A(x-1,2),\ldots, A(1,x)\in \{2^a,2^b\}$ for all positive integers $x$ . Hence, all $A(i,j)\in \{2^a, 2^b\}$ for all positive integers $i,j$ . Hence, $|\mathcal{S}| \le 2$ is proven.

We'll Induct on  $n$ . For  $n=1$ , note that  $$ f(m+2)-f(m)-f(2)=2^{a_{m}}+2^{a_{m+1}}-2^{a_1} $$  is a non-negative power of two. By the lemma earlier we are done. Now suppose this holds for some  $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ , note that  $$   \{a_m,a_{m+1},\dots,a_{m+n} \}=\{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n \} \cup \{ x\} $$  for some non-negative integer  $x$ . Then note that,  $$ f(m+n+2)-f(m)-f(n+2)=2^{a_{m+n+1}}+2^x-2^{a_{n+1}} $$  by the lemma earlier we have  $a_{n+1}=a_{m+n+1}$  or  $x$ . Both yields  $$ \{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{n+1} \} \subset \{a_m,a_{m+1},\dots,a_{m+n+1} \} $$  hence the statement also holds for  $n+1$ . We are done by Induction.
-----**Lemma 3.** Let  $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ . If  $a_{n+1} \notin \{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n \}$ , then  $a_1=a_2=\dots=a_n$ .**Proof.** If  $n=1$  we are done, suppose  $n>1$ . Note that  $a_1 \in \{ a_{n+1},a_{n+2}\}$ , hence  $a_1=a_{n+2}$ . 

Now for all  $i=1,2,\dots,n$  we will prove that  $a_1=a_i=a_{n+1-i}$ , by strong Induction on  $i$ . For  $i=1$ , note that  $a_1 \in \{ a_n,a_{n+1}\}$ , hence  $a_1=a_n$ . Suppose this holds for all  $i=1,2,\dots,k$  where  $1 \le k <n$  is an integer. Note that,  $$ \{ a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{k+1}\} \subset \{ a_{n+1-k},a_{n+2-k},\dots,a_{n+1},a_{n+2}\} $$  by Induction Hypothesis we have  $a_1=a_2=\dots=a_k$  and  $a_1=a_{n+1-k}=\dots=a_{n}$ . Hence we must have  $a_{k+1} \in \{a_{n+1},a_{n+2}\}$ , which forces  $a_{k+1}=a_1$ . Next we have  $$ \{ a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{k+1}\} \subset \{ a_{n-k},a_{n+1-k},\dots,a_{n+1}\} $$  hence, by the fact before, we must have  $a_{n-k}=a_1$ . Thus it also holds for all  $i=1,2,\dots,k+1$ . Our Induction is finished and indeed  $a_1=a_2=\dots=a_n$ .
-----
As a consequence of lemma  $3$ , we notice that if there exist  $k<\ell \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$  such that   $$ a_{k+1} \notin \{ a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k\}, \ a_{\ell+1} \notin \{ a_1,a_2,\dots,a_\ell\} $$  then this implies  $a_1=a_2=\dots=a_\ell$ . But this contradicts  $a_{k+1} \notin \{ a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k\}$ . 

Thus for all  $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$  we have  $a_n \in \{ 2^a,2^b\}$  where  $a,b$  are not necessarily distinct non-negative integers. Thus for all  $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$  we have  $$ f(m+1)-f(m)-f(1)=2^{a_m} \in \{2^a,2^b\} $$  now we'll prove by Induction that, for all  $m,n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ . We have  $$ f(m+n)-f(m)-f(n) \in\{2^a,2^b \} $$  we'll Induct on  $n$ . We've proven the base case  $n=1$ . Suppose this holds for all  $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$  and fixed  $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ . Note that,  $$ f(m+n+1)-f(m)-f(n+1)=(f(m+n+1)-f(m+n)-f(1))+(f(m+n)-f(m)-f(n))-(f(n+1)-f(n)-f(1)) $$  where each of the three terms in the  $RHS$  is either  $2^a$  or  $2^b$ . Since the  $LHS$  must also be a non-negative power of two, it's easy to conclude by lemma  $1$ , that  $$ f(m+n+1)-f(m)-f(n+1) \in \{ 2^a,2^b\} $$  hence it also holds for  $n+1$ . Our Induction is finished, thus  $|\mathcal{S}| \le 2$ .

Let  $ABC$  be an acute triangle with  $AB < AC$ , and let  $\Gamma$  be the circumcircle of  $ABC$ . Points  $X$  and  $Y$  lie on  $\Gamma$  so that  $XY$  and  $BC$  meet on the external angle bisector of  $\angle BAC$ . Suppose that the tangents to  $\Gamma$  at  $X$  and  $Y$  intersect at a point  $T$  on the same side of  $BC$  as  $A$ , and that  $TX$  and  $TY$  intersect  $BC$  at  $U$  and  $V$ , respectively. Let  $J$  be the centre of the excircle of triangle  $TUV$  opposite the vertex  $T$ .

Prove that  $AJ$  bisects  $\angle BAC$ .
solution_md:
Let the excircle be tangent to  $UV$  at  $D,$  external angle bisector intersects  $BC$  and  $\Gamma$  at  $P$  and  $N,$  bisector of  $\angle BAC$  intersects  $BC$  at  $Q,$   $TA$  intersects  $BC$  at  $R,$   $AY$  and  $NX$  intersects at  $M,$   $AX$  and  $NY$  intersect at  $K,$  tangents from  $A$  to the excircle are  $AT_1$  and  $AT_2.$  (Polars are taken wrt  $\Gamma$  and issogonal lines are wrt  $\angle BAC$ )

Since  $NN//BC$  homothety at  $T$  taking  $\Gamma$  to the excircle sends  $N$  to  $D$  hence  $T,N,D$  are collinear.

Using DIT on degenerate quadriteral  $XXYY$  with circumcircle  $\Gamma$  and line  $BC$  we get  $(B,C),(U,V),(P,P)$  reciprocal pairs hence there exist a point  $Z$  on  $BC$  such that  $ZP^2=ZB\cdot ZC=ZU\cdot ZV$  but since  $(P,Q;B,C)=-1,$   $Z$  is the midpoint of  $PQ$  hence  $(Q,Q),(B,C),(U,V)$  are reciprocal pairs. Since  $(AB,AC)$  and  $(AQ,AQ)$  are issogonal,  $(AU,AV)$  are also issogonal.

By La Hire and  $(P,Q;B,C)=-1$  we get that polar of  $P$  passes through  $T,Q$  and from Brokard on  $AXYN$  we get that it also passes through  $K,M$  hence  $T,K,M,Q$  are collinear. 

Take DDIT on  $AYNX$  with perspector  $T,$  we get that  $(TA,TN),(TX,TY),(TK,TM)$  are reciprocal pairs and projecting onto  $BC$  we get  $(R,D),(U,V),(Q,Q)$  are also pairs and since  $(AU,AV)$  and  $(AQ,AQ)$  are issogonal,  $(AR,AD)$  is also issogonal. 
Take DDIT with perspector  $A$  on degenerate quadriteral  $TUDV$  with inconic as the excircle, we get  $(AT,AD),(AU,AV),(AT_1,AT_2)$  are reciprocal pairs and since  $(AT\equiv AR,AD)$  and  $(AU,AV)$  are issogonal wrt  $\angle BAC$ ,  $(AT_1,AT_2)$  is also issogonal hence  $AJ$  bisects  $\angle BAC$  and we are done.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Let  $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$  denote the set of positive integers. Let  $f : \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$  be a function satisfying the following property: for  $m,n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ , the equation
\[
f(mn)^2 = f(m^2)f(f(n))f(mf(n))
\]holds if and only if  $m$  and  $n$  are coprime.

For each positive integer  $n$ , determine all the possible values of  $f(n)$ .
solution_md:
The answer is everything with the same set of prime factors as  $n$ . First we show these work. Fix any  $n,k$  with the same set of prime factors. We claim we can make a function where  $f(n) = k$ . 

Consider the unique function so that for all positive integers  $m$ ,  $f(m) = f(\mathrm{rad}(m))$ , for all primes  $p \mid n$ ,  $f(p) = p^{\nu_p(k)}$ , for all other primes  $p$ ,  $f(p) = p^{1434}$ , and for all different primes  $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_t$ , we have  $f(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_t) = f(p_1) f(p_2) \cdots f(p_t)$ .   

We claim such a function works. Note that clearly  $f(n) = \prod_{p \mid n} p^{\nu_p(k)} = k$  (where  $p$  is prime),  $f(x^2) = f(x), f(f(x)) = f(x)$  from the fact that  $f(m) = f(\mathrm{rad}(m))$ . So the FE reduces to \[ f(mn)^2 = f(m) f(n) f(mf(n)) \iff \gcd(m,n) = 1\] Note that  $f$  is multiplicative, so if  $\gcd(m,n) = 1$ , the LHS is  $f(m)^2 f(n)^2$  and the RHS is  $f(m) f(n) f(m) f(f(n)) = f(m)^2 f(n)^2$ , as desired. Note that for any  $x$  and prime  $p$  that  $\nu_p(f(x)) \le \nu_p(f(p))$ . Now, if  $p$  is a prime dividing both  $m$  and  $n$ , the  $\nu_p$  of the RHS of the equation is clearly more than  $\nu_p(f(p)^2)$  but the LHS is not, absurd. Therefore, if  $\gcd(m,n) > 1$ , the equation fails, so this solution is valid. 


Firstly, note that  $m = 1$  gives  $f(n)^2 = f(1) f(f(n))^2$ , so  $f(f(n)) \mid f(n)$ . Thus,  $f(n) \ge f(f(n)) \ge f^3(n) \ge f^4(n)  \ge \cdots $ , so  $f(n), f^2(n), f^3(n), \ldots, $  must be eventually constant, so there's a fixed point  $t$  of  $n$ , so  $P(1,t)$  gives  $f(1) = 1$ . 

Thus,  $f(n) = f(f(n))$  for all  $n$  and  $P(n,1)$  gives  $f(n)^2 = f(n^2) f(n)$ , so  $f(n) = f(n^2)$ . 

Rewrite the FE as \[ f(mn)^2 = f(m) f(n) f(mf(n)) \iff \gcd(m,n) = 1\] Let  $P(m,n)$  be the assertion of this. 

Swapping  $m,n$  gives that  $f(mf(n)) = f(nf(m))$  when  $\gcd(m,n) = 1$ . 

Claim:  $f(m)  = 1 \iff m = 1$ . 
Proof: If  $f(m) = 1$  for some  $m \ne 1$ , then  $P(m,m)$  gives  $f(m^2)^2   \ne f(m^2) f(f(m)) f(mf(m))$ . However, clearly  $f(m^2) = f(m) = f(f(m)) = 1$  and  $f(mf(m)) = f(m) = 1$ , so both sides go to  $1$ , absurd.  $\square$ Claim:  $\gcd(m,f(m)) > 1$  for all  $m > 1$ . 
Proof: If not for some  $m$ ,  $P(m,f(m))$  with  $P(f(m), m)$  gives  $f(m f(m)) = f(f(m)^2) = f(m)$ .  $P(m, f(m))$  now gives  $f(m f(m))^2 = f(m)^2 f(mf(m))$ , so  $f(mf(m)) = 1$ , absurd because  $m > 1$ .  $\square$ Claim:  $\mathrm{rad}(m) \mid f(m)$ . 
Proof: We prove this by showing that all primes  $p \mid m$  divide  $f(m)$ . 

Let  $m = p^k \cdot d$  where  $p \nmid d$ . Note that by the above claim,  $p \mid f(p^k)$ .   $P(p^k, d)$  gives that  $f(p^k) \mid f(m)^2$ , so  $p \mid f(m)$ .  $\square$ Claim: If  $\gcd(m,f(n)) > 1$ , then  $\gcd(n,f(m)) > 1$  (and equivalently if  $\gcd(m,f(n)) = 1$ , then  $\gcd(n,f(m)) = 1$ ). 
Proof: If  $\gcd(m ,f(n)) > 1$  and  $\gcd(n,f(m)) = 1$ ,  $P(m,f(n))$  gives that  $f(mf(n))^2 \ne f(m) f(n) f(mf(n))$ , so  $f(mf(n)) \ne f(m) f(n)$ .  $P(n,f(m))$  gives that  $f(n f(m))^2 = f(m) f(n) f(n f(m))$ , so  $f(nf(m)) = f(m) f(n)$ . However, since  $\gcd(n,f(m)) = 1$ , it is clear that  $\gcd(n,m) = 1$  as well, so from  $P(m,n)$  with  $P(n,m)$ , we have that  $f(mf(n)) = f(nf(m)) = f(m) f(n)$ , absurd.  $\square$ Claim: For any two primes  $p,q$ , if  $p \mid f(q)$ , then  $pq$  divides  $f(n)$  for all  $n$  not coprime to  $pq$ . 
Proof: Basically note that  $\gcd(p,f(q))  > 1$ , so  $\gcd(q,f(p)) > 1$ , so  $q \mid f(p)$ . Now,  $\gcd(nq,f(p)) > 1$ , so  $\gcd(p, f(nq)) > 1$ , so  $p \mid f(nq)$  and since  $q$  divides  $f(nq)$ ,  $pq \mid f(nq)$ . The rest is similar.  $\square$ Now suppose for some  $n$  that some prime dividing  $f(n)$  did not divide  $n$ . This implies that if  $p\mid f(n)$  is such a prime, then since  $\gcd(f(n), p) > 1$ ,  $\gcd(f(p), n) > 1$ , so  $f(p)$  cannot be a power of  $p$ . 

Suppose some other prime  $q$  divided  $f(p)$ . 

Let  $T$  and  $U$  be positive integers so that  $T$  is the minimal value of  $\nu_p(f(mpq))$  over all positive integers  $m$  and  $U$  is the minimal value of  $\min(\nu_p(f(mp^k)), \nu_p(f(mq^k)))$  as  $m,k$  range over positive integers so that  $\gcd(m,pq) = 1$ . 

Claim:  $U \ge T$ Proof: Suppose otherwise. Note that for any  $x$  that is not coprime to  $p,q$ , we have that  $pq \mid f(x)$ . This means that  $\nu_p(f(x)) = \nu_p(f(f(x))) \ge T$ , which actually shows that  $U \ge T$  must hold by choosing some  $x$  as either  $mp^k$  or  $mq^k$  for some  $m,k$  where  $\nu_p(f(x)) = U$ .  $\square$ The claim implies that for any positive integer  $x$  that is not coprime to  $pq$ ,  $\nu_p(f(x)) \ge T$  (because if  $x$  is divisible by exactly one of  $p,q$ , then  $\nu_p(f(x)) \ge U \ge T$  and otherwise if  $pq \mid x$ , then from the minimality of  $T$ ,  $\nu_p(f(x)) \ge T$ ). 
Claim:  $T = 0$ . 
Proof: Suppose  $\nu_p(f(r p^x q^y)) = T$  for some  $r$  coprime to  $pq$ .  $P(r p^x, q^y): f(r p^x q^y) = f(r p^x) f(q^y) f(r p^x f(q^y))$ . Note that the RHS has  $\nu_p$  of at least  $T + T + T = 3T$  but the LHS has a  $\nu_p$  of  $T$ , so  $T \ge 3T \implies T = 0$ .  $\square$ This is a contradiction because  $p$  must divide  $f(mpq) \forall m \in \mathbb N$ .

SolutionThe answer is all positive integer $k$ that has the same set of prime divisor as $n$ (i.e., $\operatorname{rad}(f(n)) = \operatorname{rad}(n)$ ).**Construction.** For any choice of $\alpha_p$ for each prime $p$ , the function $$ f(p_1^{e_1} \dots p_k^{e_k}) = p_1^{\alpha_{p_1}} \cdots p_k^{\alpha_{p_k}} $$ is multiplicative and satisfies $f(f(n)) = f(n)$ and $f(n^2)=f(n)$ , so it satisfies the functional equation. This gives the construction.**Impossibility.** Let $P(m,n)$ denote the assertion $f(mn)^{2}=f(m^{2})f(f(n))f(mf(n))$ . We say that $m\perp n$ if $m$ and $n$ are coprime. ------ **Claim.** $f(1)=1$ . *Proof.* $P(1,n)$ implies $f(n)^2 = f(f(n))^2 f(1)$ , so $f(f(n)) = f(n)/c$ , where $c=\sqrt{f(1)}$ . Using this repeatedly gives $$ f^k(n) = \frac{f^{k-1}(n)}{c} = \frac{f^{k-2}(n)}{c^2} =\dots = \frac{f(n)}{c^{k-1}}, $$ which forces $c=1$ upon taking $k$ large and noting that $c^{k-1}\mid f(n)$ . $\blacksquare$ ----- Thus, $P(1,n)$ implies $f(f(n)) = f(n)$ and $P(m,1)$ implies $f(m)= f(m^2)$ . Therefore, $P(m,n)$ is simplified to $$ f(mn)^2 = f(m)f(n) f(mf(n)). $$ ------ **Claim.** $n$ and $f(n)$ are not coprime for all $n>1$ . *Proof.* Assume $n\perp f(n)$ . Then, \begin{align*} P(n,f(n)) &\implies f(nf(n))^2 = f(n)^2 f(nf(n)) \implies f(nf(n))^2 = f(n)^2 P(f(n),n) &\implies f(nf(n))^2 = f(n)^2 f(f(n)^2) = f(n)^2 f(f(n)) = f(n)^3. \end{align*} Combining both equations gives $f(nf(n)) = f(n) = 1$ , which means $P(n,n)$ is true, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$ ----- **Claim.** For any prime $p\mid n$ , we have $p\mid f(n)$ . *Proof.* Write $n=p^at$ where $p\nmid t$ . From the claim above, we have $p\mid f(p^a)$ . Finally, $P(p^a,t)$ gives that $p\mid f(p^at)$ . $\blacksquare$ ----- **Claim.** For any $m,n$ , we have $m\perp f(n) \iff n\perp f(m)$ . *Proof.* Suppose $m\perp f(n)$ . The previous claim implies $m\perp n$ . Thus, \begin{align*} P(m,f(n)) &\implies f(mf(n)) = f(m)f(n) P(m,n) &\implies f(mn) = f(m)f(n) P(n,m) &\implies f(nf(m)) = f(m)f(n), \end{align*} so $P(n,f(m))$ holds, which means that $n\perp f(m)$ . The converse holds. $\blacksquare$ ----- We are now facing the crux of the problem **Claim.** (The crux) $f(p)$ must be a power of $p$ . *Proof.* Assume that $q\mid f(p)$ for some prime $q\neq p$ . We note that for any positive integer $n$ , we have $$ q\not\perp f(p) \implies p\not\perp f(q) \implies p\mid f(q) \implies np\not\perp f(q) \implies q\not\perp f(np), $$ so $q\mid f(np)$ . We now make a key step. Select a positive integer $n$ such that $\nu_q(f(np))$ is minimum. Let $f(np)=p^\alpha q^\beta u$ where $\alpha=\nu_p(f(np)) > 0$ and $\beta = \nu_q(f(np)) > 0$ . Then, we have $$ f(np)^2 = f(f(np))^2 = f(p^\alpha) f(q^\beta u) f(p^\alpha f(q^\beta u)). $$ The first and third terms are divisible by $q^\beta$ by minimality. However, $q\mid f(q^\beta u)$ . We claim that for any  $n$ , the possible values of  $f(n)$  are exactly those which have the same prime factors as  $n$ , or equivalently those with  $\operatorname{rad}(f(n))=\operatorname{rad}(n)$ .

We first show that these are achievable. Let  $p_1<p_2<\cdots$  be the primes. We claim that any  $f$  for which there exist positive integers  $a_1,a_2,\dots$  with \[f(n)=\prod_{p_i\mid n}p_i^{a_i}\] is a solution. For such  $f$ , we can check
\begin{align*}
    \nu_{p_i}(f(mn)^2)&=2[p_i\mid m\vee p_i\mid n]a_i
    \nu_{p_i}(f(m^2)f(f(n))f(mf(n)))&=([p_i\mid m\vee p_i\mid n]+[p_i\mid m]+[p_i\mid n])a_i
\end{align*}
which are equal if and only if  $p_i$  does not divide both  $m,n$ . Then this is a valid solution. Then for any desired  $f(n)$  with  $\operatorname{rad}(f(n))=\operatorname{rad}(n)$ , there is a solution of the outlined form achieving that value of  $f(n)$ .

We now show that these are the only possible values. Consider a solution  $f$ . Let  $P(m,n)$  denote the given condition; then we have  $P(m,n)\iff \gcd(m,n)=1$ .**Claim:  $f(1)=1$**
We have \[P(m,1)\implies f(m)^2=f(m^2)f(f(1))f(mf(1))\] Now for any prime  $p$ , pick  $m$  such that  $\nu_p(f(m))$  is minimal. Then we get \[\nu_p(f(f(1)))=2\nu_p(f(m))-\nu_p(f(m^2))-\nu_p(f(mf(1)))\leq 0\implies \nu_p(f(f(1)))=0\] Then since this holds for all  $p$ , we must have  $f(f(1))=1$ . Then \[P(1,1)\implies f(1)=1\]**Claim:  $P(m,n)$  is equivalent to  $f(mn)^2=f(m)f(n)f(mf(n))$**
We have
\begin{align*}
    P(m,1)\implies& f(m^2)=f(m)
    P(1,m)\implies& f(f(m))=f(m)
\end{align*}
Then \[P(m,n)\iff f(mn)^2=f(m)f(n)f(mf(n))\]**Claim: For all primes  $p$  and  $a\geq 1$ ,  $p\mid f(p^a)$**
We have \[f(mf(n))=f(m)f(n)\iff P(m,f(n))\iff \gcd(m,f(n))=1\] This is enough to imply that \[\gcd(m,f(n))=1\iff f(mn)=f(m)f(n)\iff \gcd(n,f(m))=1\text{ when }\gcd(m,n)=1\] We also have that
\begin{align*}
&\gcd(m,f(n))=1
\implies &P(m,f(n))\quad\wedge\quad P(f(n), m)
\implies &f(mf(n))=f(m)f(n)\quad\wedge\quad f(mf(n))^2=f(m)f(n)f(f(m)f(n))
\implies &f(f(m)f(n))=f(m)f(n)
\implies &f(f(m)f(n))=f(f(m))f(n)
\implies &\gcd(f(m),f(n))=1
\end{align*}
We also note that \[f(m)=1\implies P(m,m)\implies \gcd(m, m)=1\implies m=1\] Now, for any prime  $p$  and  $a\geq 1$ , we have  $f(p^a)\neq 1$  and \[\gcd(f(p^a),f(p^a))=f(p^a)\implies \gcd(p^a,f(p^a))\neq 1\implies p\mid f(p^a)\]**Claim: For primes  $p,q$ , if we define  $p\sim q$  if  $p\mid f(q)$ , then  $\sim$  is an equivalence relation**
We already have  $p\sim p$ . We have for distinct  $p,q$  with  $p\sim q$ , since  $\gcd(p,q)=1$ , that \[p\mid \gcd(p,f(q))\implies \gcd(q,f(p))\neq 1\implies q\sim p\] We have for distinct  $p,q,r$  with  $p\sim q$  and  $q\sim r$  that \[r\mid\gcd(f(p),f(q))\implies \gcd(p,f(q))\neq 1\implies p\sim q\] Then  $\sim$  is an equivalence relation. Now for any equivalence class  $S$ , we will define  $\mathfrak P(S)$  as the set of positive integers all of whose prime factors are in  $S$  and  $\mathfrak P_1(S)$  as the set of positive integers in  $\mathfrak P(S)$  divisible by every prime in  $S$ .**Claim: For any equivalence class  $S$ , for all  $m\neq 1$  with  $m\in\mathfrak P(S)$ ,  $f(m)\in\mathfrak P_1(S)$ .**
Take  $p_1\in S$ . Since all primes in  $S$  divide  $f(p_1)$ ,  $S$  must be finite. Now let  $S=\{p_1,p_2,\dots,p_k\}$ . We now have for every  $i$  and  $a\geq 1$ , for all  $j$  we have \[p_i\mid \gcd(f(p_j),f(p_i^a))\implies \gcd(p_j,f(p_i^a))\neq 1\implies p_j\mid f(p_i^a)\] Then  $f(p_i^a)$  is divisible by every prime in  $S$ . Now for any  $m\neq 1$  with  $m\in\mathfrak P(S)$ , pick  $p\mid m$  and let  $a=\nu_p(m)$ . Then  $P\left(\frac{m}{p^a},p^a\right)$  implies that  $f(m)$  is divisible by every prime in  $S$ . Now suppose FTSOC  $f(m)$  is divisible by  $q$  in an equivalence class  $T\neq S$ . Since  $\gcd(m,q)=1$ , we have \[q\mid \gcd(q,f(m))\implies \gcd(m,f(q))\neq 1\] But since  $f(q)\in\mathfrak P_1(T)$ , this implies that some prime divisor of  $m$ , which must be in  $S$ , is in  $T$ , which is a contradiction. Then no such  $q$  exists, and we have  $f(m)\in\mathfrak P_1(S)$ .**Claim: Every equivalence class  $S$  contains exactly  $1$  prime**
Suppose FTSOC  $S=\{p_1,p_2,\dots,p_k\}$  with  $k\geq 2$ . Pick  $m\in\mathfrak P(S)$  such that  $\nu_{p_1}(f(m))$  is minimal. Since  $f(f(m))=f(m)$  and  $f(m)\in \mathfrak P_1(S)$ , we can WLOG assume  $m\in\mathfrak P_1(S)$ . Write \[m=p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}\dots p_k^{a_k}\] We now have
\begin{align*}
    &P(p_1^{a_1},p_2^{a_2}\dots p_k^{a_k})
    \implies &f(m)^2=f(p_1^{a_1})f(p_2^{a_2}\dots p_k^{a_k})f(p_1^{a_1}f(p_2^{a_2}\dots p_k^{a_k}))
    \implies &\nu_{p_1}(f(p_1^{a_1}f(p_2^{a_2}\dots p_k^{a_k})))=2\nu_{p_1}(f(m))-\nu_p(f(p_1^{a_1}))-\nu_{p_1}(f(p_2^{a_2}\dots p_k^{a_k}))
    \implies &\nu_{p_1}(f(p_1^{a_1}f(p_2^{a_2}\dots p_k^{a_k})))\leq 0
\end{align*}
which is a contradiction. Then we must have  $k=1$ .**Claim: For all  $m$ ,  $\operatorname{rad}(f(m))=\operatorname{rad}(m)$**
We will induct on  $\omega(m)$ . We already have that this is true when  $\omega(m)=0,1$ . Now consider  $m$  with  $\omega(m)=k$  for some  $k\geq 2$ , assuming that we already have that this is true when  $\omega(m)<k$ . Pick prime  $p\mid m$  and let  $a=\nu_p(m)$ . Then \[\operatorname{rad}\left(f\left(\frac{m}{p^a}\right)\right)=\operatorname{rad}\left(\frac{m}{p^a}\right)=\frac{\operatorname{rad}(m)}{p}\] Then
\begin{align*}
&P\left(\frac{m}{p^a},p^a\right)\quad\wedge\quad P\left(\frac{m}{p^a},f(p^a)\right)
\implies &f(m)^2=f\left(\frac{m}{p^a}\right)f(p^a)f\left(\frac{m}{p^a}f(p^a)\right)\quad\wedge\quad f\left(\frac{m}{p^a}f(p^a)\right)=f\left(\frac{m}{p^a}\right)f(p^a)
\implies &f(m)=f\left(\frac{m}{p^a}\right)f(p^a)
\implies &\operatorname{rad}(f(m))=\operatorname{rad}(m)
\end{align*}
This completes the induction.

We now have that  $\operatorname{rad}(f(m))=\operatorname{rad}(m)$  for all  $m$ , as desired.

We claim that  $S = \{m\}$  or  $S = \{m, 3m\}$  for any  $m$  are the only solutions. These clearly work.**Claim:  $v_p(s)$  is constant over all  $s \in S$****Proof:** FTSOC if this was not true, let  $m = \min_{s \in S} (v_2(s))$  and  $M = \max_{s \in S} (v_2(s))$ . We may find  $a, b$  such that  $v_2(b) = m$  and  $v_2(b) = M$ . In that case  $a \mid b + 2c$  is impossible since  $v_2(2c) > v_2(b) = m$  but  $v_2(a) = M$ .

Note that sequence  $S' = \{ ms : s \in S\}$  works if and only if sequence  $S$  works for any  $m$  since scaling each element does not affect the divisibility rule. Therefore, WLOG let the greatest common divisor of the elements of  $S$  be zero. By the claim, all elements of  $S$  are odd.

If  $|S| = 1$ , then  $S = \{1\}$ . This corresponds to the  $S = \{m\}$  solution.

If  $|S| = 2$ , let  $S = \{a, b\}$  for some  $\gcd(a, b) = 1$  and WLOG let  $b > a$ . Note  $b \mid a + 2b \iff b \mid a$  is impossible by size, so  $b \mid a + 2a$ . Since  $b > a$ , we must have  $b = 3a$ . This corresponds to  $S = \{m, 3m\}$  solution.

If  $|S| \ge 3$ , let the elements of  $S$  be  $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_n$ . For each  $1 \le i \le n - 1$ , since  $a_1, \dots, a_{n-1} < a_n$ , there exists exactly one unique  $j$  such that  $a_i + 2 a_j \equiv 0 \pmod{a_n}$ . Consider a graph  $G$  on vertices  $\{1, \dots, n-1\}$  and draw an edge  $i \rightarrow j$  for each such relation. Note that the indegree of each vertex on  $G$  is at most one since there is an unique  $i$  such that  $a_i + 2a_j \equiv 0 \pmod{a_n}$ .  Therefore,  $G$  is a collection of cycles  $-2k \rightarrow k \pmod{a_n}$ . 

The only self-edges on  $G$  are when  $a_i + 2a_i \equiv 0 \pmod{a_n}$ . Since  $a_i < a_n$  and both are odd, this happens at most once when  $3a_i = a_n$  for some  $i$ . As a result, there must be a cycle  $C$  of length at least  $2$  on  $G$ .

Let  $C$  have elements  $a_{b_1} \leftarrow a_{b_2} \leftarrow \dots \leftarrow a_{b_k} \leftarrow a_{b_1}$ . With indices modulo  $k$ , each,
\[a_{b_{i+1}} \equiv -2 a_{b_i} \pmod{a_n}\]
However, since each  $a_{b_i}$  satisfy  $0 < a_{b_i} < a_n$  and each  $a_{b_i}$  is odd, for  $a_{b_{i+1}}$  to be odd, we must have each  $a_{b_i} < \frac{a_n}{2}$  and  $a_{b_{i+1}} = a_n - 2a_{b_i}$ . This is a contradiction since  $|a_{b_i} - \frac{a_n}3|$  is now strictly increasing.

Let \(ABC\) be a triangle with incenter \(I\) such that \(AB<AC<BC\). The second intersections of \(AI\), \(BI\), and \(CI\) with the circumcircle of triangle \(ABC\) are \(M_{A}\), \(M_{B}\), and \(M_{C}\), respectively. Lines \(AI\) and \(BC\) intersect at \(D\) and lines \(BM_{C}\) and \(CM_{B}\) intersect at \(X\). Suppose the circumcircle of triangles \(XM_{B}M_{C}\) and \(XBC\) intersect again at \(S\neq X\). Lines \(BX\) and \(CX\) intersect the circumcircle of triangle \(SXM_{A}\) again at \(P\neq X\) and \(Q\neq X\), respectively.

Prove that the circumcenter of triangle \(SID\) lies on \(PQ\).

*Proposed by Thailand*
solution_md: Note that $S$ is the Miquel point of $BM_CM_BC$ , which is cyclic. Thus there is an inversion $\Phi$ at $S$ , followed by a reflection around line $SIO$ such that: - $\Phi(B)=M_B$ and $\Phi(C)=M_C$ by Miquel inversion, - $\Phi(I)=O$ from $SBOM_B$ and $SCOM_C$ being cyclic, - $\Phi(A)=M_A$ since $S$ is also the Miquel point of $AM_AM_BB$ , - Circle $(ABC)$ is fixed under $\Phi$ by above, - $\Phi(SXPQM_A)=KA$ where $K=BC\cap M_BM_C$ as $\Phi(X)=K$ , - $\Phi(P)=(SKC)\cap KA \neq K$ , and call this $P'$ , - $\Phi(P)=(SKB)\cap KA \neq K$ which we call $Q'$ , - $\Phi(D)=(SAOM_A) \cap (M_BXM_CS)$ other than $S$ , call this $D'$ , - and the center of $(SID)$ goes to the reflection of $S$ over $OD'$ . We thus want to show that $OD'$ passes through the center of $(SP'Q')$ . An equivalently way of stating this is that the radical axis $\ell$ of $(SP'Q')$ and $(ABC)$ is perpendicular to line $OD'$ .**Claim:** Line $\ell$ is parallel to line $KA$ . *Proof.* Let $W = SQ' \cap M_CB$ and $Z =SP' \cap M_BC$ . Then, radical axis on $(SQ'M_CB)$ , $(ABC)$ , and $(SP'Q')$ and the symmetric version give that line $WZ$ is line $\ell$ . However, note a spiral similarity at $S$ takes $Q'BM_C$ to $P'CM_B$ by Miquel. Thus it takes line $SQ'$ to line $SP'$ and line $MC_B$ to line $M_BC$ . Hence it takes $SQ' \cap M_CB$ to $SP' \cap M_BC$ , or just $W$ to $Z$ . But as it also takes $Q'$ to $P'$ , the collinearities gives that the spiral similarity sending $P'Q'$ to $WZ$ is a homothety, so $\ell$ is parallel to $P'Q'$ as desired. $\blacksquare$ Now, consider the image of $D'$ under inversion about $(ABC)$ , which we will call $A'$ . Note that $A' = AM_A \cap (IM_BM_C)$ by inverting $D'$ . By radical axis, the problem is now equivalent to the following claim applied in triangle $M_AM_BM_C$ .**Claim:** Let $ABC$ be a triangle with orthocenter $H$ . Let $E'$ , $F'$ , and $H'$ be the reflections of $H$ around $BC$ , $AC$ , and $AB$ . Lines $E'F'$ and $BC$ meet at $T$ , and let $AH$ meet $BHC$ again at $A'$ . Line $TH'$ meets $(ABC)$ again at $J$ . show $A'H = A'J$ . *Proof.* We essentially reflect everything around line $BC$ . Set $J'=TH\cap (BHC)$ to be the reflection of $J$ over $BC$ . Then, $TE'\cdot TF' = TB\cdot TC = TH\cdot TJ'$ so $E'HJ'F'$ is cyclic. However, this clearly has center $A$ by orthocenter reflection, so $AH=AJ'$ . Thus reflecting back, $A'H' = AJ$ . $\blacksquare$

Let  $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots$  be an infinite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers such that for each  $n \geqslant 1$  we have  $$ a_n \in \left\{ \frac{a_{n-1} + a_{n+1}}{2},\ \sqrt{a_{n-1} \cdot a_{n+1}} \right\}. $$  Let  $b_1, b_2, \ldots$  be an infinite sequence of letters defined as  $$ b_n = 
\begin{cases}
A & \text{if } a_n = \frac{1}{2}(a_{n-1} + a_{n+1}) 
G & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases} $$  Prove that there exist positive integers  $n_0$  and  $d$  such that for all  $n \geqslant n_0$  we have  $b_{n+d} = b_n$ .

*Proposed by Josef Tkadlec, Czech Republic*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>**Claim 1:**  $a_{n+1}-a_n=c.gcd(a_n,a_{n+1}),\forall n\geq0, c=\frac{a_1-a_0}{gcd(a_1,a_0)}$ Proof: Use induction
If  $gcd(a_n)_{n\geq0}=d$ , then we can look at the sequence  $(\frac{a_n}{d})_{n\geq0}$ , so WLOG  $gcd(a_n)_{n\geq0}=1$ Thus, for all prime  $p$ , there exists a minimal  $n_p$  that  $a_{n_p}$  is not divisible by  $p$ , and for large enough  $p$ ,  $n_p=0$ Let  $n_0=\max n_p$ **Claim 2:** For all odd prime  $p$ ,  $n\geq n_p$ , either  $v_p(a_{n+1})=v_p(a_n)=0$  or  $v_p(a_{n+1})\neq v_p(a_n)$ Proof: Fix  $p$ . it is true for  $n_p$ . Assume the claim is true for all  $n\geq i\geq n_p$ .
If  $a_n$  or  $a_{n+1}$  is not divisible by  $p$ , we don't care. If not, call  $m$  the nearest indice to  $n+1$  that  $a_m$  is divisible by  $p$ . We can prove (by induction) that  $v_p(a_{i+1})-v_p(a_i)=v_p(a_i)-v_p(a_{i-1})$  if  $b_i=G$ , else  $v_p(a_{i+1})-v_p(a_i)=-(v_p(a_i)-v_p(a_{i-1}))$  for all  $m\leq i\leq n$ Thus  $v_p(a_{n+1})\neq v_p(a_n)$ , by induction we proved the claim
Note that if  $q|a_{n+1}$ ,  $q\nmid a_n$  for some  $q$  prime then  $b_n=A$ Also note that  $a_{n+1}>2gcd(a_n,a_{n-1})$ If for all  $n\geq n_0$ ,  $b_n=A$  the problem statement is true
Assume there are infinitely many  $n$  that  $b_n=G$ Consider  $N\geq n_0$  that  $b_N=A,b_{N+1}=G$ , we have that all prime divisor of  $a_{N+1}$  divides  $a_N$  $a_{N+1}=2a_N-a_{N-1}$ ,  $v_p(a_N)\neq v_p(a_{N-1})$  for all odd  $p|a_N$ Then  $v_p(a_{N+1})=\min\{v_p(a_N),v_p(a_{N-1})\}$ , so  $a_{N+1}=2^kgcd(a_N,a_{N-1})$  for some  $k\geq 2$ But by Claim 1, we have  $a_{N+1}=\frac{2^k}{2^k-c}a_N$ If  $c$  is even, then  $a_n$  is odd for all  $n$  (contradiction because  $k\geq 1$ ), so  $c$  is odd
Let  $a=2^k-c$ , then  $(a,c)=1$ Let  $f(n)$  be a function that  $f(N)=0$ ,  $f(n+1)=f(n)$  if  $b_{n+1}=G$ ,  $f(n+1)=f(n)+1$  if  $b_{n+1}=A$ By induction, we can derive that  $a_{n+1}=a_n.\frac{a+(f(n)+1)c}{a+f(n)c},\forall\;n\geq N$ Let  $c_m=|\{n\geq N, f(n)=m\}|$  for all  $m\geq 0$ Then we have  $a_N.\prod^m_{i=0}\left(\frac{a+(i+1)c}{a+ic}\right)^{c_i}\in\mathbb Z,\forall\;m\geq0$ Let  $x_m=a_N.\prod^m_{i=0}\left(\frac{a+(i+1)c}{a+ic}\right)^{c_i}$  is a positive integer,  $x_{m+1}=x_m.\left(\frac{a+(m+2)c}{a+(m+1)c}\right)^{c_{m+1}}$ , but  $(a+(m+2)c,a+(m+1)c)=1$  so  $(a+(m+1)c)^{c_{m+1}}|x_m$  
Note that  $x_m\leq a_N.\left(\frac{a+(m+1)c}{a}\right)^{\max_{0\leq i\leq m}c_i}<(a+(m+1)c)^{1+\max_{0\leq i\leq m}c_i}$ , so sequence  $(c_m)$  is bounded
Let  $d$  be the largest value that appears infinitely many times in the sequence (c_m)
From this we can see that there are constants  $A,M$  that  $x_m\leq A(a+(m+1)c)^d,\forall\;m\geq M$  and  $c_m\leq d,\forall\;m\geq M$ Let  $M\leq k_1<k_2<...$  be the sequence of indices that  $c_{k_i+1}=d$ For any  $i$ ,  $(a+c(k_i+1))^d|x_{k_i}$ , so there exists  $1\leq t_i\leq A$  that  $x_{k_i}=t_i(a+(k_i+1)c)^d$ If  $k_{i+1}-k_i=1$  then  $t_i=t_{i+1}$ . Consider  $k_{i+1}-k_i>1$ Then  $\frac{x_{k_i+j+1}}{x_{k_i+j}}\leq \left(\frac{a+(k_i+j+2)c}{a+(k_i+j+1)}\right)^d$  for all  $0\leq j\leq k_{i+1}-k_i-1$  and the smaller sign is strict for  $j=1$ Multiply all of these inequalities, we have  $x_{k_{i+1}}<x_{k_i}.\left(\frac{a+(k_{i+1}+1)c}{a+(k_i+1)c}\right)^d$ Which means  $t_{i+1}<t_i$ So we have the sequence  $(t_i)$  is non-increasing, so it is eventually constant when  $i\geq M_1$  for some  $M_1$ Note that we proved if  $k_{i+1}-k_i>1$  then  $t_{i+1}<t_i$ , so for all  $i\geq M_1$ ,  $k_i+1=k_{i+1}$ So it mans  $c_m=d$  for all  $m\geq k_{M_1}$ , finishing the problem
[/hide=Solution]</details>

We will prove a stronger result: namely, for  $i_1, i_2, \dots$  the indices for which  $b_{i_k} = A$ , for sufficiently large  $n$ ,  $i_{n+1} - i_n = d$  for some constant  $d$ .

Let  $r = a_1 - a_0$ . It is not hard to see inductively that the quotients  $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \tfrac{a_0+(k+1)r}{a_0+kr}$  for some positive integer  $k$ , where  $k$  does not decrease as  $n$  increases. In particular, let  $c_k \in \mathbb N \cup \{\infty\}$  denote the number of positive integers  $n$  such that \[\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{a_0+(k+1)r}{a_0+kr}.\] We may assume that  $\gcd(a_0, r) = 1$ , so all these fractions are in reduced terms. It is not hard to see the closed form \[a_{c_0+\cdots+c_k} = a_0 \left(\frac{a_0+r}{a_0}\right)^{c_0} \cdots \left(\frac{a_0+(k+1)r}{a_0+kr}\right)^{c_k} = a_0  \prod_{i=0}^{k+1} (a_0+ir)^{c_{i-1} - c_i}.\] We set  $c_{k+1} = 0$  in this expression.

We define a new sequence  $x_i$  by  $x_k = a_{c_0+c_1+\cdots+c_k}$  for each  $k$ . In particular, since  $x_k \cdot \left(\frac{a_0+(k+2)r}{a_0+(k+1)r}\right)^{c_{k+1}}$  is an integer, the denominator of the latter fraction in reduced terms divides  $x_k$ ; in particular,  $(a_0 + (k+1)r)^{c_{k+1}} \mid x_k$ .

Define a new sequence  $\{y_i\}$  by  $y_k = \frac{x_k}{(a_0+(k+1)r)^{c_{k+1}}}$ . From the given recursion, we have \[y_{k+1} = y_k(a_0+(k+2)r)^{c_{k+1}-c_{k+2}}.\] Write  $d_i = a_0 + ir$  for short. The idea now is to consider a sequence of *local maximum indices*  $i_1, i_2, \dots$ , which satisfy the following constraints:


- If  $\{c_n\}$  is bounded,  $i_k$  is sufficiently large and  $c_{i_k}$  is the maximum among the set of values that  $\{c_n\}$  attains infinitely many times, and
- If  $\{c_n\}$  is unbounded,  $i_k$  satisfies  $c_{i_k} > c_j$  for all  $j < i_k$ .

Then, observe that 
\begin{align*}
\frac{y_{i_{k+1} - 2}}{y_{i_k - 2}} &= d_{i_k}^{c_{i_k}} \cdot \left(\frac{d_{i_k + 1}}{d_{i_k}}\right)^{c_{i_k + 1}} \cdots \left(\frac{d_{i_{k+1}}}{d_{i_{k+1}-1}}\right)^{c_{i_{k+1}-1}} \cdot \frac 1{d_{i_{k+1}}^{c_{i_{k+1}}}}. 
&< d_{i_k}^{c_{i_{k+1}}} \cdot \left(\frac{d_{i_k + 1}}{d_{i_k}}\right)^{c_{i_{k+1}}} \cdots \left(\frac{d_{i_{k+1}}}{d_{i_{k+1}-1}}\right)^{c_{i_{k+1}}} \cdot \frac 1{d_{i_{k+1}}^{c_{i_{k+1}}}} = 1.
\end{align*}
Here we use the property that  $c_j < c_{i_{k+1}}$  for any  $i_k < j < i_{k+1}$ , which follows by definition of the local maximum indices. Hence the subsequence  $\{y_{i_j - 2}\}$  over all  $j$  is a strictly decreasing sequence of integers, contradiction.

Let  $n$  and  $T$  be positive integers. James has  $4n$  marbles with weights  $1$ ,  $2$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $4n$ . He places them on a balance scale, so that both sides have equal weight. Andrew may move a marble from one side of the scale to the other, so that the absolute difference in weights of the two sides remains at most  $T$ .

Find, in terms of  $n$ , the minimum positive integer  $T$  such that Andrew may make a sequence of moves such that each marble ends up on the opposite side of the scale, regardless of how James initially placed the marbles.
solution_md: We claim that $T = 4n$ . $n = 1$ is obvious, so assume $n > 1$ . Let $S = 1 + 2 + \dots + 4n$ , $E = 1 + \dots + 2n$ , and $s(S)$ denote the sum of a set $S$ . Note that $E > 4n$ . ------------------- **Bound** Note that $T$ is equal to twice the maximal distance that one of the scale hsa from $\frac{S}{2}$ . Since one of $x, x - 4n$ has distance at least $2n$ , the bound follows. ------------------- **Construction** Call a number *small* if its in $[1, \dots, 2n]$ and *big* if its in $[2n+1, \dots, 4n]$ . Call a scale configuration $(A, B)$ with weight sets $A \sqcup B = \{1, 2, \dots, 4n\}$ valid if the weight difference $s(A) - s(B)$ has magnitude less than $T$ .**Claim:** Suppose that $(S_0 \sqcup L_0, S_1 \sqcup L_1)$ and $(S_0' \sqcup L_0, S_1' \sqcup L_1)$ are both valid configurations where $L_i$ consists of only large numbers. Then there exists a way to go from one configuration to the other. *Proof.* Starting with $(S_0, L_0)$ , we need to move the small numbers in $M_0 = S_1 \setminus S_1' \subseteq S_0$ and $M_1 = S_0 \setminus S_1' \subseteq S_1$ , while preserving the validity of our configuration. We do this by removing elements from $M_i$ . Since the interval has size $4n$ , the current sum $s(S_i)$ has distance at least $2n$ from an endpoint. Now consider the set $M_i$ which moving elements that when moved decrease the length of $s(S_i)$ to this endpoint. If $M_i$ is empty, we may repeatedly move elements of $M_{1-i}$ until we are done by continuity. Otherwise, we may remove an element of $M_{1-i}$ . $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** We may form any integer in $[0, 1, \dots, E]$ as the sum of a subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, 2n\}$ . *Proof.* Define $S_0 = \{\}$ , then we generate $S_{i+1}$ from $S_i$ by replacing some $i$ with $i+1$ when possible and adding the element $1$ when not possible. $\blacksquare$ Now, let $(L_0, \{2n+1, \dots 4n\} \setminus L_0)$ be the initial large number sets on each side. We now move large elements into and out of $L_0$ to get $L_i$ . To make our movement valid, we require by our lemma that there exists an $t \in [0, E]$ such that \[ s(L_i) + t, s(L_{i+1}) + t \in [S - 2n, S + 2n] \] This $t$ means that we can use our earlier claims to construct a small set $S_{i+1}$ with sum $t$ that allows us to move between the two sets. We must also require $s(L_i) \in [S-E-2n, S+2n]$ . This allows us to simplify the above condition, as we need one of $s(L_i), s(L_{i+1})$ to lie in $[S-E, S]$ for each $i$ . Now, note that the sums initially lie in the range $[S-E, S]$ . Starting with $L_0$ , we need to move the elements $M_0 = L_0, M_1 = L_1$ . We may also do this greedily; Note that $s(L_i)$ has a distance at least $4n$ from some endpoint. If the corresponding $M_i$ that decreases the distance to that endpoint is empty, we may empty $M_{1-i}$ while preserving both conditions. Otherwise, we may remove an element from $M_i$ while preserving both conditions.

The answer is  $4n$ .**Lower Bound.** Trivial.  Either before of after when  $4n$  is moved to an opposite side, the difference must be at least  $4n$ .**Construction.** Like IMO 2020 P3, the idea is to pair  $\{1,4n\}$ ,  $\{2,4n-1\}$ ,  $\dots$ . Call a configuration **peaceful** if for any  $1\leq i\leq 4n$ , marbles with weight  $i$  and  $4n+1-i$  are on the same side of the scale. The process consists of two key steps.



- **Turn the starting configuration into a peaceful configuration.**

The algorithm does as follows: at each step, if there is  $k$  such that marble  $k$  and marble  $4n+1-k$  are on different sides (say  $k$  is on the left and  $4n+1-k$  is on the right), we fix this by either moving  $k$  or moving  $4n+1-k$ . Repeat this until the configuration is peaceful.

We claim that this is possible while maintaining the fact that the difference between two sides is in  $[-4n, 4n]$ . To see this, suppose that that the total weight of left minus right side is  $\Delta\in [-4n,4n]$ . Then,
[list]
- Moving  $k$  from left to right changes the difference to  $\Delta-2k$ . This works if  $\Delta-2k\geq -4n$ , which is equivalent to  $\Delta\geq 2k-4n$ .
- Moving  $4n+1-k$  from right to left changes the difference to  $\Delta+2(4n+1-k)$ . This works if  $\Delta+2(4n+1-k)\leq 4n$ , which is equivalent to   $\Delta\leq 2k-4n+2$ .
[/list]
Since  $\Delta$  is always even, one of the conditions hold, and one may perform either of the two bullet points while keeping the difference in range  $[-4n, 4n]$ .
- **Move all marbles in a peaceful configuration to the opposite side.**

First, note that at this point, the sum of weights on both sides must be a multiple of  $4n+1$ . Hence, if we ever reach a peaceful configuration, the difference between two sides must be a multiple of  $4n+1$ , but it is in  $[-4n, 4n]$ , so it is actually  $0$ , i.e., there are equal numbers of pairs in form  $\{k, 4n+1-k\}$  on both sides.

We claim that we can swap the pair  $\{2n, 2n+1\}$  with any pair  $\{x, 4n+1-x\}$  (WLOG, assume  $x\leq 2n$ ) from the opposite side. To do that, we make the sequence of swaps:
\begin{align*}
x, 4n+1-x &\mid 2n,2n+1  &\text{diff} &= 0 
x, 4n+1-x, 2n &\mid 2n+1 &\text{diff} &= 4n 
x, 2n &\mid 2n+1, 4n+1-x &\text{diff} &= 2x-4n-2 
x, 2n, 2n+1 &\mid 4n+1-x &\text{diff} &= 2x 
2n, 2n+1 &\mid 4n+1-x, x &\text{diff} &= 0.
\end{align*}
Once we push  $\{x,4n+1-x\}$  to another side, by repeating the same process, one can move another pair $\{y, 4n+1-y\}$  back to the same side. This process exchanges two pairs, each to its opposite side, and we may repeat this  $n$  times to move everything to its opposite side.


Finally, we reverse moves in (i) so that one can turn the resulting configuration in (ii) into the configuration corresponding to the starting position, but with each marble moved to the opposite side compared to the starting position.

stem_md: Find all periodic sequence  $a_1,a_2,\dots$  of real numbers such that the following conditions hold for all  $n\geqslant 1$ :  $$ a_{n+2}+a_{n}^2=a_n+a_{n+1}^2\quad\text{and}\quad |a_{n+1}-a_n|\leqslant 1. $$   *Proposed by Dorlir Ahmeti, Kosovo*
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{\mathrm{constant}}$  sequences and  $\boxed{a_n=(-1)^n c}$  for all  $|c|\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . It can be checked that these work.

Let  $x_n:=a_{n+1}-a_n$  and  $y_n:=a_{n+1}+a_n$ . Note that  $(x_n)$  and  $(y_n)$  are both periodic. Also,  $x_{n+1}=x_n(y_n-1)$  and  $y_{n+1}=y_n(x_n+1)$ . We prove that one of  $(x_n)$  or  $(y_n)$  consists of only  $0$ 's, which finishes.

Here is a solution found by Johan Konter (NDL deputy) and me (COL deputy) based mostly in dynamics. I'll post Johan's write-up.

We begin by shuffling the given equation as  $a_n^2-a_n=a_{n+1}^2-a_{n+2}$ . If we now subtract  $a_{n+1}$  we get  $$ a_n^2-a_n-a_{n+1}=a_{n+1}^2-a_{n+1}-a_{n+2}. $$  If we define the left-hand side as  $b_n$ , then this reads as  $b_n=b_{n+1}$ . So this sequence is constant, say  $b_n=d-\frac{3}{4}$ . This is to say that  $a_{n+1}=a_n^2-a_n-(d-\frac{3}{4})$ . We can rewrite this as  $a_{n+1}-\frac{1}{2}=(a_n-\frac{1}{2})^2-d$ . Now we substitute  $c_n=a_n-\frac{1}{2}$ , to get the recurrence  $$ c_{n+1}=c_n^2-d. $$  The rest of the solution is now to find the periodic orbits of this dynamical system, with the intuition coming from the cobweb plot (or Verhulst diagram).

First note that  $c_{n+1}-c_n=(c_n^2-d)-(c_{n-1}^2-d)=(c_n-c_{n-1})(c_n+c_{n-1}).$  So if  $c_i>0$  for all  $i$ , then the sequence is monotone; contradicting the periodicity. So there exists a  $k$  such that  $c_k\leq 0$ , for which we then find that  $0\leq c_k=c_{k-1}^2-d\geq -d$ . Hence  $d\geq 0$ , as the notation suggests. Now
consider the roots of  $x=x^2-d$ , which we call  $p=\frac{1-\sqrt{1+4d}}{2}<0$  and  $q=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4d}}{2}>0$ . If  $c_n$  is equal to  $p$  or  $q$ , then the period is 1, whose solution we check at the end. If  $c_n>q$ , then  $c_{n+1}=c_n^2-d>c_n$ . So the sequence is increasing from this point forward, again contradicting the periodicity. Now we only need to consider  $q>c_n\geq -d$ .

If  $q>c_n>p$ , then  $c_{n+1}=c_n^2-d<c_n.$  Since the sequence cannot always be decreasing, not all  $c_n$  can be in this interval. So there must be an n such that  $p>c_n\geq -d$ .

If for certain  $n$  and  $k$   we have  $p>c_n>c_k\geq -d$ , then  $p<c_{n+1}<c_{k+1}\leq d^2-d$ - However if  $c_{k+1}$  is positive, then  $d^2-d\geq c_{k+1}>0$  so  $d>1$ . Hence  $c_k^2-d=c_{k+1}>0$  implies that  $c_k<-\sqrt{d}<-1$ . But then  $c_{k+1}-c_k>1$ , contradicting the second condition. We conclude that  $p<c_{n+1}<c_{k+1}\leq 0$ . But then applying the function again we get  $p>c_{n+2}>c_{k+2}\geq -d$ .

In particular, if  $c_{n+2}\neq c_n$ , then the sequence  $c_{n+2i}$  is (strictly) monotone, contradicting the periodicity yet again. So in this case the period is 2. 

The solutions with period 1 are any constant sequence. For a sequence with period 2 we notice that  $a_{n+2}$  and  $a_n$  cancel in the original equation, so  $a_n^2=a_{n+1}^2$  Since  $a_n = a_{n+1}$  would have period 1, this means that  $a_n = -a_{n+1}$  for all  $n$ . So the sequence alternates between  $a$  and  $-a$  for some  $|a| \leq \frac{1}{2}$  by the second condition.

The answer is constant sequences and  $r,-r,r,-r,\dots$  where  $|r|\leq \frac{1}{2}$  only, which clearly work.

Subtract  $a_{n+1}$  from both sides to rearrange the equation as  $$ a_{n+2}-a_{n+1}=(a_{n+1}-a_n)(a_{n+1}+a_n-1). $$  Suppose we have a cycle of length at least  $3$ .

Claim:  $a_i< 1$  for all  $i$ . Let  $M$  be the maximum value of a term in the cycle. If any term next to the  $M$  is also  $M$ , then the entire cycle is  $M$ , contradiction. Otherwise, the value increased then decreased as it went through  $M$  due to maximality. Consider  $$ a_{n+2}-a_{n+1}=(a_{n+1}-a_n)(a_{n+1}+a_n-1). $$  This means that for that step,  $a_{n+1}+a_n-1$  was negative, as the sign of the difference of consecutive terms changed. In particular, if  $a_{n+1}=M$ , then  $a_{n}\geq M-1$ , so  $M+(M-1)-1<0$ , so  $M<1$ .

Note that the recurrence above implies that  $$ \prod_{cyc} (a_{n+1}+a_n-1)=1 $$  by multiplying it across the entire cycle. Note that since  $a_i<1$ , the factors are all less than  $1$ .

If every term in the product has magnitude at least  $1$ , then they all have magnitude exactly  $1$ , so  $a_i+a_{i+1}=0$ , but this is just a  $2$ -cycle. Thus, assume some factor has magnitude less than  $1$ , that is,  $a_k+a_{k+1}$  is positive for some  $k$ .

Claim 2: If  $a_k+a_{k+1}\geq 0$ , then  $a_{k+1}+a_{k+2}\geq 0$  as well. Note that  $$ a_{k+2}=a_k+a_{k+1}^2-a_k^2 $$    $$ a_{k+2}+a_{k+1}=(a_k+a_{k+1})(a_{k+1}-a_k+1). $$  Furthermore,  $a_{k+1}-a_k+1\geq 0$  since  $|a_{k+1}-a_k|\leq 1$ , which shows the claim.

Thus, if  $a_k+a_{k+1}$  is positive for any  $k$ , going around the circle,  $a_i+a_{i+1}\geq 0$  for all  $i$ . However, clearly violates  $\prod_{cyc} (a_{n+1}+a_n-1)=1$  as all factors have magnitude at most  $1$  while at least one term has magnitude less than  $1$ , contradiction.

Thus all cycles have length at most  $2$ . For  $1$  it's constant, and if  $a\rightarrow b\rightarrow a$ , then  $a^2=b^2$ , so  $a=r$  and  $b=-r$  for some  $r$ , as desired.

Remark: Quite straightforward imo, the subtracting  $a_{n+1}$  is natural as the difference between consecutive terms is already used in the problem. Then this allows us to bound things and then we just keep pushing these bounds which solves the problem. Then, the multipliers between the differences involve  $a_k+a_{k+1}$ , so from there we just add that to the original equation to get information about that as well. Furthermore, it essentially has to be some form of bounding, because given a long cycle the condition becomes an arbitrarily high degree polynomial, which is very difficult to solve exactly.

All the sequences are constant sequence, or  $c, -c, c, -c, \ldots$   $(|c| \leq 1/2)$ .  
Let  $k$  be the period of the sequence (i.e.  $a_n = a_{n+k}, \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ ).  

Assume that there exists  $a_n = -a_{n+1}$ . Then  $a_n = a_{n+2}$ , and  $a_{n+1} = a_{n+3}, \ldots$  so the sequence is  $c, -c, c, -c, \ldots$ .  

Now, assume that  $a_n + a_{n+1} \ne 0, \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ .  
We have  
\[
\frac{a_{n+2} + a_{n+1}}{a_{n+1} + a_n} = a_{n+1} - a_n + 1, \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}^+.
\]  
Therefore,  
\[
(a_{k+1} - a_k + 1)(a_k - a_{k-1} + 1)\cdots(a_2 - a_1 + 1) = 1.
\]  

Since  $a_{n+1} - a_n + 1 \geq 0, \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ , then by AM–GM, we have  
\[
(a_{k+1} - a_k + 1)(a_k - a_{k-1} + 1)\cdots(a_2 - a_1 + 1) \leq \left(\frac{a_{k+1} - a_k + 1 + a_k - a_{k-1} + 1 + \cdots + a_2 - a_1 + 1}{k}\right)^k = 1.
\]  

Therefore the equal signs must be occurred, i.e.  
\[
a_{k+1} - a_k + 1 = a_k - a_{k-1} + 1 = \cdots = a_2 - a_1 + 1 = 1,
\]  
which implies that the sequence is constant.

Rewrite the equation as  $$ a_{n+2}+a_{n+1}=(a_{n+1}+a_n)(a_{n+1}-a_n+1). $$  -----**Case 1.** There exists  $N\in\mathbb N$  such that  $a_{N+1}+a_N=0$ . Then by induction  $a_{n+1}+a_n=0$  for all positive integers  $n\ge N$ . Thus, there exists  $c\in\mathbb R$  such that  $a_n=(-1)^n c$  for all positive integers  $n\in\mathbb N$ . Suppose the sequence  $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$  has period  $p$ . Then for all positive integers  $n$ ,  $$ a_n=a_{n+2pm}=(-1)^{n+2pm}c=(-1)^nc. $$  By assumption we have  $1\ge|a_2-a_1|=2c$  so  $|c|\le\frac{1}{2}$ . It follows that  $\boxed{a_n=(-1)^nc\quad\forall n\in\mathbb N}$ , which is indeed a solution whenever  $c\in\mathbb R$  and  $|c|\le\frac{1}{2}$ .
-----**Case 2.**  $a_{n+1}+a_n\ne 0$  for all positive integers  $n$ . Let  $m$  be an arbitrary positive integer. Since the sequence  $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$  is periodic, there exists a positive integer  $p$  such that  $a_{n+p}=a_n$  for all positive integers  $n$ . Since we can change  $p$  to  $mp$ , we can assume that  $p\ge m$ . By assumption, for all positive integers  $n$  we have  $a_{n+1}-a_n\ge -1$  so  $a_{n+1}-a_n+1\ge 0$ . Hence by AM-GM  $$ 1=\frac{a_{p+2}+a_{p+1}}{a_2+a_1}=\prod_{i=1}^p(a_{i+1}-a_i+1)\le\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^p(a_{i+1}-a_i)}{p}+1\right)^p=\left(\frac{a_{p+1}-a_1}{p}+1\right)^p=1. $$  It follows that equality holds everywhere, so  $a_{i+1}=a_i$  for all  $i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p+1\}$ . Thus,  $a_i=a_1$  for all  $i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p+1\}$ , and in particular  $a_m=a_1$ . As a result, if we denote  $c=a_1$ , it follows that  $\boxed{a_n=c\quad\forall n\in\mathbb N}$ , which is indeed a solution whenever  $c\in\mathbb R$ .

stem_md:
Decide whether for every sequence  $(a_n)$  of positive real numbers, 

     $\frac{3^{a_1}+3^{a_2}+\cdots+3^{a_n}}{(2^{a_1}+2^{a_2}+\cdots+2^{a_n})^2} < \frac{1}{2024}$  

is true for at least one positive integer  $n$ .
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{\mathrm{yes}}$ .

Let  $b_n:=\frac{(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_n})^2}{3^{a_1}+\cdot+3^{a_n}}$ . We prove that  $(b_n)$  is unbounded. Suppose FTSOC  $(b_n)$  is bounded from above by  $M$ .**Claim 1.**  $(a_n)$  is unbounded.
*Proof.* If  $a_n\leq T$  for all  $n$ , we have  $b_n\geq\frac{n^2}{n3^T}$ , which is unbounded.  $\square$ Let  $E:=\log_{4/3} M$ , so  $4^\alpha>M3^\alpha$  iff  $\alpha>E$ .**Claim 2.**  $(b_n)$  is eventually increasing.
*Proof.* Take  $N\geq M3^E$  with  $a_N>E$ . We prove that for all  $n\geq N$ ,  $b_n<b_{n+1}$ .

Suppose FTSOC there exists  $n\geq N$  with  $b_n\geq b_{n+1}$ . We have
\begin{align*}
(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_{n+1}})^2&\leq b_n(3^{a_1}+\cdots+3^{a_{n+1}})
&=b_n3^{a_{n+1}}+b_n(3^{a_1}+\cdots+3^{a_n})
&\leq M3^{a_{n+1}}+(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_n})^2
\end{align*}
so
\[
4^{a_{n+1}}+2\cdot 2^{a_{n+1}}(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_n})\leq M3^{a_{n+1}}.
\]
Since  $4^{a_{n+1}}\leq M3^{a_{n+1}}$ , we have  $a_{n+1}\leq E$ . But now  $2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_n}\geq n\geq M3^E>M3^{a_{n+1}}$ , a contradiction. Thus  $(b_n)$  is eventually increasing.  $\square$ Hence  $(b_n)$  has a limit. Take  $n$  sufficiently large so that  $a_{n+1}>E$ ,  $a_{n+1}=\max\{a_1,\,\ldots,\,a_{n+1}\}$ , and  $0<b_{n+1}-b_n\leq 1$ . Then
\begin{align*}
(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_{n+1}})^2&=b_{n+1}(3^{a_1}+\cdots+3^{a_{n+1}})
&=b_{n+1}3^{a_{n+1}}+b_{n+1}(3^{a_1}+\cdots+3^{a_n})
&\leq M3^{a_{n+1}}+(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_n})^2+(3^{a_1}+\cdots+3^{a_n})
\end{align*}
so
\[
4^{a_{n+1}}+2\cdot 2^{a_{n+1}}(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_n})\leq M3^{a_{n+1}}+(3^{a_1}+\cdots+3^{a_n}).
\]
Since  $4^{a_{n+1}}>M3^{a_{n+1}}$ , it follows that  $2\cdot 2^{a_{n+1}}(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_n})<3^{a_1}+\cdots+3^{a_n}$ . However,
\[
2^{a_{n+1}}(2^{a_1}+\cdots+2^{a_n})\geq 4^{a_1}+\cdots+4^{a_n}>3^{a_1}+\cdots+3^{a_n},
\]
a contradiction. Thus  $(b_n)$  is unbounded and the conclusion follows.  $\square$

The answer is yes, it must be true for at least one positive integer  $n$ . In fact, the limit of the sequence as  $n \rightarrow +\infty$  is  $0$ .

If  $(a_n)$  is bounded above by  $M > 0$ , we have  $$ \dfrac{3^{a_1}+3^{a_2}+\cdots+3^{a_n}}{(2^{a_1}+2^{a_2}+\cdots+2^{a_n})^2} \leq \dfrac{n\cdot 3^M}{n^2}, $$  which approaches  $0$  as  $n \rightarrow +\infty$ .

Then,  $$ \dfrac{3^{a_1}+3^{a_2}+\cdots+3^{a_n}}{(2^{a_1}+2^{a_2}+\cdots+2^{a_n})^2} \leq \dfrac{n\cdot 3^{b_n}}{(n-1 + 2^{b_n})^2}. $$  Fix a real number  $\alpha \in \left(\log_4(3), 1\right)$ . Then, two cases appear:
Case 1: If  $3^{b_n} \leq n^{\alpha}$ , then  $\dfrac{n\cdot 3^{b_n}}{(n-1 + 2^{b_n})^2} < \dfrac{n^{\alpha + 1}}{(n-1 + 2^{b_n})^2}$ .
Case 2: If  $3^{b_n} > n^{\alpha}$ , then  $n < (3^{b_n})^{1/\alpha} = (3^{1/\alpha})^{b_n}$ , and  $\dfrac{n\cdot 3^{b_n}}{(n-1 + 2^{b_n})^2} < \dfrac{(3^{1/\alpha})^{b_n}}{(n-1 + 2^{b_n})^2}$ .
Therefore,   $$ \dfrac{3^{a_1}+3^{a_2}+\cdots+3^{a_n}}{(2^{a_1}+2^{a_2}+\cdots+2^{a_n})^2} \leq \max\left(\dfrac{n^{\alpha + 1}}{(n-1 + 2^{b_n})^2}, \dfrac{(3^{1/\alpha})^{b_n}}{(n-1 + 2^{b_n})^2}\right). $$  Because  $\alpha + 1 < 2$  and  $3^{1/\alpha} < 4$ , both of these goes to  $0$  as  $n$  approaches  $+\infty$ .

Combining both cases, the problem is finished.

Let  $ABC$  be a triangle with incentre  $I$ , and let  $\Omega$  be the circumcircle of triangle  $BIC$ . Let  $K$  be a point in the interior of segment  $BC$  such that  $\angle BAK < \angle KAC$ . The angle bisector of  $\angle BKA$  intersects  $\Omega$  at points  $W$  and  $X$  such that  $A$  and  $W$  lie on the same side of  $BC$ , and the angle bisector of  $\angle CKA$  intersects  $\Omega$  at points  $Y$  and  $Z$  such that  $A$  and  $Y$  lie on the same side of  $BC$ .

Prove that  $\angle WAY = \angle ZAX$ .

*Proposed by David Brodsky, Uzbekistan*

To see why, we use a phantom point type argument: we know  $P{}$  *should* lie on the perpendicular bisectors of  $AK'{}$  and  $WX{}$  (and such a point is unique); but the claimed arc midpoint  $P'$  already lies on the former by definition, and so it suffices to show it lies on the latter. The rest is spam simplifying the condition until it's trivial: as  $L{}$  lies on the perpendicular bisector of  $WX{}$ , it is equivalent to show that  $LP'\perp WX$  i.e.  $LP'\perp YZ$  i.e.  $\angle (AK',LP')=\angle(AK',YZ)$ , the last of which is easy to angle chase in terms of arcs on  $(ABC)$  (the latter is  $\tfrac{\angle AKC}{2}=\tfrac{\angle AC+\angle BK'}{4}$ ). Explicitly it reduces to arcs  $BL{}$  and  $CL{}$  being congruent, true.

Now we extend  $LP{}$  to meet  $(AK'WX)$  at the arc midpoint  $M{}$ , so that  $AM{}$  is the desired bisector of  $\angle WAX$ . It seems (again thanks to our diagram) like  $AM{}$  bisects  $\angle K'AL$ , which would make a lot of sense since this characterization is "symmetric" and it would therefore bisect  $\angle YAZ$  as well by identical logic. Indeed
\[\angle K'AL=\angle K'PL=\angle K'PM=2\angle K'AM,\]
meaning  $\angle WAX$  and  $\angle K'AL$  share a bisector, and therefore with  $\angle YAZ$  as well.  $\square$

**Solution.** Let  $AI$  meet the circumcircle again at  $M_A$ . We claim that  $\angle YAZ$  and angle  $\angle KAM_A$  share an angle bisector. If the same where true for  $\angle WAX$ , then the result would follow. Consider the point  $S'$  along ray  $KC$  such that  $AK=KS$ . Then  $K$ ,  $Y$ , and  $Z$  all lie along the perpendicular bisector of  $AS$ . Preform  $\sqrt{bc}$ -inversion. Then  $S$  is taken to some point  $S'\in (ABC)$  and the perpendicular of  $AS$  is taken to the circle  $\omega$  centered at  $S'$  passing through  $A$ . Then  $Y'$  and  $Z'$  are taken to the intersections of  $\omega$  and  $\Gamma$  and  $K'$  is taken to the intersection of  $\omega$  and  $ABC$ . And let  $\omega$  meet  $AM_A$  at  $D$  as this line is preserved under reflection. The result we must show remains that  $\angle DAK'$  and  $\angle Y'AZ'$ . Since these points all lie on a circle, it suffices that  $Y'Z'\parallel K'D$ . Since  $Y'Z'$  is perpendicular to the line connecting the centers  $S'M_A$  we must show that  $S'M_A\perp K'D$ . We claim that in fact  $K'$  and  $D$  are reflections about  $S'M_A$  which follows from  $\angle DM_AS'=\angle K'M_AS'$  and  $\angle S'DM_A=180^{\circ}-\angle S'AM_A=\angle S'K'M_A$ .

By the converse of the radical axis theorem, line  $AK$ ,  $(ABC)$ ,  $(WAX)$  and  $(YAZ)$  concur at some point  $R$ .

Let  $L$  be the center of  $(BIC)$ . Let  $P$  and  $Q$  be the midpoints of minor arc  $WX$  in  $(WAX)$  and minor arc  $YZ$  in  $(YAZ)$ , respsectively.**Claim:** Point  $Q$  is the incenter of  $\triangle ALR$ .**Proof:** It suffices to show that  $\overline{QL}$  bisescts  $\angle ALR$  and that  $\angle RQL = 90^{\circ} + \angle QAR$ :


- To show the former: it's easy to show by angle chasing that for any point  $R$  on  $(ABC)$ , the angle bisectors of lines  $AR$  and  $BC$  are parallel/perpendicular to the angle bisectors of  $\angle ALR$ . But the angle bisectors of lines  $AR$  and  $BC$  are  $\overline{WX}$  and  $\overline{YZ}$ , respsectively; moreover,  $\overline{QL}$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{YZ}$ . So,  $\overline{QL}$  is one of the angle bisectors of  $\angle ALR$ .
- To show the latter: let  $Q'$  be the antipode of  $Q$  in  $(AYZ)$ . We have
\[\angle RQL = 180^{\circ} - \angle RQQ' = 90^{\circ} + \angle RQ'Q = 90^{\circ} + \angle QAR.\]

Analogously, point  $P$  is the  $A$ -excenter of  $\triangle ALR$ , so  $P$  and  $Q$  both lie on the angle bisector of  $\angle LAR$ . With a little bit of angle chasing, the final result follows.

Let  $I$ ,  $I_B$ , and  $I_C$  be the incenters of  $ABC$ ,  $ABK$ , and  $ACK$ , respectively, and let  $J$ ,  $J_B$ , and  $J_C$  be the  $A$ -excenters of  $ABC$ ,  $ABK$ , and  $ACK$ , respectively. Note that  $I_B$ ,  $J_C$ ,  $I_C$ , and  $J_B$  are the intersection points of lines  $WX$  with  $BI$  and  $CJ$ , and  $YZ$  with  $CI$  and  $BJ$ , and  $A$ ,  $I_B$ ,  $J_B$  and  $A$ ,  $I_C$ ,  $J_C$  are collinear.

Since  $\angle BAI=\angle JAC=\frac12\angle BAC$  and  $\angle AIB=\angle ACJ=90^\circ+\frac12\angle ACB$ ,  $\triangle AIB\sim\triangle ACJ$ , and  $A$  is the Miquel point of quadrilateral  $BICJ$ . But this holds for any triangle and its incenter and one excenter, so  $A$  is also the Miquel point of  $BI_BKJ_B$  and  $KI_CCJ_C$ . A similar angle chase also shows that  $A$  is the Miquel point of  $I_BII_CK$  and  $J_BKJ_CJ$ . Hence, the points  $I_B$ ,  $I_C$ ,  $J_B$ ,  $J_C$  satisfy  $\frac{II_C}{I_CC}=\frac{I_BK}{KJ_C}=\frac{BJ_B}{J_BJ}$  and  $\frac{BI_B}{I_BI}=\frac{J_BK}{KI_C}=\frac{JJ_C}{J_CC}$ .

Now notice that \[\frac{J_BZ\cdot J_BY}{I_CZ\cdot I_CY}=\frac{J_BB\cdot J_BJ}{I_CI\cdot I_CC}=\frac{AJ_B^2}{AI_C^2}\] from power of a point and the spiral similarities we found earlier. However, from law of sines, we also know \[\frac{J_BZ}{I_CZ}\cdot\frac{J_BY}{I_CY}=\frac{AJ_B^2}{AI_C^2}\cdot \frac{\sin\angle ZAJ_B}{\sin\angle ZAI_C}\cdot\frac{\sin\angle J_BAY}{\sin\angle I_CAY},\] so we must have  $\sin\angle ZAJ_B\cdot\sin\angle J_BAY=\sin\angle ZAI_C\cdot\sin\angle I_CAY$ . If we rewrite this as \[\sin\angle ZAJ_B\cdot\sin(\angle J_BAI_C+\angle I_CAY)=\sin(\angle ZAJ_B+\angle J_BAI_C)\cdot\sin\angle I_CAY,\] which simplifies to  $\sin\angle ZAJ_B\cdot\cos\angle I_CAY=\cos\angle ZAJ_B\cdot\sin\angle I_CAY$ , it is apparent that  $\angle ZAJ_B$  must equal  $\angle I_CAY$ , since this is the same as saying  $\sin(\angle ZAJ_B-\angle I_CAY)=0$ . By an analogous argument, we also have  $\angle WAI_B=\angle J_CAX$ .

To finish, we simply have \[\angle WAY=\angle WAI_B+\angle I_BAI_C+\angle I_CAY=\angle J_CAX+\angle J_BAJ_C+\angle ZAJ_B=\angle ZAX,\] as desired.
